paths.title: From Babel's plain to Abraham's altar
paths.theme: Early Genesis geography — Babel/Ur into Abraham altar country (no Eden pin)
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Babel — one language becomes many; peoples scatter across the earth.
stops.caveats: Babylon dig geography. Beat is Gen 11 scattering, not every brick as the tower.
stops.narration:
Long ago, on a wide river plain, the whole human story seemed to be in one place. Then, Genesis says, everything changed. In Genesis 11:1–9 (LSB), one language breaks into many, and people scatter across the earth. From that scattering, the Bible's story narrows to one family that Yahweh calls. There is no map pin for Eden here, only the places Scripture names next.

Thousands of years later, from 1899 to 1917, German diggers led by Koldewey's team for the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft worked at Babylon. They uncovered the famous Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way. They found Nebuchadnezzar's city walls and palaces, the remains of the Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat, and building inscriptions pressed into clay in wedge-shaped cuneiform writing.

Here the ground and the Bible line up well. Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon matches the empire that destroyed Jerusalem (2 Kings 25), and inscriptions record Cyrus taking the city later. Many people link the Tower of Babel to the Etemenanki ziggurat. That link is traditional and plausible, but it is background, not proof that Genesis 11 is a news report.

So stand here and remember the scattering, not every brick as the tower itself. The journey now follows one family out of the crowd.

stops.panel_truth_line: Erech — named among early cities of the plain in the table of nations.
stops.caveats: Gen 10 urban context; do not over-claim every stratum as patriarchal-period proof.
stops.narration:
Before Abram ever left home, the world was already busy with cities. Erech is one of them. Genesis 10:10 (LSB) names it among the early cities of the plain in the list of nations. That matters. When Yahweh later calls a man out of Ur, he is leaving a crowded human story, not an empty land.

Most scholars think biblical Erech is the ancient city of Uruk, today called Warka. That is the majority view. Over many years, German teams dug here, from early work by Koldewey and Andrae, to the Lenzen campaigns, to continuing studies by the German Archaeological Institute. Iraqi heritage officials care for it too, and in 2016 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing for the Ahwar marshes region.

What lies here is amazing. Uruk was the leading Early Bronze city of southern Mesopotamia. Diggers found the sacred areas of Eanna and Anu, huge Late Uruk buildings, cylinder seals used to run the city's business, and some of the earliest writing anywhere. Ziggurat and city wall remains still rise over the dry plain.

Here the evidence is a mix of clear and unclear. Uruk shows the early city life named in Genesis 10, but it is not a dig that reads that chapter like a diary. Not every layer proves the time of the patriarchs.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ur — Abram's homeland. Yahweh says: Go to the land I will show you.
stops.caveats: Major dig; patriarchal chronology debated. Haran: no pin yet—name in narration only.
stops.narration:
This is where a big journey begins. Ur was Abram's homeland, and here Yahweh tells him: go to the land I will show you (Genesis 11:27–32; Genesis 12:1, LSB). Scripture says the family traveled by way of Haran before moving toward Canaan. Haran has no stop on this map yet, so we only name it as we pass.

From 1922 to 1934, the Joint Expedition to Ur, with Woolley, dug deep into this city. They found the Royal Cemetery, including the burial of Puabi. They uncovered the Great Ziggurat built by Ur-Nammu, neighborhoods where people lived, and clay tablets. Woolley also found a thick layer of flood mud and linked it to Noah.

The ground and the Bible line up well here in one important way. Ur really was a major Sumerian city, fitting the tradition that Abraham came from Ur of the Chaldeans. Its ziggurat helps us picture the temple towers behind the Babel story.

But be honest about the flood layer. It was a local flood deposit, not proof of a worldwide flood. And scholars still debate exactly when the patriarchs lived.

Still, picture Abram turning his back on a great city, simply because Yahweh spoke.

stops.panel_truth_line: Shechem — Abram's first altar in the land after Yahweh promises it to his offspring.
stops.caveats: Tell Balata locus; altar itself is not excavated as Abram's stones.
stops.narration:
After a long road, Abram arrives in the land. At Shechem, Yahweh promises this land to his offspring, and Abram builds his first altar there (Genesis 12:6–7, LSB). The Maker of the world is also the Promise-Maker. Worship answers his word, and it happens in a real place.

Today the old city is a mound called Tell Balata. Sellin dug here in 1913–1914 and 1926–1927. Later, from 1956 to 1973, Wright led the Drew-McCormick and ASOR excavations. They uncovered massive Middle Bronze walls, a temple-fortress, a gate complex, layers of destruction, and later Iron Age homes.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Shechem was a major city in both the Bronze and Iron Ages. That makes it a fitting stage for the great covenant gathering in Joshua 24 and the Abimelech story in Judges 9.

One honest note: no one has dug up Abram's altar stones. Proving a single family's visit is beyond what archaeology can do. But standing here, you can picture a traveler stopping in a strong city's shadow to build an altar and call on Yahweh.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethel — tent and altar; a return point in Abram's walk.
stops.caveats: Traditional dig site; patriarchal sojourn geography.
stops.narration:
Abram's walk is not a straight line. At Bethel he pitches his tent and builds an altar, and later he comes back to this same spot to call on Yahweh again (Genesis 12:8; Genesis 13:3–4, LSB). The promise is lived out in ordinary camps and repeated worship, not only at the finish line.

Most maps place Bethel at a mound near the village of Beitin. Albright and Kelso led digs here in 1934, 1954, 1957, and 1960. They found Bronze and Iron Age remains, including religious and household objects that Kelso published. People have linked Beitin to Bethel since the days of the explorer Robinson and of Albright.

Still, this is not a closed case. Beitin is the majority view, but other spots have been suggested, such as near el-Bireh. No sign with the city's name has been found on the site. So we visit Bethel here as the traditional dig site, while keeping the question open.

Either way, picture a tent and a pile of stones on a hilltop, and a man who keeps coming back to pray.

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — Mamre sojourn; later Machpelah burial geography.
stops.caveats: Mamre has no separate pin; Hebron carries sojourn/burial tradition.
stops.narration:
Hebron is a place of both living and dying in Abram's story. He settles near the oaks of Mamre here, and later Genesis tells how Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah to bury Sarah (Genesis 13:18; Genesis 23:1–20, LSB). The promise includes people laid to rest still believing that Yahweh's word stands. Mamre has no separate stop on this map, so Hebron carries both the camp and the burial story.

On the ancient mound, Tel Rumeida, digs took place in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, with huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Ancient Hebron was a fortified city in the hills, a fitting setting for the patriarch traditions. It later became David's first capital. This is background geography, not a photo of Abraham himself.

What about the cave? It lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has not been excavated. So we honor it from the outside, and remember a family that buried its dead in hope.

stops.panel_truth_line: Beersheba — covenant well and southern edge of the patriarchal walk.
stops.caveats: Tel Beersheba is Iron Age famous; patriarchal well traditions mapped with that caveat.
stops.narration:
At the southern edge of the land, the road reaches a well. At Beersheba, Abraham makes a covenant about a well, and later Isaac worships Yahweh here too (Genesis 21:22–34; Genesis 26:23–25, LSB). Look back over this whole path: from Babel's scattering to this southern well, Yahweh orders the nations, calls one man, and plants worship in a named land.

From 1969 to 1976, Tel Aviv University dug at Tel Beersheba. They found a planned Iron Age town with a water system, walls, and storehouses. Their most famous find was a horned altar. It had been taken apart, and its stones were reused in a storehouse wall.

That altar matches the shape of altars described in the Bible. It also fits the way Amos and the books of Kings criticize worship at Beersheba. The town's careful layout fits a time when Judah's kings controlled the Negev desert.

But here the evidence is mixed for our story. Tel Beersheba is famous for its Iron Age town, long after Abraham. So we map the well stories here with that caveat. Still, in a dry land, a well meant life, and a covenant meant peace. Yahweh had promised that through Abraham all the families of the earth would be blessed (Genesis 12:3). Paul calls that promise the gospel announced ahead of time (Galatians 3:8). It was kept in Jesus, through whom Yahweh's love reaches every scattered nation from Babel on.

paths.title: Flood memory — warning, waters, mountains of Ararat
paths.theme: Genesis Flood with honest Ararat/Durupınar caveats + ministry teaching sites
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Nineveh — Ashurbanipal library world; flood-tablet culture (tablet now in BM).
stops.caveats: Context only. Flood Tablet is parallel literature, not Scripture or Genesis GPS.
stops.narration:
Genesis tells the flood story in its own voice. Yahweh sees how wicked people have become. He warns, he judges by water, and he keeps Noah's household safe (Genesis 6:5–8; Genesis 7:11–24, LSB). Why start this path at Nineveh? Because this city's library shows the wider world that remembered floods too.

Between 1845 and 1851, Layard dug here, and Rassam continued into the 1850s–1880s. They found Sennacherib's Southwest Palace, carved wall pictures of the siege of Lachish, giant winged guardian statues, and Ashurbanipal's library of clay tablets full of epic poems and royal records. One of those tablets tells a flood story. It now sits in the British Museum.

Some finds here match the Bible strongly. Assyrian records and the Lachish carvings back up Sennacherib's 701 BC campaign against Judah (2 Kings 18–19). Nineveh fell in 612 BC, fitting what the prophets foresaw.

Recent history left scars too. While ISIS controlled Mosul from 2014 to 2017, Nineveh suffered documented destruction, and normal digging stopped because of war.

One honest note: the flood tablet is parallel literature. It is not Scripture, and it does not point to where Noah's story happened.

stops.panel_truth_line: Babylon's plain — Mesopotamian world that remembered catastrophic floods.
stops.narration:
The people of Mesopotamia lived between two great rivers, and they remembered terrible floods. Genesis speaks into that world with a different message. It shows Yahweh's judgment, his instructions to Noah, and, after the waters, his promise to keep the seasons going (Genesis 6:11–22; Genesis 8:20–22, LSB).

Babylon was one of the great cities of that river world. From 1899 to 1917, Koldewey's team for the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft dug here. They found the Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, Nebuchadnezzar's walls and palaces, the remains of the Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat, and building inscriptions in cuneiform.

Some of this lines up strongly with the Bible's later history. Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon matches the empire that destroyed Jerusalem (2 Kings 25). Inscriptions record Cyrus taking the city later. Many connect the Tower of Babel to the Etemenanki ziggurat, but that is traditional background, not proof.

For this path, though, the evidence is mixed. Babylon is here for cultural context. It is not where Noah landed. Think of it as a window into a world that told flood stories, so we can hear how Genesis tells its own.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ararat region — Gen 8:4 reception geography. Strong caveats.
stops.caveats: Tradition for "mountains of Ararat," not a verified wreck.
stops.narration:
Genesis 8:4 (LSB) says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Hebrews 11:7 later remembers Noah as a man who, by faith, became an heir of righteousness. This stop asks us to hold that verse honestly, without the fake certainty of tourist claims.

What has been studied here? There have been geological surveys of Mount Ararat and archaeological work at sites in the wider region. There have also been many popular claims since the 1800s that someone found "ark wood." None of these claims has been accepted in peer-reviewed archaeology as Noah's ark. No credible dig has uncovered an ark here.

So why stop at all? Because the New Testament writers point back to the flood in their teaching. This region is part of how people have received and remembered that story. Think of it as tradition about the "mountains of Ararat," not a confirmed wreck.

The evidence here is mixed and comes with strong caveats. But the main point of Hebrews does not depend on finding a boat. It praises a man who trusted Yahweh's warning about things not yet seen.

stops.panel_truth_line: Contested Durupınar and popular ark claims — caution, not endorsement.
stops.caveats: REQUIRED contested-hypotheses stop. Do not endorse ark-found claims.
stops.narration:
Some places are famous not for what was found, but for what people claimed. This is one of them. In eastern Turkey, near Doğubayazıt, there is a boat-shaped landform called the Durupınar formation. Searchers have also explored other spots around Ararat.

The Bible's flood story stands (Genesis 8:4; 2 Peter 2:5, LSB). But some map claims do not.

At Durupınar, people have said they found wood, metal rivets, and inner rooms. None of these claims has held up under independent scientific checking as the remains of a ship. Geologists agree on a plainer answer. The shape comes from a fold in the rock, a block of limestone, and flowing clay in an area of landslides and earthflows.

This stop is more about the story than the shovel, because the evidence here is thin. It is on the path for a reason: to show how a claim can feel exciting and still be wrong. We are not saying the ark was found here, and we do not endorse such claims.

Second Peter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness. Honesty about evidence is a good way to honor him.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ark Encounter — ministry reconstruction of Gen 6–9. Attraction, not dig.
stops.narration:
Not every stop on this path is a dig. In Williamstown, Kentucky, in Grant County, stands the Ark Encounter. It is a ministry's life-size reconstruction based on the story of Noah in Genesis 6–9.

Genesis 6:14–22 (LSB) describes Yahweh's instructions for building the ark. Jesus later compares the days of Noah to the coming of the Son of Man (Matthew 24:37–39, LSB). People went on with ordinary life, and then judgment came.

Be clear about what this place is. It is an attraction built by a ministry. It is not an excavation, and it is not a found wreck. It can help visitors imagine the size of the story, but it is not evidence that the ark was found.

So walk through it as you would a model or a museum display. Let it make you think about Jesus' warning: to be ready, and to take Yahweh's word seriously before the waters rise.

stops.panel_truth_line: Creation Museum — Eden-to-Flood teaching. Attraction, not dig.
stops.narration:
This path ends at a teaching center, not a dig site. The Creation Museum is in Petersburg, Kentucky, in Boone County. It is a ministry attraction that teaches the story from Eden to the Flood.

Its displays draw on Genesis 1:1–31, the account of creation, and Genesis 7:1–5, where Yahweh tells Noah to enter the ark (LSB). First Peter 3:20 adds a striking detail about God's character: he waited patiently in Noah's days while the ark was being built.

Remember what kind of place this is. It is an attraction meant to teach. It is not an excavation, and it does not hold proof found in the ground.

So what should we carry away from this whole path? Not a fake hull on a mountain ridge. The last word belongs to Yahweh: holy toward evil, yet patient, because he does not wish for any to perish (2 Peter 3:9). Noah's family was carried safely through the waters. Peter says Christ suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, to bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18). The door is still open.

paths.title: Fossil witness — soft tissue, feathers, and careful claims
paths.theme: Creature-find pins with plain-honest soft-tissue caveats
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: London Archaeopteryx — feathered fossil inviting wonder at created kinds.
stops.caveats: Use pin sources only. Wonder + honesty, not invented proofs.
stops.narration:
In 1861, workers in a limestone quarry in Bavaria, Germany, near Langenaltheim and Solnhofen, found something that still makes people stop and stare. It was a fossil of a crow-sized animal. It had clear feathers and wings. But it also had teeth, claws on its wings, and a long bony tail.

This is Archaeopteryx. The British Museum bought it, and today it is kept in the Natural History Museum in London.

Genesis 1:20–23 (LSB) tells of God filling the skies with flying creatures and the seas with living things, and calling them good. This fossil invites that same kind of wonder at the creatures he made.

But wonder needs honesty. We will not invent lab results or proofs that our sources do not include. What we have is a preserved animal from long ago, with its feathers pressed into stone so clearly that you can still see them.

Sometimes the best response is simply to look closely and be amazed.

stops.panel_truth_line: B-rex soft-tissue report — provisional framing required.
stops.caveats: Soft-tissue interpretation contested. Keep provisional language from creature pack.
stops.narration:
Deep in Montana, northwest of the town of Jordan in Garfield County, south of Fort Peck Reservoir in the Charles M. Russell National Wildlife Refuge, scientists dug up a T. rex known as MOR 1125, or "B-rex."

What happened next surprised many. Researchers treated pieces of bone in acid to remove the minerals. Inside, they reported flexible, branching structures that looked like blood vessels, and shapes that looked like cells. Later studies reported tiny fragments of protein.

Scientists still debate how such material could last so long, and some offer other explanations. These are published claims, not a closed courtroom case, so we keep our words careful and provisional.

Genesis 1:24–25 (LSB) speaks of God making the land animals. Job 12:7–10 (LSB) says to ask the beasts, and they will teach you. One thing they teach is humility. The right response to a surprising find is not to shout "case closed," but to keep looking, keep asking, and stay honest about what we do not yet know.

stops.panel_truth_line: Brachylophosaurus collagen-report conversation — careful claims only.
stops.narration:
North of Malta, Montana, in Phillips County, on state trust land, a team went looking for something specific. They dug up the leg of a duck-billed dinosaur, a Brachylophosaurus known as MOR 2598, on purpose to test for original proteins.

In 2009, researchers reported collagen fragments and vessel-like structures from its thigh bone. Later teams reported more protein pieces called peptides. These results are widely cited. They are also debated.

So we use careful words here, just as with B-rex. Something surprising was reported, and scientists are still working out what it means.

Genesis 1:31 (LSB) says God saw all that he had made, and it was very good. A surprise about how well something was preserved can deepen our reverence. But that only works if we refuse hype. Overstating a result does not honor the Creator. Telling the truth, including the parts still being argued, does.

stops.panel_truth_line: SUE — well-documented T. rex that draws careful looking.
stops.caveats: Museum specimen per pin; not a proof object by itself.
stops.narration:
In 1990, a fossil hunter named Sue Hendrickson spotted bones in a cliff near Faith, South Dakota, on Cheyenne River Sioux Reservation land in Ziebach County. Those bones turned out to be one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found.

The dinosaur, named SUE after her, did not have a quiet life after discovery. There was a legal fight over who owned it. In 1997 it was sold at auction and bought for the Field Museum in Chicago, where it is on display today.

Genesis 1:24–25 (LSB) tells of God making the creatures of the land. SUE is a well-documented T. rex that rewards careful looking, and looking carefully is a form of honesty.

One honest note: SUE is a museum specimen. By itself, it is not a proof object for any side of an argument. It is a creature to study and wonder at.

Caring about creation means refusing two bad habits: sneering at wonder, and believing whatever we wish were true.

stops.panel_truth_line: Creation Museum — ministry framing of creature exhibits.
stops.narration:
This path ends back in Petersburg, Kentucky, in Boone County, at the Creation Museum. It is a ministry attraction that presents creature exhibits through its own teaching. It is not a dig.

Genesis 1:20–31 (LSB) describes God filling the sea, sky, and land with living things. Psalm 104:24 (LSB) bursts out in praise at how many works Yahweh has made, all with wisdom.

Think back over the fossils on this path: feathers in limestone, surprising reports from inside dinosaur bones, and a famous T. rex in a museum. Some results are clear. Others are still debated.

Here is the balance to carry home. Be plain and honest about the limits of what any single fossil report can prove. And hold on to Scripture's Creator, who did not stay distant from what he made. The Bible teaches that all things were made through the Son, and that through him God makes peace with his world by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:16–20).

paths.title: Earliest sacred places — wonder without a fake Eden
paths.theme: Early sacred/urban places + ministry teaching; no Eden GPS
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Göbekli Tepe — early monumental ritual architecture; not Eden or Noah's altar.
stops.caveats: Do NOT claim Göbekli proves Genesis chronology or is Eden.
stops.narration:
High above the Harran plain in Türkiye stands one of the most famous early monumental sites on earth. At Göbekli Tepe, people built huge round, oval, and rectangular enclosures with tall T-shaped stone pillars. Carvings of wild animals and simple human forms cover them. UNESCO dates them to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, about 9600–8200 BC.

Digging began in 1995 under Klaus Schmidt, who led until 2014. The German Archaeological Institute and the Şanlıurfa Museum continue the work through the Taş Tepeler program.

There was a pause many visitors ask about. On June 13, 2016, Türkiye's Ministry of Culture and Tourism closed the site so crews could build two permanent roofs over the open trenches. This was for visitor safety and long-term protection, under a shelter project with the EU. The site stayed closed through 2017 and reopened in 2018. Excavation lead Celal Uludag later said work stopped while the roofs went up.

Genesis 1:1–2:3 (LSB) tells of creation. Göbekli Tepe is not a named biblical site. It is not Eden, and it is not Noah's altar. It does not prove any Genesis timeline. It is simply a reason to wonder at early sacred building.

stops.panel_truth_line: Eridu — early southern Mesopotamian urban/sacred tradition.
stops.caveats: Iraqi dig frame; not a patriarchal GPS proof.
stops.narration:
In the far south of Mesopotamia lies Eridu, one of the earliest city and worship centers of that land. Genesis begins with creation and moves to the scattering at Babel (Genesis 1:1–31; Genesis 11:1–9, LSB). Early cities like this remind us that Scripture's world is real earth, not a mythic nowhere.

People have dug here in waves. Taylor worked here in the 1850s. In the 1940s and 1950s, Iraqi excavations led by Fuad Safar with Seton Lloyd went deeper. In 2016, Eridu became part of the UNESCO Ahwar World Heritage listing, along with Ur and Uruk, as old Sumerian cities on the edge of the marshes.

Diggers found a long series of temples to the god Enki, also called Ea, stacked one on top of another. They also found an Ubaid-period settlement and the remains of a ziggurat.

The evidence here is mixed for our path. Eridu gives cultural and historical background. It is not tied to a particular verse, and it is not a map pin that proves the patriarchs' travels. But it shows how far back people were building sacred places.

stops.panel_truth_line: Babel / Babylon — Gen 11 scattering geography that is pinned.
stops.narration:
Eden stays in the words of Scripture. We do not have a pin for it. But Babel is on the map. Genesis 11:1–9 (LSB) tells how people tried to build a tower, and how Yahweh scattered them.

At Babylon, from 1899 to 1917, Koldewey's team for the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft dug up the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way. They found Nebuchadnezzar's city walls and palaces, the remains of the Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat, and building inscriptions in cuneiform.

Here the ground and the Bible line up well. Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon matches the empire that destroyed Jerusalem (2 Kings 25). Inscriptions record Cyrus taking the city later.

What about the tower? Many link the Tower of Babel to the Etemenanki ziggurat. That is a traditional and plausible background, but it is not proof that Genesis 11 is a news report.

On a path about the earliest sacred places, this stop marks a turning point. We leave the places we cannot map and stand at one we can.

stops.panel_truth_line: Creation Museum — attraction teaching Gen 1–3 (label as attraction).
stops.caveats: Ministry attraction, not dig. Textual Eden—no pin.
stops.narration:
In Petersburg, Kentucky, in Boone County, the Creation Museum teaches the opening chapters of Genesis. It is a ministry attraction, not a dig.

Genesis 1:1–2:3 (LSB) tells of the creation week. Genesis 2:8–15 (LSB) describes a garden planted in Eden, with rivers flowing out of it. Many people wish they could find that garden on a map. But Eden stays in the text. There is no pin for it.

That is the point of this stop. Good teaching can help our imagination, picturing a world fresh from God's hand. But teaching does not invent a GPS location for Eden.

So enjoy the displays for what they are: an attraction meant to help people think about the start of the story. Then carry the honest takeaway with you. Some things we can dig for. Some things we receive only by reading.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ark Encounter — optional close on Flood teaching (attraction, not dig).
stops.narration:
This path can close in Williamstown, Kentucky, in Grant County, at the Ark Encounter. It is a ministry attraction built to teach the Flood story. It is not a dig.

Genesis 1:31 (LSB) says God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. Genesis 6:9–22 (LSB) shows how far the world fell from that, and how God told Noah to build an ark.

Why end here? Because there is very little on the map for the creation week itself. There is no place to stand and point to the seventh day. This path has been the honest substitute: real early sacred sites, a mapped Babel, and clearly labeled teaching attractions.

So visit this place as a reconstruction, not a discovery. Let it help you picture the story, and remember the difference between what helps us imagine and what the ground has shown. What the Bible teaches is clear: the God who made a very good world did not give up on it. Yahweh shut Noah's family safely inside the ark (Genesis 7:16), and he sent his Son, not to condemn the world, but so the world might be saved through him (John 3:17).

paths.title: Isaac's wells and Jacob's ladder
paths.theme: Patriarchal promise geography: wells, Bethel dream, Jacob's well
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Beersheba — covenant well / Isaac's southern life.
stops.caveats: Iron Age tel; patriarchal well traditions with caveat.
stops.narration:
Isaac's life is a quieter story than his father's, and much of it happens around wells. At Beersheba, Isaac re-digs wells and calls on the name of Yahweh in the south (Genesis 26:23–33, LSB). In a dry land, water meant life, and worship meant trust.

From 1969 to 1976, Tel Aviv University dug at Tel Beersheba. They found a planned Iron Age town with walls, storehouses, and a water system. They also found a horned altar. It had been taken apart, and its stones were reused in a storehouse wall.

That altar matches the shape of altars in the Bible. It also fits the way Amos and the books of Kings criticize worship at Beersheba. The neat town plan fits a time when Judah's kings controlled the Negev.

But the evidence is mixed for Isaac's story. This town comes from the Iron Age, much later. We place the well traditions here with that caveat.

Picture Isaac with a shovel, reopening what had been filled in, and stopping to pray.

stops.panel_truth_line: Tel Haror — Gerar candidate (**candidate caveat**).
stops.caveats: REQUIRED: Gerar identification is candidate, not settled.
stops.narration:
Isaac stays in the land of Gerar during a famine, and there he digs wells, only to have local herders quarrel over them (Genesis 26:1–6; Genesis 26:17–22, LSB). But where was Gerar? We hold that question humbly.

One strong candidate is Tel Haror, beside a stream called Nahal Gerar. Ben-Gurion University's team under Oren led digs here from 1982 to 1992, with more work around 2010. The team found a large, walled Canaanite city from the Middle Bronze Age, with a sacred area. There were also Late Bronze and later Iron Age remains.

The digging is real. But the name is not proven. Calling this place Gerar is probable, yet no inscription confirms it. So this is a candidate, not a settled answer. Its size in the Middle Bronze Age fits a regional center in the Negev corridor where the patriarchs traveled.

Imagine Isaac moving from one well to the next after each fight, until at last he finds room. Whether or not this is the exact spot, the story is about patience and trust.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethel — Jacob's ladder dream.
stops.narration:
Jacob leaves home on a long and lonely road. At Bethel he sleeps, and in a dream he sees a stairway. Yahweh stands above it and renews the promise given to Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 28:10–22, LSB).

Most maps place Bethel at the mound near the village of Beitin. Albright and Kelso dug here in 1934, 1954, 1957, and 1960. They found Bronze and Iron Age remains, including religious and household objects that Kelso published. People have linked this site to Bethel since the explorer Robinson and Albright.

The ground and the Bible line up well here, with one caution. Beitin is the majority view, but other places, such as near el-Bireh, have been proposed. No sign with the city's name has been found. So we treat this as the traditional dig site, not a closed debate.

Later, on the way home, Jacob wrestles at a place called Penuel (Genesis 32). That place has no stop of its own, so we only tell it in words as we travel on.

stops.panel_truth_line: Shechem — Jacob's return / altar geography.
stops.narration:
Jacob has been through a long night. Earlier on the road he wrestled at Penuel, a place we can only name, since it has no stop on this map. Now he comes back to Shechem and builds an altar, and later Yahweh calls him on to Bethel (Genesis 33:18–20; Genesis 35:1–7, LSB). After the struggle, Jacob returns to a life of worship in the land.

The old city of Shechem is the mound called Tell Balata. Sellin dug here in 1913–1914 and 1926–1927, and Wright led the Drew-McCormick and ASOR digs from 1956 to 1973. They uncovered huge Middle Bronze walls, a temple-fortress, a city gate, layers of destruction, and later Iron Age homes.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Shechem was a major city in the Bronze and Iron Ages, a fitting stage for the covenant gathering in Joshua 24 and for the Abimelech story in Judges 9.

But no shovel can prove that one family stopped here. That is beyond what archaeology can reach. What we can do is stand where a strong city once rose and picture a limping man who chose to build an altar.

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — patriarchal burial country.
stops.narration:
The story of Isaac and Jacob ends where it began for Abraham's family: at Hebron, burial country. Isaac dies here, old and full of days, and his sons bury him. Later Jacob asks to be buried with his fathers in the cave they bought (Genesis 35:27–29; Genesis 49:29–33, LSB). The promise includes graves bought in hope.

On the ancient mound, Tel Rumeida, digs ran in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, including huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Ancient Hebron was a fortified city in the hills. That fits the setting of the patriarch stories, and it later became David's first capital. This is background geography, not a portrait of the patriarchs themselves.

The cave of Machpelah lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has never been dug as an excavation. So this stop is about burial tradition. Picture a family returning again and again to bury its dead in a land they did not yet own, trusting it would one day be theirs.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jacob's Well / Sychar — living memory of Jacob's well into John 4.
stops.narration:
Centuries after Jacob, a weary traveler sits down beside a well. John 4:5–6 (LSB) says Jesus came to a town called Sychar, near the land Jacob had given to his son Joseph, and Jacob's well was there. Genesis 33:18–20 (LSB) tells of Jacob settling near Shechem. John simply uses the well's name. He does not build extra meanings beyond what the text says.

What is here today? A deep well, traditionally called Jacob's, still draws water at the pass by Shechem. Over it stand church buildings from Byzantine, Crusader, and modern times. Church builders probed here in the 1800s and 1900s. Nearby is Tell Balata, ancient Shechem, which saw major digs from 1913 to 1934 and 1956 to 1974.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. There really is a deep well at this pass, and ancient Shechem really is next door. Together they frame the geography John describes.

But the well cannot prove the conversation with the Samaritan woman. It shows the place, not the words. The tradition links this spot near Askar and Balata to the story. Imagine lowering a bucket into water that people have drawn from for ages.

stops.panel_truth_line: Horned altar from Beersheba — cultic Beersheba witness (museum object).
stops.caveats: Artifact pin; museum object, not a dig stop pretending to be Isaac's stones.
stops.narration:
This stop is not a place but an object. In a museum stands a four-horned altar made of cut stone blocks, rebuilt from pieces found at Tel Beersheba. Beersheba was a major city in Judah's south, where the kingdom ran its affairs.

Genesis 26:23–25 (LSB) tells how Isaac went up to Beersheba, where Yahweh appeared to him, and Isaac built an altar and called on his name. The altar in the museum helps us picture worship in Beersheba country.

But be careful about what it shows. It is an excavated witness to worship in this region. It is not Isaac's altar, and it does not mark the exact spot where he prayed. It comes from Judah's later city, and the evidence for linking it to the patriarchs is mixed at best.

So look at its four horns, one at each corner, and remember that people in this southern land long kept a memory of worship here. The object gives context. It does not pretend to be Isaac's stones. The promise behind those altars went further. Jesus told Nathanael he would see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man (John 1:51), the ladder Jacob dreamed of after leaving Beersheba (Genesis 28:10–12), fulfilled in a person. Yahweh kept his word to these fathers by sending the One who opens the way to him.

paths.title: When Yahweh shook Judah
paths.theme: Assyria 701 BCE — Lachish to Jerusalem to Nineveh
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Lachish was Judah’s southwest fortress city. In Hezekiah’s day Assyria besieged it — the open wound before Jerusalem.
stops.caveats: Assyrian siege of Lachish is among the best-documented Judah campaign sites (reliefs + tell). Tour beat is Scripture + site geography — not a claim that every wall course visible today is the 701 BCE face.
stops.narration:
Stand where Judah's fortress in the southwest once watched over the coastal road. In King Hezekiah's days, Assyria came down like a slow storm. City after city heard the rumor: Sennacherib is coming (2 Kings 18:13–17; Isaiah 36:1–2, LSB). Lachish was no village. It was the strong wall before Jerusalem, and here it became an open wound.

From 1932 to 1938, the Wellcome-Marston Expedition dug at Lachish. Near the gate they found the Lachish Letters, messages written on broken pottery. They found evidence of a siege ramp, a destruction layer they tied to Sennacherib, a palace-fort, and the Fosse Temple.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The letters speak of a military crisis that fits Judah's last years. And the Assyrian siege of Lachish is also carved on Sennacherib's palace walls at Nineveh. That gives us a rare triple witness: the Bible, Assyrian art and writing, and the dig itself.

One honest note: this is one of the best-recorded battle sites in Judah. But not every stone you see today is the wall that faced the attack in 701 BC. The story here is Scripture and geography together.

stops.panel_truth_line: Samaria fell first. Judah’s fear at Lachish was rational — the same empire had already emptied the northern capital.
stops.caveats: Flashback stop — not part of the 701 BCE Judah siege sequence. Herodian/NT Sebaste overlays the hill; keep OT exile beat clear from later Roman city fabric.
stops.narration:
Look north in your mind, to Samaria, Israel's capital on its hill. Years before Lachish shook, this city learned what Assyria does when a kingdom will not bend. The king of Assyria came up, and after hard years the city was taken. People were carried away (2 Kings 17:5–6; 2 Kings 17:18–23, LSB). The same empire that later threatened Judah had already emptied the northern capital.

From 1908 to 1910, the Harvard Expedition dug at Samaria. They uncovered the beginnings of a palace from the time of Omri's royal family, pieces of carved ivory, and the Samaria Ostraca, notes in Hebrew written on pottery. Many names on them include part of the name Yahweh.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The Bible says Omri founded this capital, and the dig shows a major royal center from that era. The notes show the palace tracking wine and oil, and the names fit the Northern Kingdom world of Kings and Amos.

This is a flashback stop, not part of the 701 BC siege story. A later Roman city called Sebaste, from Herod's time and the New Testament era, sits on the same hill. Keep that later city separate from the older story of exile.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jerusalem — where Yahweh set His Name — hears Assyrian taunts. Hezekiah spreads the threat before Yahweh.
stops.caveats: Do not treat Large Stone Structure / ‘palace of David’ (CBG-22) as settled in this tour — crisis beat is Zion under threat + prayer, not palace ID. Keep Yahweh’s Name / deliverance center, not archaeology overclaim.
stops.narration:
Now the story tightens on Jerusalem, the City of David, where Yahweh set his Name. Assyrian messengers stand outside the walls and use words as weapons. They mock the people's hope. They list the gods of conquered lands as proof that Jerusalem's God will fail too. And King Hezekiah takes the threatening letter and spreads it out before Yahweh in prayer (2 Kings 18:17–19:19; Isaiah 37:14–20, LSB).

From 1961 to 1967, Kenyon dug on the Ophel and in the City of David. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that helped explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on the southeast ridge known as David's city. But how big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still argued about, with some scholars thinking small and others much larger.

Some people claim a certain large stone building was David's palace. This tour does not treat that as settled. The heart of this stop is not a building at all. It is a city under threat, a king on his knees, and Yahweh's Name as the center of hope.

stops.panel_truth_line: Gihon is Jerusalem’s lifeblood. Under siege, Hezekiah’s people prepared water — trust in Yahweh with calloused hands.
stops.caveats: Tunnel attribution and exact cut chronology have scholarly debate on phases; tour may say ‘tradition tied to Hezekiah’ and ‘water brought inward’ without over-precise engineering claims. Siloam pool (JER-NT-01) is the outlet end — optional secondary open, not required for this stop.
stops.narration:
Walk down toward the spring called Gihon, the lifeblood of Jerusalem on its eastern slope. In a siege, courage without water is a short story. Hezekiah understood that. He stopped up the outer springs and brought water inward (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:2–4; 2 Chronicles 32:30, LSB). Trust in Yahweh and hard work went together.

From 1995 into the 2010s, the Reich–Shukron team dug here. They found the Spring Tower and other defenses around Gihon. They clarified the Siloam Tunnel, often called Hezekiah's Tunnel. They found a channel known as Channel II, small clay seals called bullae, and in 2004 a pool of Siloam from the Second Temple period at the tunnel's far end.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. An inscription found in the tunnel in 1880 matches the Bible's description of Hezekiah bringing water into the city. Many teams have studied the tunnel since.

One honest note: scholars debate the tunnel's phases and exactly when it was cut. So we say this work is tied by tradition to Hezekiah, and that water was brought inward, without claiming every engineering detail. Later generations still connect his work to this tunnel through the rock.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nineveh — home of the empire that shook Judah. Yahweh judges the oppressor in His time. Empires are borrowed breath.
stops.caveats: Zoom-out stop far from Judah. Nahum’s oracle is theological judgment on Nineveh; do not imply the tour ‘proves’ every Nahum detail by the ruin mounds alone. Isaiah 37 deliverance is Judah-side; Nineveh’s later fall is a separate historical horizon — narration already holds both carefully.
stops.narration:
The path now pulls far to the east, to Nineveh, jewel of the empire that crushed Lachish and taunted Jerusalem. For a while it seemed unstoppable, with broad walls, proud kings, and a war machine that moved whole nations like cattle. Judah's rescue in Hezekiah's day cracked the myth of endless power, though it did not end Assyria's story overnight (Isaiah 37:36–38, LSB). The prophet Nahum later announces Yahweh's judgment on this city (Nahum 1:1–8; Nahum 3:1–7, LSB). Empires live on borrowed breath.

Layard dug here from 1845 to 1851, and Rassam continued into the 1850s–1880s. They uncovered Sennacherib's Southwest Palace, with carved wall scenes of the siege of Lachish, giant winged guardian statues, and Ashurbanipal's library of tablets.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Assyrian records and the Lachish carvings support Sennacherib's 701 BC campaign against Judah (2 Kings 18–19). The libraries shed light on the world of Isaiah and Nahum. Nineveh fell in 612 BC, matching what the prophets foresaw.

During ISIS control of Mosul from 2014 to 2017, Nineveh suffered documented destruction, and war stopped the digging. One honest note: Nahum's words are judgment from Yahweh. The ruin mounds alone do not prove every detail he spoke.

Nahum's message also holds comfort: Yahweh is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble, and he knows those who take refuge in him (Nahum 1:7). The book of Isaiah, whose prophet stood with Hezekiah in this crisis, also speaks of a Servant wounded for our wrongs, by whose wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The New Testament names that Servant as Jesus (1 Peter 2:24). Empires fall; Yahweh's word and his rescue last.

paths.title: Out of slavery — a people Yahweh redeems
paths.theme: Exodus liberation: Goshen → sea → Sinai → Nebo → Gilgal
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Goshen / Rameses — Israel in bondage; Passover instituted before departure.
stops.narration:
The story of rescue begins in the eastern Nile Delta, in the area of Pi-Ramesses and Qantir. Here Israel lives in bondage. Exodus 1:8–14 (LSB) tells of hard slavery. Then Yahweh hears their groans and sends Moses. Before the people leave, the Passover is set up: a lamb's blood marks their doors (Exodus 12:1–13, LSB).

This is where human redemption begins in the Bible's story. It starts as freedom from slavery, and it moves into belonging to Yahweh.

The evidence here is mixed. This stop uses a general map of the Exodus and wilderness route, not an exact dig that proves each detail. Still, picture families inside their homes on that night, with blood on the doorframes, waiting for the word to go.

stops.panel_truth_line: Succoth — first camp after departure from Rameses.
stops.caveats: Itinerary geography; not every camp excavated as named.
stops.narration:
The first camp after leaving Rameses is Succoth (Exodus 12:37–42; Numbers 33:5, LSB). A possible location is in Wadi Tumilat, at a site called Tell el-Maskhuta in Egypt.

Picture a great crowd on the move, their bread still unleavened because there was no time to let it rise. Redemption here looks like feet moving under Yahweh's command.

The evidence is mixed. This stop follows the travel list in the Bible, and not every camp on that list has been dug up and named. Tell el-Maskhuta is a candidate, not a certainty. But the meaning is clear: on the very first night of freedom, the people were already walking where Yahweh led.

stops.panel_truth_line: Yam Suph — crossing tradition geography. Keep contested chariot-claim pins out.
stops.caveats: Crossing location debated. Do NOT use Wyatt CBG-16.
stops.narration:
The Bible names this place Yam Suph, the sea Israel crossed. Exodus 14:15–31 (LSB) tells how Yahweh opens a way, the people walk through, and the pursuers fall. Then in Exodus 15:1–18 (LSB), they sing. A people is rescued by Yahweh's power.

Where did it happen? That is debated. This map shows a representative spot among the lakes of the northeast Nile Delta and the land bridge there. Others argue for the Gulf of Suez or the Gulf of Aqaba.

There are also popular claims that chariot wheels have been found under the water. Those claims are contested, and we keep them off this map on purpose.

So stand here with an open question about the exact location, and a clear answer about the story's point: when there was no way forward, Yahweh made one.

stops.panel_truth_line: Marah — bitter water made sweet; early wilderness testing.
stops.caveats: Itinerary pin; exact oasis ID traditional/schematic.
stops.narration:
Just days after the great rescue, the people reach Marah, and the water is bitter. Yahweh makes it sweet, and this becomes an early test in the wilderness (Exodus 15:22–26, LSB).

Where was Marah? Traditional candidates lie in the corridor from Ayun Musa to Hawara in western Sinai. The exact oasis is traditional and approximate, so this stop is a pin from the travel story, not a proven site.

The evidence is mixed, but the lesson is plain. Rescued people still have to learn trust, one camp at a time. Seeing the sea split did not mean they would never be thirsty or afraid again.

stops.panel_truth_line: Elim — twelve springs and seventy palms; mercy after bitterness.
stops.narration:
After the bitter water comes a surprise. At Elim there are twelve springs and seventy palm trees, and the people camp by the water (Exodus 15:27, LSB). It is mercy after bitterness.

The traditional candidate for Elim is Wadi Gharandel in western Sinai. This is an approximate oasis stop, and the evidence is mixed.

Think about what this short verse shows. Yahweh does not only split seas. He also gives ordinary mercy on the road: water, palm trees, and a place to rest. Sometimes the next stop after a hard day is simply a place to breathe.

stops.panel_truth_line: Sinai / Horeb — redeemed slaves meet Yahweh and receive covenant word.
stops.caveats: Traditional Jebel Musa locus; exact Sinai ID debated.
stops.narration:
At last the people come to the mountain. At Sinai, also called Horeb, slaves who were rescued meet Yahweh and receive the words of his covenant (Exodus 19:1–8; Exodus 20:1–17, LSB).

Notice the order. Yahweh rescues first, and then he gives commands. Grace comes before obedience. Later readers see that pattern fulfilled even more deeply in Christ.

Where is the mountain? The traditional site is Jebel Musa, near St. Catherine in southern Sinai. But the location is debated, and the evidence is mixed. So we stand here at the traditional spot while keeping the question open.

Picture a crowd at the foot of a mountain, hearing that the God who freed them now wants them as his own people.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nebo / Pisgah — Moses sees the land he will not enter.
stops.narration:
Moses climbs a mountain and looks out over the land he will not enter. On Mount Nebo, from the ridge of Pisgah, Yahweh shows him the promise, and there Moses dies (Deuteronomy 34:1–8, LSB).

Today you can stand at the Mount Nebo memorial in Jordan, on the Pisgah ridge. This is the traditional viewpoint, and here the geography and the Bible fit well.

It is a quiet, sad, and hopeful moment. A faithful servant finishes his work looking toward what Yahweh promised. He does not see it fulfilled, but Yahweh's word still stands. The people will go on without him, because the promise never depended on one man.

stops.panel_truth_line: Gilgal — Jordan crossing memory; entry beat into the land.
stops.caveats: Gilgal ID has scholarly debate; wilderness-pack entry geography.
stops.narration:
The long journey ends with a crossing. After passing through the Jordan, the people camp at Gilgal. They set up stones as a memorial, and they keep the Passover in the land (Joshua 4:19–24; Joshua 5:10–12, LSB).

Gilgal lay in the Jordan Valley, west of Jericho, but scholars debate exactly where. There are several candidates, so the evidence here is mixed.

Think back to the start of this path: a lamb's blood on doors in Egypt. Now a rescued people eats the Passover again, this time in the land. The stones are there so children will ask what they mean. And the whole story points beyond itself, to a greater rescue still to come. Yahweh rescued Israel because he loved them and kept his oath (Deuteronomy 7:8). Paul calls Jesus our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), whose death sets people free from a deeper slavery than Egypt's.

paths.title: The week that changed the world
paths.theme: Passion → empty-tomb geography → Emmaus
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethany — friends, perfume, and Lazarus near Passion week.
stops.caveats: Lazarus tomb traditions are reception history.
stops.narration:
Before the hardest week, there is a village of friends. Bethany, near Jerusalem, is where Lazarus lived with Martha and Mary. John tells how Jesus raised Lazarus from the dead, and later how perfume was poured on him at a meal (John 11:1–44; John 12:1–8, LSB). The story of rescue reaches its high point among people who ate with Jesus and buried their dead.

From 1949 to 1953, Franciscan archaeologists dug here, with conservation work later. They found tomb complexes and remains of Byzantine and Crusader churches built over earlier Jewish tombs. They also found signs of village life and pilgrim facilities linked to the Lazarus tradition.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background and tradition. Christians have remembered Bethany as the village of Lazarus, Martha, and Mary without a break. A tomb has been honored here since Byzantine times.

But the dig does not prove that Lazarus was raised. What it supports is the place name and the pilgrim map of John 11. The Lazarus tomb traditions are part of how later believers received the story. Picture a quiet home, a grieving family, and a friend who came.

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — approach, teaching, Gethsemane prayer geography.
stops.caveats: Broad Olivet/Gethsemane tradition; multiple commemorations exist.
stops.narration:
The Mount of Olives rises just east of Jerusalem. Jesus comes over it as he approaches the city, weeps over Jerusalem, and later prays in Gethsemane before his arrest (Luke 19:28–44; Matthew 26:30–46, LSB). Here the Redeemer's obedience looks like sweat and surrender.

From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at a place called Dominus Flevit, Latin for "the Lord wept." They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with bone boxes called ossuaries and tunnel-like tombs. There were inscriptions too, and some people read them as Christian, though those readings are debated. A Byzantine monastery and church here remembered Jesus weeping over the city.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows how Jews buried their dead on this hill in Jesus' time. That is the real landscape around Gethsemane and the place tradition links to the Ascension in Acts. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated. The main value is the real cemetery.

There are many places on this hill that honor these events, and the traditions are broad. But picture the city spread out below, and a man who wept for it before he died for it.

stops.panel_truth_line: Caiaphas tradition — trial geography; keep ossuary/house caveats.
stops.narration:
After his arrest, Jesus is brought to the high priest Caiaphas. Human courts think they are judging him. The Gospels show the true Judge standing silent for sinners (Matthew 26:57–68; John 18:12–24, LSB).

In November and December 1990, construction work in south Jerusalem's Peace Forest, near North Talpiot, caused a burial cave from the Second Temple period to collapse open. The Israel Antiquities Authority sent Zvi Greenhut to save what was inside. He found several ossuaries, or bone boxes. One was an ornate limestone box. Its inscription is commonly read with the name Caiaphas, and the longer label is understood as "Joseph son of Caiaphas." Ronny Reich studied the writing, and Joseph Zias and Tzipora Kahana studied the bones. Greenhut published the find in 1992. The Israel Museum now shows the box as context for the high priest's family, from about AD 18–36.

The evidence is strong for a high-status priestly family named Caiaphas buried in Jerusalem at the right time. The fine box fits an important family. But it is not a signed label saying "this is the exact man in John 18." Names could be shared. So we keep that caution, and we do not claim to know the location of Caiaphas' house.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — the house He cleansed and taught near in His last days.
stops.caveats: Herodian western-wall / Robinson's Arch dig tourism geography.
stops.narration:
In his last days, Jesus walks into the temple, cleanses it, and teaches near its courts (Luke 19:45–48; Mark 11:15–18, LSB). The week of redemption runs through real streets and courts.

Stand at the western side of the Temple Mount, by the stub of Robinson's Arch. From 1968 to 1978, B. Mazar led digs here, with later seasons on the Ophel and work along the southwest corner. They uncovered a street from Herod's time running under the arch. On it lay huge cut stones that crashed down when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70. They also found Ophel walls, ritual baths, and grand stairways climbing toward the temple.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These are the approaches people used to reach the temple Jesus cleansed. Up on the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf. That is why the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere, and why tunnels and southern-wall digs stay outside the sacred area.

Imagine the noise of the market, then a sudden crash of tables, and a voice calling this house a place of prayer.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pilgrimage Road — City of David ascent toward the Temple.
stops.caveats: Excavated stepped street; Passion connections are geographic context.
stops.narration:
Passover is near, and Jerusalem fills with crowds. Jesus sends disciples ahead to prepare the meal in an upper room. Later, his accusers will not enter the governor's headquarters so they can still eat the Passover (Luke 22:7–13; John 18:28, LSB). The Lamb of God moves through a feast city toward the cross.

From the 1990s until now, with major sections uncovered in the 2000s and 2010s, archaeologists in the City of David have exposed a grand stepped street. Paved in the Early Roman period, it climbs from the Siloam area toward the Temple Mount. Shops lined it, and a drainage channel ran beneath. Coins found under the paving, including some from Pontius Pilate's time, date its building to about AD 30–40s.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. This street shows the pilgrim route and city life of Jerusalem in the lifetimes of Jesus and the apostles. The coins place the paving in the years of Pilate or Agrippa.

That does not prove any single walk from the Gospels. But it is a real street that pilgrims of Jesus' day used. Picture it crowded with families, lambs, and baskets, all heading up for the feast.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethesda — healing pools in the Passion-week city.
stops.caveats: Pool complex identified with John 5 tradition.
stops.narration:
Earlier in his ministry, Jesus came to a pool in Jerusalem called Bethesda, where many sick people lay. He told a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years to get up and walk, and he did (John 5:1–9, LSB). Later, in John 19:16–18 (LSB), the same city leads Jesus out to be crucified. The city that will crucify him had already seen his mercy.

Near St. Anne's Church, people discovered this pool complex in the 1800s. Major digs took place from the 1870s through the 1960s, and study continues. They found two pools with covered walkways, called porticoes. There were phases of a healing shrine, and some think a Roman healing temple was built here later, though that is debated. A Byzantine church remembered the miracle. Water works from the Second Temple and Early Roman periods were found too.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. John describes a pool with five porticoes near the Sheep Gate, and a real complex of several basins fits that. The exact shape of the "five porticoes" and the miracle itself are matters of interpretation.

What archaeology shows is a major pool site, right where John places the healing. Picture someone waiting by the water for years, and then hearing a single command.

stops.panel_truth_line: Golgotha — crucifixion of Jesus. Human redemption's center.
stops.caveats: No separate Holy Sepulchre pin; empty-tomb narrated here and at Emmaus.
stops.narration:
This is the center of the whole story. At Golgotha, also called Calvary, Jesus is crucified. Matthew and John tell of that day (Matthew 27:33–54; John 19:16–30, LSB). When he dies, the curtain in the temple is torn, and a Roman centurion confesses who he really was. God redeems people by the blood of his Son.

Where did it happen? In Jerusalem, the traditional site is commonly marked inside the area of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Many Protestants honor another tradition at the Garden Tomb.

The ground and the Bible line up well with Jerusalem as the place. There is no separate map stop for the Holy Sepulchre itself, so the empty tomb is told here and at Emmaus.

Stand still for a moment. The week that began with friends at Bethany and crowds on the road comes to this hill. Everything before points here, and everything after flows from it.

stops.panel_truth_line: Emmaus — risen Lord opens Moses and the Prophets. Debated village ID.
stops.caveats: REQUIRED: multiple Emmaus candidates; this pin uses Nicopolis tradition area.
stops.narration:
On the first Easter, two followers walk home to a village called Emmaus, sad and confused. A stranger joins them and explains Moses and the Prophets. Only when he breaks bread do they realize it is the risen Lord (Luke 24:13–35, LSB). Matthew 28:1–10 (LSB) tells of the women who find the tomb empty. The story of redemption ends with an empty tomb and a living Lord.

Which village was Emmaus? That is debated. This stop uses the tradition at Emmaus Nicopolis. Digs and surveys here began in the 1880s, with major church excavations in the 1900s and work off and on since. They found a Roman and Byzantine city, churches remembering the Luke 24 meeting, mosaics, and earlier settlement.

But other candidates exist: Motza or Qaloniyeh, el-Qubeibeh, and Abu Ghosh. Luke gives a distance of 60 stadia, but some manuscripts say 160. Nicopolis has a strong tradition among Byzantine pilgrims. Archaeology shows a real town remembered as Emmaus, but it does not settle which village Luke meant.

So the village is uncertain. The meeting is not. Picture two tired travelers suddenly running back the way they came. This is the heart of the whole week: Christ died for our sins and was raised on the third day, just as the Scriptures said (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). God shows his own love in this, that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8).

paths.title: Born under promise — Bethlehem to the Temple
paths.theme: Incarnation geography: Bethlehem → Nazareth → Temple pilgrimage
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — David's town; the child promised by Micah is born.
stops.narration:
Long before Jesus was born, the prophet Micah named a small town as the birthplace of a coming ruler (Micah 5:2, LSB). Bethlehem was David's town. Luke and Matthew tell how the promised child is born here (Luke 2:1–20; Matthew 2:1–6, LSB). The Redeemer enters history as a real baby in a real town.

Over a cave long believed to be Jesus' birthplace stands the Church of the Nativity, with building phases from the emperors Constantine and Justinian. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors. No clear first-century "manger house" layer has been published as a smoking gun.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as tradition. Christians have honored a cave in Bethlehem since at least the 300s AD. Archaeology confirms that early pilgrim memory. It has not found a census record or anything from the birth itself.

The claim that Jesus was born in Bethlehem comes from the text. The digs show the history of the shrine. Some claim a certain "Jesus house," but that is contested, and we leave it aside. Picture a small town, a crowded night, and a promise kept.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nazareth — upbringing town; He grows in wisdom and stature.
stops.narration:
After the excitement of his birth, Jesus grows up in Nazareth. Luke says he grew in wisdom and stature (Luke 2:39–52, LSB), and Matthew notes that he was called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23, LSB). God becoming human includes years of ordinary life before Jesus' public work began.

In 2009, the Israel Antiquities Authority dug near the Marian Center. They found remains of a courtyard house, partly cut from rock and partly built, dated to the first century. There were storage pits and household features. It is one of the first well-published houses in Nazareth from Jesus' time.

The evidence here is mixed but meaningful. This dig shows that Nazareth was a small Jewish village in the early first century. That answers extreme claims that Nazareth did not exist then. But it does not show that this was the house of Jesus or Mary. It only shows that houses like this stood when the Gospels say Jesus grew up there.

First-century Nazareth was a humble place, and the finds are modest too. Picture a boy helping around a simple courtyard home, growing up quietly in a village most people never noticed.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — presentation geography in His Father's house.
stops.caveats: Herodian west; presentation narrated from Temple approaches.
stops.narration:
When Jesus is still a baby, Mary and Joseph bring him to the temple in Jerusalem. There an old man named Simeon and an aged prophet named Anna recognize him. They hold hope in their arms (Luke 2:22–38, LSB).

We tell that story from the approaches on the temple's western and southern sides, by Robinson's Arch. From 1968 to 1978, B. Mazar dug here, followed by later seasons on the Ophel and work at the southwest corner. They uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, huge fallen stones from Rome's destruction in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths used for washing before worship, and great stairways leading up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These were the routes families walked to reach the temple courts. Up on the platform, though, licensed excavation is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf. So the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere, and tunnels and southern-wall digs stay outside the sacred area.

Picture a young couple climbing these stairs with a tiny child, not knowing that two faithful old people inside had waited their whole lives for this day.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pilgrimage Road — Passover pilgrimage feel for the boy Jesus.
stops.caveats: Stepped street as pilgrimage geography context for Luke 2.
stops.narration:
When Jesus is twelve, his family goes up to Jerusalem for Passover, as they do every year. On the way home, they discover he is missing. After three days they find him in the temple, and he asks them why they were searching, since he had to be in his Father's house (Luke 2:41–50, LSB).

Since the 1990s, with major sections uncovered in the 2000s and 2010s, archaeologists in the City of David have exposed a grand stepped street. It climbs from the Siloam area toward the Temple Mount. Shops lined it, and a drainage channel ran beneath. Coins under the paving, including some from Pontius Pilate's time, date its building to about AD 30–40s.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The street shows the pilgrim route and city life of Jerusalem during the lives of Jesus and the apostles. The coins place the paving in the years of Pilate or Agrippa, so it was finished after the boyhood story.

That means it is not proof of any single Gospel walk. It gives us the feel of pilgrimage. Picture crowds of families climbing toward the temple, and one boy who knew exactly where he belonged.

stops.panel_truth_line: Siloam / City of David water — pilgrim world of Jerusalem.
stops.caveats: Siloam pool excavations as pilgrim-city geography.
stops.narration:
Jerusalem at feast time was a pilgrim city, full of travelers and water for washing. Luke 2:41–49 (LSB) shows Jesus as a boy among those crowds. Later, John 9:1–11 (LSB) tells how Jesus sent a man born blind to wash in the Pool of Siloam, and he came back seeing. God becoming human means Jesus truly shared our places.

In 2004–2005, the Reich–Shukron team uncovered a large pool here at a spot called Birkat el-Hamra, with more exposure work in the 2020s. It is stepped and plastered, from the late Second Temple or Early Roman period, with a stone plaza to the north and stairs for going down into the water. Work continues with the Israel Antiquities Authority and the City of David.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. A huge pool at Siloam fits John's account of the blind man washing. It does not prove the miracle, but it shows a large public pool stood here in Jesus' time, very likely used by pilgrims for ritual washing.

There has been drama under the streets too. In March 2008, Israel's High Court of Justice briefly stopped a dig in Silwan near the pool after residents said work ran under their homes without proper notice. Living neighborhoods and archaeology meet here.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — He settles here as ministry base after the childhood/promise arc.
stops.caveats: Synagogue visible today is later rebuild — say teaching base carefully.
stops.narration:
After the stories of his birth and childhood, Jesus makes Capernaum his base by the sea (Matthew 4:13; Luke 4:31, LSB). This path has been about birth and belonging. A separate tour around the lake covers his teaching days here.

In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of Capernaum's white limestone synagogue. They documented its architecture, which set the stage for later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. The dig confirmed that a grand synagogue ruin stands in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base.

But be careful. The synagogue you can see today is a later building, from the 300s–400s AD. Whether an earlier, first-century phase lies under its floors is debated. So we say this was Jesus' teaching base, without claiming these exact white walls heard his voice.

Think back along this path: a baby in Bethlehem, a boy in Nazareth, a child in the temple. Now a grown man settles in a lakeside town, ready to begin. The angel had told the shepherds why he came: a Savior is born, who is Christ the Lord (Luke 2:11). Yahweh kept his word, sending his Son at just the right time to redeem us and make us his children (Galatians 4:4–5).

paths.title: Good news for the nations
paths.theme: Acts: Joppa/Caesarea through Greece to Rome — humanity invited
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Joppa — Peter's vision doorway; clean/unclean wall begins to fall.
stops.narration:
On a rooftop in Joppa, Peter prays and sees a vision that shakes his old ideas about clean and unclean. Then messengers from a Roman officer arrive at the door (Acts 10:9–23, LSB). The risen Lord is sending good news beyond the habits that kept Judea separate.

Joppa is today's Jaffa, an old port with many layers. Kaplan dug here from 1955 to 1974, and new projects by the Israel Antiquities Authority, UCLA, and others have continued since the 1990s. Earlier work found a Late Bronze gate with Egyptian inscriptions. Above it lie the remains of Iron Age, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman port cities. This is the harbor where Jonah sailed from in the Old Testament, and where Peter raised Tabitha and saw his vision in Acts.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Joppa is confirmed as Jaffa, and its harbor has a record from the Bronze Age to Roman times. The setting of Acts is secure at the level of the city. The exact "house of Simon the tanner" shown to visitors is pilgrim tradition.

Picture Peter on a flat roof by the sea, hungry and praying, as God opens a door that would change everything.

stops.panel_truth_line: Caesarea — Cornelius's household hears and receives the Spirit.
stops.caveats: Governor's port city; dig is Herodian/Roman.
stops.narration:
Peter travels north to Caesarea and enters the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer. While Peter is still speaking, the Spirit falls on everyone listening. God shows no partiality (Acts 10:24–48, LSB). The rescue God offers now opens publicly to the nations.

Caesarea Maritima was the governor's port city. From 1959 to 1964, an Italian mission dug its theater, built in Herod's time. In June 1961 they found a limestone block that had been reused in stairs in the 300s AD. It names "Pontius Pilatus," calls him prefect of Judea, and mentions a building named for the emperor Tiberius. It is the only known stone inscription from Pilate's own time that names him, and it calls him prefect of Judea.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone confirms Pilate's name, his title, and his post in Judea during Tiberius' reign. That matches the Gospels and the ancient historians Tacitus and Josephus. It does not tell the story of Jesus' trial, but it is strong evidence that the governor was real and tied to this city.

Picture this proud Roman city, the seat of power, and inside one home, a Gentile family hearing the good news and believing.

stops.panel_truth_line: Antioch — disciples called Christians; a sending church for the nations.
stops.narration:
Believers scattered by persecution reach Antioch and start telling Greeks about Jesus. A church grows, and here the disciples are first called Christians. Later this church sends out Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:19–26; Acts 13:1–3, LSB). The good news creates one people from many peoples.

From 1932 to 1939, a Princeton team led excavations at Antioch on the Orontes. They uncovered Roman and Byzantine city remains, a famous collection of mosaics, a racecourse called a circus, and villas. Very little early Christian building can be recovered, because the modern city sits on top.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. Antioch was a major Roman capital in Syria, a fitting hub for the mission in Acts. Remains of early house churches are rare under modern Antakya. But the mosaics and the city's size set the scene for the debates about Gentile believers that Paul describes in Galatians 2.

Picture a busy, mixed city where people from many backgrounds sat at one table, and neighbors needed a new name for them.

stops.panel_truth_line: Philippi — Lydia's heart opens; a jailer believes; Europe hears.
stops.narration:
Paul crosses into Macedonia and reaches Philippi. By a river, a businesswoman named Lydia opens her heart to the message. Later, after an earthquake at the prison, a jailer and his household believe (Acts 16:11–34, LSB). Different stories, one Lord. The good news is planted in European soil.

Since 1914, the French School and the Greek archaeology service have dug at Philippi, with major campaigns between and after the world wars. They found the forum, the theater, an eight-sided church complex called the Octagon, and paving from the Via Egnatia road. Visitors are shown a "prison of Paul," but that is traditional. There are also baptism sites by the Gangites river, by tradition, and inscriptions from the Roman colony.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Acts calls Philippi a Roman colony on the main road, and that matches exactly. The finds do not prove the stories of Lydia or the jailer. But the colony, the road, and the river all fit.

Picture Paul and his friends sitting by a river on the Sabbath, speaking with a few women, and a church beginning quietly there.

stops.panel_truth_line: Thessalonica — synagogue proclamation and civic upset.
stops.narration:
In Thessalonica, Paul goes into the synagogue and reasons from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believe. Others stir up a crowd, and the city is thrown into an uproar (Acts 17:1–9, LSB).

Since the 1960s, urban building work in modern Thessaloniki has revealed the old Roman forum, which is still being studied. Diggers found the public square, a small theater called an odeon, a covered underground walkway, inscriptions, and buildings tied to emperor worship. This was the civic heart of the city where Paul preached.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. Thessalonica was a major free city on the Via Egnatia. Acts 17:6 uses a special title, "politarchs," for its city officials. Local inscriptions found elsewhere in the city confirm that title. It is a strong match, and the forum gives a real stage for the events in Acts.

Picture a busy square, angry voices, and officials being told that these men were turning the world upside down. The message was already changing things.

stops.panel_truth_line: Berea — noble listeners examine the Scriptures daily.
stops.narration:
Sent away from Thessalonica by night, Paul and Silas reach Berea. The people here are eager, but they also check what they hear, examining the Scriptures every day to see if it is true (Acts 17:10–12, LSB). Faith is not fear of the text.

Modern Veria sits on top of ancient Berea. Through the 1900s and 2000s, salvage digs have taken place off and on, and an area linked to the synagogue tradition is cared for as a monument. Finds include Roman and Byzantine city remains, markers of the Jewish community's memory, and early Christian monuments. It is less grand than Philippi, but the town has been lived in continuously.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. Berea was a real Macedonian town on Paul's route. There is no dramatic single find, as at Philippi. What supports the story is the geography and the presence of a Jewish community far from Judea.

Picture people gathered with scrolls open, listening closely, then saying, "Let's look it up," and doing it day after day.

stops.panel_truth_line: Athens — Areopagus sermon; Creator and Judge who raised Jesus.
stops.caveats: Ancient Agora pin; Areopagus narrated from Athens geography.
stops.narration:
In Athens, Paul is stirred by a city full of idols. He speaks at the Areopagus about the Creator of all, who will judge the world and has raised Jesus from the dead. Some sneer. Some believe (Acts 17:16–34, LSB). The nations are told they answer to the risen Lord.

Since 1931, the American School has dug the Athenian Agora, the city's ancient marketplace. They uncovered covered colonnades called stoas, temples, altar areas, the council house, the Altar of the Twelve Gods, a Roman concert hall, and a huge number of inscriptions. There are also possible areas linked to the approaches to Paul's speech.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The Agora and the Areopagus hill are the physical stage of Acts 17. Paul mentions an altar to an unknown god. Altars of that kind are known in Greek religion, recorded by the writer Pausanias and found elsewhere. So Luke's detail fits real practice. Of course, no find proves Paul's speech word for word.

Picture the marble buildings, the philosophers, and one traveler telling them that the God they did not know is near.

stops.panel_truth_line: Corinth — port city church in a famously tangled culture.
stops.narration:
