Corinth was a busy port city with a famously tangled culture. Paul stays here for a year and a half, working and teaching, and a church takes root (Acts 18:1–11, LSB). Even in a noisy port, God plants holiness.

Since 1896, the American School of Classical Studies has dug at Corinth. They uncovered the forum, the bema or judgment platform, the temple of Apollo, the theater, a healing shrine called the Asklepieion, and shops. They also found a paving stone inscription saying that a man named Erastus, an official called an aedile, laid the pavement at his own expense.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The bema fits the setting where Paul is brought before the governor Gallio in Acts 18. Many people link the Erastus inscription to the Erastus in Romans 16:23 and 2 Timothy 4:20. His titles differ, and that is debated, but many think it is likely the same man. The city itself matches Paul's long stay in a bustling Roman colony.

Picture Paul working with his hands as a tentmaker and reasoning in the synagogue every Sabbath, in a crowded city that needed good news.

stops.panel_truth_line: Rome — Paul arrives; the gospel is not ashamed in the empire's heart.
stops.caveats: Catacombs pin as Rome locus; Pauline Rome traditions span multiple pins.
stops.narration:
The path that began on a rooftop in Joppa ends in the empire's capital. Paul arrives in Rome under guard. He lives under house arrest, but he keeps welcoming visitors and preaching. He is chained, but the word is not (Acts 28:11–31, LSB). Earlier he had written that he was not ashamed of the gospel (Romans 1:14–16, LSB).

This stop uses the catacombs as Rome's map point. Since the 1850s, starting with de Rossi and continuing under a papal commission, researchers have studied and protected these underground Christian burial networks. They hold paintings of the Good Shepherd, fish, and people praying with raised hands, along with grave inscriptions and the crypt of the popes at Callixtus.

Be honest about the dates. Most of this comes from the 100s to 300s AD, after Paul's lifetime. The catacombs show how Roman Christians later remembered their dead and their apostles. They do not prove Acts 28. Traditions about Paul in Rome are spread across several places.

The evidence for this stop is mixed. But picture a prisoner in a rented house in the world's greatest city, still speaking freely about Jesus. His message was the one he had written to Rome: the gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes (Romans 1:16). From a rooftop in Joppa to the capital, the invitation kept widening, and it still reaches whoever hears it today.

paths.title: Joseph — rejected, exalted, saving many
paths.theme: Genesis 37–50: betrayal, Egypt, preservation, reconciliation
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — family base before the sale.
stops.narration:
Every big story starts somewhere ordinary. For Joseph, it starts at home in Hebron. His father Jacob sends him, the favored son, to check on his brothers in the fields (Genesis 37:14, LSB). Jacob does not know that those brothers will sell Joseph.

On the ancient mound of Hebron, called Tel Rumeida, digs took place in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, including huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. Ancient Hebron was a fortified city in the hill country. That fits the setting of the patriarch stories, and the city later became David's first capital. The famous cave of Machpelah lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has not been dug.

None of this shows us Joseph himself. It shows the kind of place his family called home base. Picture a young man setting out from these hills on an errand for his father, with no idea how far the road would take him.

stops.panel_truth_line: Dothan — Joseph finds his brothers near Dothan.
stops.caveats: Pin is Elisha-labeled (2 Kgs 6); use as place geography, not Elisha event.
stops.narration:
Joseph walks a long way looking for his brothers. At last he finds them near Dothan (Genesis 37:17, LSB). It is here, far from home, that the brothers will turn against him.

This map pin at Dothan was first labeled for a different story, about the prophet Elisha in 2 Kings 6. That is another chapter on the same map. Here we use it simply as the place, not for the Elisha event.

The evidence for this stop is mixed, and the facts are few. But the moment is powerful. Picture the brothers looking up and seeing Joseph coming in the distance. For him it is the end of a long search. For them it is a chance to get rid of the brother they envy.

stops.panel_truth_line: Shechem — brothers first pastured toward Shechem.
stops.narration:
Joseph's brothers take the flocks to pasture near Shechem, and Jacob sends Joseph to see how they are doing (Genesis 37:12–14, LSB). The road of envy begins in ordinary pasture country.

The ruins of ancient Shechem are at a mound called Tell Balata. Sellin dug here in 1913–1914 and 1926–1927, and Wright led the Drew-McCormick and ASOR excavations from 1956 to 1973. They uncovered massive Middle Bronze walls, a temple-fortress, a gate complex, destruction layers, and later Iron Age homes.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Shechem was a major city in the Bronze and Iron Ages. It is a fitting stage for the covenant gathering in Joshua 24 and the Abimelech story in Judges 9.

But no dig can prove that one shepherd family passed by. That kind of proof is beyond what archaeology can reach. What we can picture is the wide grazing land around a strong city, where brothers watched their sheep and nursed a grudge that was about to boil over.

stops.panel_truth_line: Avaris — Nile Delta / Hyksos-period capital zone for Joseph-in-Egypt backdrop.
stops.caveats: Do NOT claim "Joseph's house found." Backdrop only.
stops.narration:
Joseph is sold as a slave and taken to Egypt. He serves in a household there and suffers unfairly, but Yahweh is with him. In time, Pharaoh puts him in charge of the whole land (Genesis 39:1–6; Genesis 41:39–45, LSB).

Avaris, in the Nile Delta, helps us picture that world. Austrian archaeologists dug at Tell el-Dab'a from 1966 to 2011 and beyond. They uncovered the Hyksos capital of Avaris, with a settlement culture that came from Canaan and nearby lands. They found palaces, temples, and paintings in a style like those from Crete.

The evidence here is mixed. The dig shows that many people from the Levant lived in the Delta. That makes a story of a family like Joseph's settling in Egypt more believable. But no biblical person has been identified here.

So be careful. We do not claim that "Joseph's house" was found. This is the backdrop only. Still, imagine a young foreigner from the hills of Canaan, living in a busy Egyptian city full of people who had come from his part of the world.

stops.panel_truth_line: On / Heliopolis — Asenath daughter of Potiphera priest of On.
stops.narration:
Pharaoh gives Joseph a new name and a wife, Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, a priest of On. Joseph has two sons there, and he names them in ways that remember both his suffering and his blessing (Genesis 41:45; Genesis 41:50–52, LSB). Even in a foreign land, the family line goes on. A slave market cannot cancel God's promise.

On is the city later called Heliopolis, today the Matariya and Ain Shams area of northeast Cairo. Schiaparelli's Italian Mission dug here in 1903–1906, and Egyptian teams with partners continue today. The city was devoted to the sun god Ra and Atum. An obelisk of Senusret I still stands in the open at Matariya, marking the old temple area. Teams have found temple foundations, work areas, and graves from many periods.

Scholars agree strongly that biblical On is this Egyptian city, called Iunu. Archaeology confirms it was a major center of sun worship. That does not prove the Joseph story on its own. The prophet Ezekiel also mentions this city by the same name.

Picture Joseph, once thrown in a pit, now marrying into one of Egypt's most important priestly families.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pi-Ramesses / Qantir — later Ramesside overlay of Goshen memory geography.
stops.caveats: Later capital overlay; Goshen memory geography with caveat.
stops.narration:
Later in the story, Joseph's family settles in the best of Egypt's land, in the region of Rameses (Genesis 47:11, LSB). Much later, their descendants are forced to build store cities, including one called Rameses (Exodus 1:11, LSB). Later names sit on the same Delta world that Israel will one day leave.

Since 1980, mostly German teams have dug at Qantir, the site of Pi-Ramesses. They found remains of the capital built by the Ramesside kings, with stables, bronze workshops, and palaces. It lies close to Avaris, the Hyksos city at Tell el-Dab'a.

The evidence is mixed. The dig supports a store city named Ramesses in the right part of the Delta for the Exodus tradition. It gives a believable New Kingdom setting. But on its own, it does not prove the Exodus happened.

One more caution: this capital is later than Joseph's time, laid on top of the older memory of Goshen. Picture the same green Delta land changing over the generations, from a place of welcome to a place of hard labor.

stops.panel_truth_line: Memphis — major Egyptian urban backdrop (context stop).
stops.caveats: Context stop for Egyptian power geography.
stops.narration:
Joseph is thirty years old when he enters Pharaoh's service. Later a famine spreads, and Jacob sends his sons south to Egypt to buy grain (Genesis 41:46; Genesis 42:1–3, LSB). Hunger drives the brothers into the shadow of a great empire.

Memphis helps us picture that power. Its ruins at Mit Rahina are part of a UNESCO World Heritage property, listed since 1979. Petrie dug here from 1908 to 1913, and Egyptian teams have worked here ever since. They found the temple area of the god Ptah, giant statues of Ramesses II, a palace area of King Apries, and city remains spanning thousands of years. Nearby, the burial lands from Giza to Saqqara to Dahshur hold Egypt's earliest great stone tombs.

Scholars agree that the biblical city called Noph or Moph is Memphis at Mit Rahina. As a capital, it stands behind many later prophetic messages against Egypt. Those verses name the city, but not every detail must be proven by the ruins.

This is a context stop, showing Egyptian power. Picture ten hungry brothers arriving in a land of giant statues and temples, about to bow before a brother they do not recognize.

stops.panel_truth_line: Beersheba — Jacob offers sacrifices on the way to Egypt.
stops.narration:
Jacob is old now, and he is going to Egypt to see Joseph. On the way, he stops at Beersheba and offers sacrifices. God speaks to him at night and tells him not to be afraid (Genesis 46:1–4, LSB). At the end of Genesis, Joseph tells his brothers: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to keep many people alive (Genesis 50:20, LSB).

From 1969 to 1976, Tel Aviv University dug at Tel Beersheba. They found a planned Iron Age town with walls, storehouses, and a water system. They also found a horned altar, which had been taken apart and its stones reused in a storehouse wall.

That altar matches the shape of altars in the Bible, and it fits the way Amos and the books of Kings criticize worship at Beersheba. The planned town fits a time when Judah's kings controlled the Negev.

But the evidence is mixed for Jacob's story, since the town is much later. Beersheba is the southern hinge, the last stop before Egypt. Picture an old man at an altar, afraid of a long journey, hearing that God will go down with him. Joseph's life is a picture of a greater rescue. Like Joseph, Jesus was rejected by his own and handed over, yet God raised him up (Acts 2:23–24), and there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12). What others meant for evil, God turned into life for many.

paths.title: From Susa to Zion — exile, decree, return
paths.theme: Exile, Esther's Susa, Cyrus decree, Haggai rebuild
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Babylon — exile capital.
stops.narration:
The worst has happened. Babylon's army burns Jerusalem and carries the people away (2 Kings 25:8–12, LSB). In exile, they sit by Babylon's rivers and weep when they remember Zion (Psalm 137:1–6, LSB). Judgment is real because the covenant was real.

Babylon was the exile capital. From 1899 to 1917, Koldewey's team for the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft dug here. They uncovered the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way. They found Nebuchadnezzar's walls and palaces, the remains of the Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat, and building inscriptions in cuneiform.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon matches the empire that destroyed Jerusalem in 2 Kings 25. Inscriptions also record Cyrus taking the city later, which will matter on the next stops. Many people link the ancient Tower of Babel to the Etemenanki ziggurat, but that is traditional background, not proof.

Picture the exiles walking through these grand gates as captives, surrounded by a city of wonders, and still longing for home.

stops.panel_truth_line: Babylon — Cyrus Cylinder findspot; Persian decree culture.
stops.caveats: Cylinder in BM; pin is findspot. Do not claim cylinder quotes Ezra verbatim.
stops.narration:
Ezra 1:1–4 (LSB) tells how Yahweh stirs the heart of Cyrus, king of Persia, to let the Jews go home and rebuild the house of Yahweh in Jerusalem. Yahweh moves a foreign king for the sake of his own Name.

This stop marks where a famous object was found. In 1879, Rassam discovered the Cyrus Cylinder at Babylon. It is a clay cylinder in which Cyrus the Great describes conquering Babylon and returning temples and peoples to their lands. The cylinder itself is now in the British Museum.

The evidence here is mixed but valuable. Cyrus's policy of restoring peoples matches the decree in Ezra and Chronicles that let Judeans return and rebuild. But the cylinder does not name Judah or Jerusalem. It is excellent background from the empire's own side, not a copy of Ezra's words.

Picture an ancient official reading a royal message aloud: displaced peoples may go home. And somewhere in the crowd, exiles from Judah hearing that their prayers had been answered.

stops.panel_truth_line: Cyrus Cylinder — Persian policy backdrop for Ezra 1.
stops.caveats: Artifact pin; parallel/context object, not a verse of Scripture.
stops.narration:
On this stop, look at the object itself: the Cyrus Cylinder. It is a clay cylinder of Cyrus the Great, from Babylon, describing how he restored peoples and temples after he conquered the city.

Ezra 1:1–4 (LSB) records the decree that let the exiles return. Long before, Isaiah 44:28–45:1 (LSB) spoke of Cyrus by name as the one Yahweh would use. Empires are tools in Yahweh's hand.

The evidence is mixed in a careful way. The cylinder gives the background of Persian policy for Ezra 1. It is a parallel, a piece of context. It is not a verse of Scripture, and it does not mention the Jews by name.

Still, it is remarkable to see. Picture a mighty king pressing his boasts into clay, while the Bible quietly says that the real reason behind his kindness was Yahweh keeping a promise.

stops.panel_truth_line: Susa — Esther / imperial court geography.
stops.caveats: Esther is Jewish fidelity under threat—not Gentile conversion.
stops.narration:
In the royal city of Susa, a Jewish woman named Esther becomes queen. When her people face destruction, she is told she may have come to the kingdom for such a time as this. She risks her life to go before the king so her people may live (Esther 1:1–5; Esther 4:13–16, LSB). Here rescue looks like being preserved under an empire.

French missions dug at Susa in 1884–1886 and 1897–1912, and continued through the 1900s. They found the Persian kings' palace complex, decorated with glazed bricks, and official tablets. In 1901 they also found the Code of Hammurabi, a Babylonian law stone that had been carried to Susa as war loot.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Susa was a real royal city of the Persian kings, a fitting setting for Esther and Nehemiah. The dig does not prove the details of Esther's story. The Hammurabi stone is often compared with the laws in the Torah as background.

Esther's story is about Jews staying faithful under threat. Picture a young queen standing at the edge of the throne room, knowing that one step forward could cost her everything.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pasargadae — Cyrus's Persian heartland (UNESCO).
stops.narration:
The decree in Ezra 1:1–4 (LSB) came from a real Persian world, not a fairy-tale court. Pasargadae was Cyrus's homeland capital, now a UNESCO site.

From 1961 to 1963, Stronach led major excavations here. His team studied the buildings of Cyrus the Great's capital, garden pavilions, early Persian inscriptions, and the Tomb of Cyrus. That the tomb belongs to Cyrus is traditional and widely accepted.

The evidence is mixed for linking this place to the Bible directly. But it anchors Cyrus as a real emperor with a known capital. That supports the Bible's naming of Cyrus as the king who set the exiles free.

Picture a quiet stone tomb standing in an open plain. The man buried there ruled a vast empire, and the Bible remembers him for one decision: letting a small, scattered people go home.

stops.panel_truth_line: Persepolis — later Achaemenid ceremonial capital (empire context).
stops.caveats: Empire context; not Esther's exact hall claim.
stops.narration:
Persepolis was the later ceremonial capital of the Persian kings. It helps us picture the empire behind the return from exile in Ezra 1:1–4 and the royal feasts at the start of Esther (Esther 1:1–3, LSB).

From 1931 to 1939, the Oriental Institute led excavations here. They uncovered the great audience hall called the Apadana, the palaces of Darius and Xerxes, carvings showing peoples from all over the empire bringing gifts, and thousands of clay tablets from the Fortification and Treasury archives.

The evidence is mixed for direct Bible links. These finds show how the Persian empire was run and how many nations met at its court. That is the background behind Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther. The tablets list food rations and officials. They give a sense of realism but do not name the Judean heroes of those books.

So this is not Esther's exact hall. It is the world she lived in. Picture lines of carved figures from many lands climbing the stairs, all bowing to one king, while the Bible insists that another King rules over him.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — returnees' city.
stops.narration:
The exiles have come home. In Jerusalem, they lay the foundation of Yahweh's house again. The priests blow trumpets and the people shout for joy. But some older people, who remember the first temple, weep out loud. The sounds blend so you cannot tell joy from weeping (Ezra 3:8–13, LSB). Homecoming is like that.

From 1961 to 1967, Kenyon dug on the Ophel and in the City of David. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on the southeast ridge known as David's city. But how big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still debated, with some scholars arguing for a small town and others for something larger.

Some claim a large stone building here was David's palace, but we do not overclaim that. Picture the returnees standing among ruins, some cheering, some crying, all of them home.

stops.panel_truth_line: Haggai — rebuild preaching in Jerusalem.
stops.narration:
The returned exiles have built houses for themselves, but Yahweh's house still lies unfinished. The prophet Haggai calls them to rebuild, and promises that Yahweh is with them (Haggai 1:1–8; Haggai 2:1–9, LSB). A restored people is called back to worship, not only to walls.

This stop is in Jerusalem, at the setting of the Second Temple rebuild. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

Haggai's message is short and direct. It asks people to look at their own lives and priorities. Picture families busy fixing their own roofs, and a prophet standing in the street pointing to the empty, unfinished place where Yahweh's house should be.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — Second Temple precinct memory (restored worship geography).
stops.caveats: Herodian fabric is later; use as Temple approach geography for return worship memory.
stops.narration:
Haggai promised that Yahweh would shake the nations and fill his house with glory (Haggai 2:6–9, LSB). Zechariah heard Yahweh say he would return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem (Zechariah 8:3, LSB). The rescue of God's people included holiness still unfinished, waiting for a greater glory.

The temple the returnees built was later rebuilt on a grand scale. At Robinson's Arch, on the temple's western side, B. Mazar dug from 1968 to 1978, followed by later Ophel seasons and work at the southwest corner. They found a street from Herod's time under the arch, giant stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and great stairways up to the Temple Mount.

Be honest about timing. These remains from Herod's era are later than Haggai and Zechariah. We use them as the approach to the temple, a way to remember the return and the worship that followed. The evidence for this path is mixed.

Licensed digging on the platform itself is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere. Picture the long journey from Babylon's rivers ending at these steps, with a promise still pointing forward. That promise was kept in the temple on this mount. Years later, old Simeon took the baby Jesus in his arms there and praised God, saying his eyes had seen God's salvation, a light for the nations (Luke 2:27–32). Yahweh brought his people home, and then he came to them himself.

paths.title: When the house of Yahweh stood again
paths.theme: Shiloh → Zion → post-exile rebuild → Second Temple approaches
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Shiloh — early sanctuary where Yahweh's name dwelt.
stops.narration:
Before there was a temple in Jerusalem, there was Shiloh. Each year a man named Elkanah went up there to worship Yahweh (1 Samuel 1:3, LSB). Later, Israel carried the ark of the covenant out from Shiloh into battle, and it was captured (1 Samuel 4:3–11, LSB). Shiloh taught Israel what it meant for God to dwell among them.

Danish teams dug here in the 1920s and 1930s. Finkelstein led work in 1981–1984, and the ABR team have dug since 2017. They found religious and storage remains from the Iron I period, deposits of animal bones, walls, and remains from later times. ABR has claimed finds related to the tabernacle, but those claims are debated in the wider academic world.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. There was significant activity at Shiloh in Iron I, fitting the tradition of a sanctuary in Samuel's day. The exact shape of the tabernacle has not been proven. Scholars also discuss layers of destruction alongside Jeremiah's memory of what happened to Shiloh.

Picture families climbing these hills each year to worship, long before Jerusalem's temple existed.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — David brings the ark up.
stops.narration:
The ark of the covenant has been away for a long time. Now King David brings it up to his city with shouting, music, and dancing, and with a healthy fear of Yahweh's holiness (2 Samuel 6:12–17, LSB). The ark rises to Zion.

This is the City of David, the oldest part of Jerusalem. From 1961 to 1967, Kenyon dug here on the Ophel. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied the layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge, the area known as David's city. But how big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC, in David's time, is still argued about. Some scholars think it was small. Others think it was much larger.

Some people say a large stone building here was David's palace. We do not make that claim. Instead, picture a joyful parade winding up this ridge, with a king dancing ahead of the ark as it comes home.

stops.panel_truth_line: Gihon — royal/water geography near temple mount tradition.
stops.narration:
Below the old city lies the spring of Gihon. The Bible ties this spring to a moment of royal history in 1 Kings 1:33–40 (LSB). And a psalm sings of a river whose streams make glad the city of God (Psalm 46:4, LSB). Memories of water and kingship sit beneath the mountain where people met with God.

From 1995 into the 2010s, the Reich–Shukron team dug around Gihon. They found the Spring Tower and other defenses guarding the water. They clarified the Siloam Tunnel, often called Hezekiah's Tunnel, and a water channel known as Channel II. They found small clay seals called bullae. In 2004 they uncovered the Pool of Siloam from the Second Temple period.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. An inscription found in the tunnel in 1880, studied by many teams since, matches the Bible's description of King Hezekiah bringing water into the city (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30).

On this path about Yahweh's house, Gihon is a reminder that a city needs water to live. Picture fresh water rising from the rock at the foot of the hill, and a city above that depended on it every day.

stops.panel_truth_line: Tel Motza — Iron Age temple near Jerusalem (context/contrast).
stops.caveats: NOT "Solomon's temple found." Nearby Iron Age temple only.
stops.narration:
When Solomon's temple was finished, a cloud filled the house of Yahweh, so the priests could not stand to serve (1 Kings 8:10–11, LSB). This stop visits a different temple nearby, as a contrast.

At Tel Motza, near Jerusalem, the Israel Antiquities Authority began salvage digs in the 1990s. Major exposure of a temple came in 2012–2013, led by teams including Kisilevitz and Greenhut, and work has continued. They found a large Iron Age II temple complex with stands used in worship, figurines, and grand architecture. It is a rare temple from Judah outside Jerusalem.

The evidence here is mixed in an interesting way. The temple itself is confirmed. Linking the site to biblical Mozah, mentioned in Joshua 18:26, is plausible. But the find's main value is what it shows about worship in Judah. It challenges simple ideas that there was only ever one temple in the land, so it needs careful interpretation.

One thing is clear: this is not "Solomon's temple found." It is a nearby Iron Age temple only. A neighboring temple reminds us that the Bible's claim about Yahweh's house is unique, and Motza is not that house.

stops.panel_truth_line: Haggai — "build the house."
stops.narration:
Build Yahweh's house again. That is the heart of Haggai's message to the people who came back from exile (Haggai 1:1–8; Haggai 2:1–9, LSB).

This stop is in Jerusalem, at the setting of the Second Temple rebuild. Here the geography and the Bible fit well.

On a path about Yahweh's house standing again, Haggai is the voice that gets the work moving. The returnees had started, then stopped. The prophet's words call them back to the task. Picture a half-finished building site, weeds growing over old foundations, and a prophet urging tired people to pick up their tools again.

stops.panel_truth_line: Zechariah — Zion comfort / temple visions.
stops.narration:
The prophet Zechariah received visions in the night over Jerusalem. Yahweh says he has returned to the city with compassion, and his house will be built there (Zechariah 1:16, LSB). He says he will return to Zion and dwell in Jerusalem (Zechariah 8:3, LSB).

This stop is in Jerusalem, the setting of those night visions. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

While Haggai pushed the people to build, Zechariah gave them comfort and visions of cleansing. Both hung over the rebuilding of the temple. Picture builders working through the day, and at night a prophet seeing pictures of a city made clean and filled with God's presence again.

stops.panel_truth_line: Southern Temple Mount — Herodian/Second Temple approaches.
stops.narration:
The house of Yahweh was rebuilt after the exile. When its foundation was laid, there was shouting and weeping together (Ezra 3:10–13, LSB). But the story was not finished. Malachi promised that the Lord would suddenly come to his temple (Malachi 3:1, LSB). The house stood again in history, and it still waited.

At Robinson's Arch, on the western side of the temple's great platform, you stand by the approaches of that later temple, rebuilt grandly in Herod's day. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later Ophel seasons and work at the southwest corner. They found a street from Herod's time under the arch, giant cut stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and grand stairways up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well with these approaches. These are later stones than Ezra's day, but they mark the same place of worship.

On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf. So the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere. Picture worshipers climbing these steps for generations, waiting for the Lord Malachi promised. He came. John writes that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, full of grace and truth (John 1:14). The God who filled a house of stone came near in Jesus, so that anyone may draw near to him.

paths.title: From the upper room memory to a people filled
paths.theme: Acts 1–2 Spirit outpouring geography; Cenacle gap honest
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — ascension geography.
stops.narration:
The risen Jesus is taken up into heaven from the Mount of Olives. The witnesses then walk back to Jerusalem to wait (Acts 1:9–12, LSB). They gathered in an upper room, but there is no dig site for that room, so we tell of their waiting without guessing where it was.

From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at Dominus Flevit on this hill. They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with bone boxes called ossuaries and tunnel-like tombs. Some inscriptions have been read as Christian, but those readings are debated. A Byzantine monastery and church here remembered Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows how Jews buried their dead on this hill in Jesus' time, the real landscape of the Ascension tradition in Acts. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated.

Picture a small group standing on this hill, staring up at the sky, and then turning to walk the short way back to the city, holding a promise and waiting for what comes next.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — daily temple gatherings after Pentecost.
stops.narration:
After Pentecost, the believers keep meeting in the temple every day, and they share meals in their homes with glad hearts (Acts 2:46, LSB). Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer (Acts 3:1, LSB). A people filled with the Spirit still go up to God's house to pray.

At Robinson's Arch, on the temple's western side, you can see the routes they would have walked. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later Ophel seasons and work along the southwest corner. His teams found a street from Herod's time running under the arch, and huge fallen stones from Rome's destruction in AD 70. They found Ophel walls, ritual baths used for washing before worship, and grand stairways climbing to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These are the real approaches to the temple in the apostles' lifetimes. On the platform above, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so tunnels and southern-wall digs stay outside the sacred area, and the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Picture a growing crowd of new believers, still praying at the familiar hours, climbing these steps with a brand-new joy.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pilgrimage Road — pilgrim movement archaeology in the Spirit's city.
stops.caveats: Stepped street; Pentecost narrated in Jerusalem geography.
stops.narration:
It is the feast of Pentecost, and Jerusalem is packed with pilgrims from many lands. Suddenly the Spirit comes. The disciples speak in other languages, and the crowds hear God's mighty works in their own tongues. Peter preaches, and about three thousand people believe (Acts 2:1–41, LSB).

Since the 1990s, with major sections uncovered in the 2000s and 2010s, archaeologists in the City of David have exposed a grand stepped street. Paved in the Early Roman period, it climbs from the Siloam area toward the Temple Mount. Shops lined it, and a drainage channel ran underneath. Coins found under the paving, including some from Pontius Pilate's time, date its building to about AD 30–40s.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. This street shows the pilgrim route and city life of Jerusalem in the lifetimes of Jesus and the apostles. It does not prove any single event, but it is a real road that pilgrims used.

We tell the Pentecost story here, in Jerusalem's geography. Picture this street crowded with visitors from far away, speaking a dozen languages, when suddenly they each hear a message they can understand.

stops.panel_truth_line: Siloam — City of David water / festival world.
stops.narration:
After Pentecost, the new believers devote themselves to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to breaking bread, and to prayer. They share what they have, and the Lord adds to their number day by day (Acts 2:42–47, LSB). It all happens in an ordinary city with ordinary water supplies, the same city where the Spirit fell.

In 2004–2005, the Reich–Shukron team uncovered a large pool at Siloam, at a spot called Birkat el-Hamra, with more exposure work in the 2020s. It is stepped and plastered, from the late Second Temple or Early Roman period, with a stone plaza to the north and stairs for going down into the water. Work continues with the Israel Antiquities Authority and the City of David.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The pool fits John's account of the blind man washing. It does not prove that miracle, but it shows a large public pool stood here in that era, very likely used by pilgrims for ritual washing.

Archaeology here also meets daily life. In March 2008, Israel's High Court of Justice briefly halted a dig in Silwan near the pool after residents said work ran beneath their homes without proper notice. Picture this busy pool, and a new community growing in the neighborhoods around it.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethesda — Jerusalem pool geography in the same city.
stops.caveats: John 5 pool complex in Acts' city setting.
stops.narration:
The early church in Jerusalem is full of wonder. Signs are done through the apostles, believers share their goods, and they meet with glad and sincere hearts (Acts 2:43–47, LSB). Places of mercy and places of mission share one map.

The Pools of Bethesda, near St. Anne's Church, are part of that same city. People discovered the site in the 1800s, with major digs from the 1870s to the 1960s, and study continues. They found two pools with covered walkways, healing-shrine phases, and a debated later Roman healing temple. A Byzantine church remembered Jesus' healing here, and there were water works from the Second Temple and Early Roman periods.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. John's Gospel describes a pool with five porticoes near the Sheep Gate where Jesus healed a man. A real complex with several basins fits that. The exact design and the miracle itself are matters of interpretation, but archaeology confirms a major pool site where John places the story.

So on this path about the Spirit, Bethesda reminds us that the city where the church was born had already seen Jesus' mercy. Picture the first believers walking past these pools, remembering.

stops.panel_truth_line: Joppa — doorway toward Gentile inclusion (bridge beat).
stops.caveats: Differentiate from Cornelius path: spine here is Jerusalem Spirit outpouring.
stops.narration:
The Spirit has filled the believers in Jerusalem. Now the story starts to move outward. At Joppa, Peter prays on a rooftop and sees a vision that challenges his ideas about clean and unclean (Acts 10:9–23, LSB). The same Spirit will soon fall on a Roman household. On this path, Joppa is the bridge from Jerusalem to the nations.

Joppa is today's Jaffa. Kaplan dug here from 1955 to 1974, and new projects by the Israel Antiquities Authority, UCLA, and others have continued since the 1990s. Earlier work found a Late Bronze gate and Egyptian inscriptions. Above lie the remains of Iron Age, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman port cities. This harbor is where Jonah boarded a ship, and where Peter raised Tabitha and saw his vision.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Joppa is confirmed as Jaffa, and the setting of Acts is secure at the city level. The exact "house of Simon the tanner" is pilgrim tradition.

Picture Peter, fresh from the excitement in Jerusalem, now on a quiet roof by the sea, about to learn that the Spirit's work is far bigger than he imagined.

stops.panel_truth_line: Caesarea — Spirit on the nations teaser (Cornelius household).
stops.caveats: Full Cornelius tour is under Gentiles category.
stops.narration:
In Caesarea, Peter is still speaking to Cornelius and his household when the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear. The believers who came with Peter are amazed that the gift is poured out even on Gentiles, and the household is baptized (Acts 10:44–48, LSB). The rescue God brings makes a people alive by his Spirit, from Jerusalem outward.

Caesarea Maritima was the governor's port city. From 1959 to 1964, an Italian mission dug its theater from Herod's time. In June 1961 they found a limestone block reused in stairs in the 300s AD. It names "Pontius Pilatus," calls him prefect of Judea, and mentions a building named for the emperor Tiberius. It is the only known stone inscription from Pilate's own time that names him, and it calls him prefect of Judea.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone confirms Pilate's name, title, and post in Judea under Tiberius, matching the Gospels and the historians Tacitus and Josephus. It is strong evidence that the governor was real and tied to Caesarea.

This path began with followers waiting in Jerusalem. It ends in a Roman city, with Gentiles praising God. Picture the surprise on every face in that room. Peter's message in that house was simple: everyone who believes in Jesus receives forgiveness of sins through his name (Acts 10:43). The promise of the Spirit was for Jerusalem, and for all who are far off (Acts 2:39).

paths.title: Along the lake where He taught
paths.theme: Nazareth → Capernaum → Magdala → Bethsaida → Chorazin
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Nazareth — where familiarity met unbelief. The path starts in His hometown (Luke 4).
stops.caveats: First-century Nazareth is archaeologically modest. Do NOT use Sisters of Nazareth ‘Jesus house’ (CBG-06) as proven dig consensus — optional contested footnote only. Pin NAZ-01 as primary hometown geography.
stops.narration:
This path begins where people thought they already knew the story. Nazareth was Jesus' hometown. Luke remembers how he read from the scroll in the synagogue here, and then the hard turn when his neighbors would not receive him (Luke 4:16–30, LSB). Here, familiarity met unbelief.

In 2009, the Israel Antiquities Authority dug near the Marian Center. They found a courtyard house from the first century, partly cut into rock and partly built, with storage pits and household features. It is one of the first well-published houses in Nazareth from Jesus' time.

The evidence is mixed but meaningful. The dig shows Nazareth was a small Jewish village in the early first century, answering extreme claims that it did not exist. But it does not show this was the house of Jesus or Mary. It only shows such houses stood when the Gospels say he grew up here.

First-century Nazareth was a modest place, and the finds are modest too. Some point to a different "Jesus house" at the Sisters of Nazareth convent, but that claim is contested and not accepted as proven.

Picture a village synagogue, a familiar young man reading, and neighbors who could not believe that the boy they watched grow up was something more.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — His base by the lake. Teaching and healings with authority that unsettled the town.
stops.caveats: Synagogue visible today is later rebuild over earlier remains — say ‘synagogue site / teaching base’ carefully. ‘House of Peter’ (CBG-05) is contested identification — do not require it for this stop.
stops.narration:
Down on the northwest shore of the lake, Capernaum becomes Jesus' base. Matthew notes that he settled here (Matthew 4:13, LSB). Mark tells of his teaching in the synagogue, and healings that unsettled the town. People felt his authority in the streets (Mark 1:21–34, LSB). This is where his ministry had an address.

In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of Capernaum's white limestone synagogue. They documented its architecture, preparing the way for later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. The dig confirmed that a grand synagogue ruin stands in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base.

But be careful with that building. The synagogue you see today is a later rebuild, from the 300s–400s AD, over earlier remains. Whether a first-century phase lies under its floors is debated. So we speak of the synagogue site and the teaching base, not "the very walls." Some identify a nearby "House of Peter," but that identification is contested, and this stop does not depend on it.

Picture a lakeside town buzzing with news, crowds gathering at a door at sunset, and sick people being carried through the streets.

stops.panel_truth_line: Magdala — a named shore town in the Gospel world. Real first-century streets beside the lake.
stops.caveats: Lighter direct Gospel narrative dig-proof than Capernaum. Strong narrative geography and a real first-century town; the Gospels do not locate miracle scenes here.
stops.narration:
Walk along the shore road and you reach Magdala, a real first-century town in Galilee. The Gospel world knows it through the name of Mary Magdalene, one of the women who traveled with Jesus and supported his work (Luke 8:1–3, LSB).

In 2009, the Israel Antiquities Authority carried out a salvage dig here. They uncovered a first-century synagogue with a mosaic floor and painted walls. Inside was the Magdala Stone, carved with a seven-branched lampstand called a menorah and designs linked to the temple. It is rare synagogue art from before AD 70.

The evidence here is mixed. This was a working synagogue while the temple in Jerusalem still stood. It ties Mary Magdalene's hometown to a real Jewish town center. But it does not prove any miracle story at Magdala.

Keep this stop honest. Magdala has less direct dig evidence for Gospel events than Capernaum. Its strength is the real town and its geography. The Gospels do not place miracle scenes here, so we do not invent any.

Instead, picture a woman from this lakeside town, with its streets and synagogue, leaving home to follow Jesus from village to village.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethsaida — signs and disciples’ hometown ties. Scholars still debate the exact tell; the Gospels place the town here by the lake.
stops.caveats: REQUIRED disclosure: Bethsaida ID contested (CBG-04). Primary tour pin BETHS-02 (el-Araj) with on-panel note that et-Tell remains an alternate candidate — do not declare the debate settled. Blind-man healing (JM-19) attaches to Bethsaida tradition; feeding shore (JM-12) is nearby geography, not a second mandatory pan.
stops.narration:
Bethsaida sits on the Gospel map as a town of signs and family ties. Mark tells how Jesus healed a blind man there (Mark 8:22–26, LSB), and John says it was the hometown of some of the disciples, from fishing families who followed him (John 1:44, LSB). The Gospels place the town by the lake. But where exactly it stood is debated.

This tour visits el-Araj, where an excavation project has worked since 2014–2016. The team found Early Roman material from a Jewish fishing village, such as stone vessels and fishing weights. They also found a Roman bathhouse and a Byzantine church with an inscription tradition linked to Peter. First-century walls have been reported under the church's apse.

Many scholars think a spot right on the shore fits a fishing village better, and the team argues this is Bethsaida-Julias, known from the historian Josephus and the Gospels. The case is getting stronger, but it is not settled. Another site, et-Tell, is still seriously defended. This tour does not declare the debate over.

So at this stop, the question of the site is part of the story. Picture fishermen mending nets on the shore, wherever exactly their village stood, and a man whose eyes were opened nearby.
stops.contested_note: Bethsaida identification is contested (CBG-04): el-Araj (this pin, BETHS-02) vs et-Tell (BETHS-01). This tour does not declare the debate settled.

stops.panel_truth_line: Chorazin — a town that saw works and would not turn; yet the same chapter ends with Jesus' welcome: come to Me (Matthew 11).
stops.caveats: Basalt synagogue is later Roman/Byzantine fabric on the town site — fine as the named-town locus; do not call the standing synagogue ‘the building Jesus entered.’ Closing beat is privilege without repentance.
stops.narration:
This path ends with a hard word. Chorazin is one of the towns Jesus named in his warnings. Its people saw his mighty works but would not turn (Matthew 11:20–24, LSB). Privilege without repentance is empty.

Surveys took place here in 1905–1907 and 1926, major digs in 1962–1965, and conservation in the 1980s. Teams uncovered a basalt synagogue, mostly from the 200s–300s AD, with decorated benches and a carved "Seat of Moses." They found remains of the town, a ritual bath, and olive presses, all from a Jewish village of the Roman and Byzantine periods.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The town's name has carried on in this place, making it one of the clearest of the towns Jesus warned. Earlier settlement remains exist, but the famous dark stone synagogue is later than Jesus. So it marks the named town. It is not the building he entered.

The geography of these warnings is real. And they come from love, because love tells the truth.

Picture villagers who had seen healings with their own eyes, going back to life as usual. That is the danger this stop names. But in the same chapter, Jesus also gives an open invitation: come to me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28–30). The warning and the welcome come from the same love.

paths.title: Passover lamb to the Lamb of God
paths.theme: Exodus Passover geography into John's Lamb and the cross
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Goshen / Rameses — Passover instituted; a lamb's blood marks doors.
stops.narration:
This path follows one idea from Egypt to Jerusalem: the Passover lamb. It begins in the eastern Nile Delta, in the Pi-Ramesses and Qantir area. There, the Passover is first given. A lamb's blood marks the doors (Exodus 12:1–13, LSB).

Rescue begins with blood and a meal eaten in a hurry. That is Scripture's own pattern for Passover.

The evidence for this stop is mixed. It uses a general map of the route out of Egypt, not an exact dig. But the picture is vivid. Imagine families inside their homes on that night, sandals on their feet, ready to leave, trusting that the blood on the doorframe would keep them safe.

stops.panel_truth_line: Yam Suph — a delivered people walks free.
stops.narration:
The Passover leads to a passage. At Yam Suph, the sea, Yahweh opens a way, and his people walk through. The pursuers fall, and the rescued people stand on the far shore singing (Exodus 14:15–31, LSB). Exodus 12:46 (LSB) gives instructions about the Passover lamb that later readers will remember.

Where was the crossing? It is debated. This map uses a representative spot among the northeast Nile Delta lakes and the land bridge there. Others argue for the Gulf of Suez or the Gulf of Aqaba.

There are popular claims about chariot wheels under the water, such as those tied to Wyatt. We keep those claims out on purpose.

The evidence here is mixed. But the meaning is clear. The lamb's blood marked the night of rescue, and now the rescued people are free. Picture a crowd on the far side of the water, finally safe, singing.

stops.panel_truth_line: Sinai — redeemed people meet Yahweh in covenant.
stops.narration:
The rescued people come to Mount Sinai, also called Horeb, and meet Yahweh. He calls them his own treasured people (Exodus 19:1–6, LSB). Then the covenant is sealed with blood, as Moses sprinkles it and calls it the blood of the covenant (Exodus 24:3–8, LSB). That language will be deepened in the New Testament through Christ.

The traditional site is Jebel Musa, near St. Catherine in southern Sinai. But the exact location is debated, and the evidence for this stop is mixed.

On this path, Sinai is a key step. First there was the lamb, then the crossing, and now a covenant sealed with blood. Picture a people gathered at the foot of a mountain, promising together to do all that Yahweh has said.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — the Lamb enters history as a child.
stops.caveats: Birth geography; "Lamb" title is John's later proclamation.
stops.narration:
Years later, John the Baptist will point to Jesus and say: Look, the Lamb of God (John 1:29, LSB). But the story first gives him a town and a manger. In Bethlehem, the Lamb enters history as a child (Luke 2:1–20, LSB).

The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave long believed to be Jesus' birthplace, with buildings from the eras of Constantine and Justinian. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors. No clear first-century "manger house" layer has been published as a smoking gun.

The ground and the Bible line up well as tradition. Christians have honored a cave in Bethlehem since at least the 300s AD. Archaeology confirms that early pilgrim memory, not a census record or remains from the birth. The claim that Jesus was born in Bethlehem comes from the text, including Micah 5:2.

Remember, the title "Lamb" comes later, from John. Here there is only a baby. Picture shepherds coming in from the fields to see a child who would one day be called the Lamb.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — sacrifice world of Second Temple Jerusalem.
stops.narration:
Second Temple Jerusalem was a world of sacrifice. Early in his ministry, Jesus finds people selling animals in the temple courts and drives them out (John 2:13–17, LSB). In his last week, the day comes when the Passover lamb must be sacrificed, and he sends disciples to prepare the meal (Luke 22:7–13, LSB). Passover lambs and temple courts form the world Jesus walks into.

At Robinson's Arch, on the temple's western side, you can stand near that world. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later seasons on the Ophel and along the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, and giant stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70. They found Ophel walls, ritual baths for washing before worship, and grand stairways leading up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These were the routes pilgrims climbed at Passover. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Picture these steps thick with families at Passover, many with lambs, all heading up to the courts above.

stops.panel_truth_line: Golgotha — Christ our Passover is sacrificed.
stops.caveats: Crucifixion pin; empty tomb narrated without separate sepulchre ID.
stops.narration:
At Golgotha, also called Calvary, the path of the Passover lamb reaches its goal. John tells of the day of Jesus' death, the day of Preparation (John 19:31–36, LSB). Paul later writes that Christ our Passover has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7, LSB). Scripture itself makes this link. This tour does not invent it.

The traditional site in Jerusalem is commonly marked within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre area. Many Protestants honor another tradition at the Garden Tomb.

The ground and the Bible line up well on Jerusalem as the place. There is no separate stop for the tomb, so the empty tomb is told without naming a specific site.

Think back along this path: blood on doors in Egypt, a sea crossed, a covenant sealed, a baby in Bethlehem, lambs climbing the temple steps. Now it all comes to one hill outside the city, where the Lamb of God is sacrificed.

stops.panel_truth_line: Emmaus — risen Lord opens Moses and the Prophets.
stops.caveats: Debated village ID; Nicopolis tradition area.
stops.narration:
On the road to Emmaus, two sad followers meet a stranger. Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he explains everything the Scriptures say about himself. Only later, at the table, do they see that he is the risen Jesus (Luke 24:13–35; Luke 24:25–27, LSB). The Passover finds its "yes" in a living Lord.

Which village was Emmaus? That is debated. This stop uses the Emmaus Nicopolis tradition. Digs and surveys here began in the 1880s, with major church excavations in the 1900s and work off and on since. Teams found a Roman and Byzantine city, churches remembering the Luke 24 meeting, mosaics, and earlier settlement.

Other candidates include Motza or Qaloniyeh, el-Qubeibeh, and Abu Ghosh. Luke gives a distance of 60 stadia, but some manuscripts say 160. Nicopolis has a strong Byzantine pilgrim tradition. Archaeology shows a real town remembered as Emmaus, but not which village Luke meant.

So the place is uncertain. The point is not. Picture the stranger walking beside them, opening the old story of the Passover lamb, and their hearts burning as they finally understand. John the Baptist had already named him: the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). Peter adds that we are redeemed not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish (1 Peter 1:18–19).

paths.title: "Yahweh will provide" — Isaac's mount to Golgotha
paths.theme: Abraham/Isaac path to Golgotha (Hebrews' own typology)
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Ur — family origin before the call and the later test.
stops.caveats: Patriarchal chronology debated; beat is family origin.
stops.narration:
This path is about a son given, and it begins in a household Yahweh called out of Ur. Abram's family left Ur together (Genesis 11:31, LSB). Many years later, God tests Abraham by asking him to offer his son Isaac (Genesis 22:1–2, LSB).

From 1922 to 1934, the Joint Expedition to Ur, with Woolley, dug here. They found the Royal Cemetery, including the burial of Puabi. They uncovered the Great Ziggurat of Ur-Nammu, homes, and clay tablets. Woolley also found a layer of flood mud that he linked to Noah.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Ur was a major Sumerian city, fitting the tradition that Abraham came from Ur of the Chaldeans. Its ziggurat helps us picture the temple towers behind the Babel story. But Woolley's flood layer was a local flood, not proof of a worldwide one. Scholars also still debate exactly when the patriarchs lived.

On this path, Ur is simply where the family begins. Picture a great city with a towering temple, and a family leaving it all behind, not yet knowing the hardest test still lay ahead.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethel — Abraham's altar life before Moriah.
stops.narration:
Long before the hardest test, Abraham's life was full of altars. At Bethel he pitched his tent and built an altar to call on Yahweh's name (Genesis 12:8, LSB). Years later, God would ask him for something far harder, his son Isaac (Genesis 22:1–19, LSB). A life of altars prepared a man for a deeper obedience.

Most maps place Bethel at the mound near the village of Beitin. Albright and Kelso dug here in 1934, 1954, 1957, and 1960. They found Bronze and Iron Age remains, including religious and household objects that Kelso published. The link between Beitin and Bethel goes back to the explorer Robinson and to Albright.

The ground and the Bible line up well, with a caution. Beitin is the majority view, but other spots, such as near el-Bireh, have been suggested. No sign with the city's name has been found here. So we use this as the traditional dig site, not as a closed debate.

Picture Abraham stacking stones on a hilltop, praying in a simple camp. He did not know it yet, but each small act of worship was training his heart to trust Yahweh with everything.

stops.panel_truth_line: Beersheba — Gen 22 departure/return tradition geography.
stops.narration:
After the test on the mountain, Abraham and Isaac come back down, and Abraham returns to Beersheba and lives there (Genesis 22:19, LSB). The text ties the aftermath of that story to this place. The exact peak in the land of Moriah has no pin on our map. On the next stops, we will use the Jerusalem temple tradition, with care.

From 1969 to 1976, Tel Aviv University dug at Tel Beersheba. They found a planned Iron Age town with walls, storehouses, and a water system. They also found a horned altar that had been taken apart, its stones reused in a storehouse wall.

That altar matches the shape of altars in the Bible, and it fits the way Amos and the books of Kings criticize worship at Beersheba. The neat town plan fits a time when Judah's kings controlled the Negev.

But the evidence here is mixed for Abraham's story. The town is from the Iron Age, long after him. Still, picture a father and son walking home together across the dry southern land, both of them alive, both of them changed by what happened on the mountain.

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — patriarchal sojourn country on the way toward Moriah's land.
stops.caveats: Sojourn geography; not the altar peak.
stops.narration:
Abraham had lived for years near Hebron, by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 13:18, LSB). Now God tells him to take his only son, Isaac, whom he loves, and go to the land of Moriah to a mountain God will show him (Genesis 22:2, LSB). Abraham walks with Isaac toward that mountain.

On the ancient mound of Hebron, Tel Rumeida, digs took place in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, including huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. Ancient Hebron was a fortified city in the hills, fitting the setting of the patriarch stories, and it later became David's first capital. The cave of Machpelah lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has not been dug.

This is the country where Abraham lived and traveled. It is not the place of the altar. Picture the hill country stretching out ahead, and an old man and his son walking side by side, with a long silence between them.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jerusalem — Zion geography; 2 Chr 3:1 links Moriah to Temple mount tradition.
stops.caveats: Narrate as tradition, not GPS of Gen 22 altar. Exact Moriah peak: no pin.
stops.narration:
On the mountain, Isaac asks his father where the lamb is. Abraham answers that God will provide. At the last moment, God stops him and provides a ram, and Abraham names the place "Yahweh will provide" (Genesis 22:1–14, LSB). Centuries later, 2 Chronicles 3:1 (LSB) says Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah.

So Chronicles connects the name Moriah to the temple mount. We hold that as a tradition that grew in how the story was received, not as a measured location for the altar in Genesis 22. The exact peak has no pin.

In the City of David, Kenyon dug from 1961 to 1967. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers on the city's eastern slope.

As background, there was a large Iron Age settlement on this ridge known as David's city. How big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still debated. The evidence for this stop's Moriah link is mixed.

Picture the city on its hills, and the long memory that a father's trust and God's provision belonged somewhere near here.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple west — where sacrifice language lived in Jesus' day.
stops.narration:
In Jesus' day, the language of sacrifice lived on these temple approaches. The book of Hebrews looks back at Abraham's test and says Abraham reasoned that God was able to raise people even from the dead (Hebrews 11:17–19, LSB). John 3:16 (LSB) speaks of a God who so loved the world that he gave his only Son. The New Testament writers themselves draw the line forward from Isaac to Jesus.

Here at Robinson's Arch, on the western side of the temple platform, B. Mazar dug from 1968 to 1978. Later seasons followed on the Ophel and along the southwest corner. His teams found a street from Herod's time under the arch, giant stones that crashed down when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and great stairways up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well with these approaches. Worshipers climbed here to the place where sacrifices were offered every day. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Picture the smoke rising from the temple above, and remember a father on a mountain long ago who believed God would provide.

stops.panel_truth_line: Golgotha — the Son given; the Father who did not spare His own Son.
stops.narration:
The path of "Yahweh will provide" ends here. Paul writes that God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32, LSB). John 3:16 (LSB) says God so loved the world that he gave his only Son. Christians have long read Genesis 22 toward this hill, because Hebrews and the Gospels already teach of a Father who provides by giving the Son.

The traditional site of Golgotha, or Calvary, in Jerusalem is commonly marked within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre area. Many Protestants honor another tradition at the Garden Tomb.

The ground and the Bible line up well on Jerusalem as the place of the crucifixion.

Think back over this path. It began with a family leaving Ur, a life of altars, a long walk with a son, and a ram caught in a thicket. On Moriah, Isaac was spared. On this hill, the Father did not spare his own Son. Stand here and let that difference sink in.

paths.title: The sign of Jonah
paths.theme: Joppa → Nineveh → Passion/third-day geography Jesus named
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Joppa — Jonah flees from Yahweh's face.
stops.caveats: Port geography; sea/fish has no pin—narrate between stops.
stops.narration:
Yahweh tells Jonah to go to Nineveh. Instead, Jonah goes down to Joppa, finds a ship, and pays to sail the other way, running from Yahweh's presence (Jonah 1:1–3, LSB). The sea will teach him. Nineveh will hear him.

Joppa is today's Jaffa, an old port with many layers. Kaplan dug here from 1955 to 1974, and new projects by the Israel Antiquities Authority, UCLA, and others have continued since the 1990s. Earlier work found a Late Bronze gate with Egyptian inscriptions. Above it lie the remains of Iron Age, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman port cities. This is the harbor tied to Jonah's escape, and later to Peter's stories in Acts.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Joppa is confirmed as Jaffa, with harbor remains from the Bronze Age to Roman times.

What comes next, the storm and the great fish, has no pin on our map. So we tell it in words as we travel. Picture a prophet hurrying down to the docks, buying a ticket as far away as he can go, thinking he can outrun God.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nineveh — repentance at preaching.
stops.caveats: Assyrian capital dig; repentance beat is Scripture.
stops.narration:
After his time in the sea, Jonah finally goes to Nineveh and preaches. To everyone's surprise, the people believe God. From the king down, they turn from their evil ways, and God relents from the disaster he had warned of (Jonah 3:1–10, LSB). Jesus will later call this the sign his generation needs.

Layard dug at Nineveh from 1845 to 1851, and Rassam continued into the 1850s–1880s. They found Sennacherib's Southwest Palace, carved scenes of the siege of Lachish, giant winged guardian statues, and Ashurbanipal's library of clay tablets.

The ground and the Bible line up well in Assyria's history. Assyrian records and the Lachish carvings back up Sennacherib's 701 BC campaign against Judah (2 Kings 18–19). The libraries shed light on the world of Isaiah and Nahum, and Nineveh's fall in 612 BC matches what the prophets foresaw. During ISIS control of Mosul from 2014 to 2017, the site suffered documented destruction, and war halted the digging.

The dig shows Assyria's capital. The repentance comes from Scripture. Picture a vast and proud city stopping everything to listen to one reluctant foreign prophet.

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — Jesus teaches and approaches Passion; He names Jonah's sign.
stops.narration:
Some religious leaders ask Jesus for a sign. He says no sign will be given except the sign of the prophet Jonah. As Jonah was three days and three nights in the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matthew 12:38–41; Matthew 16:4, LSB).

The Mount of Olives is where Jesus teaches and from where he approaches his Passion. From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at Dominus Flevit on this hill. They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with bone boxes called ossuaries and tunnel-like tombs. Some inscriptions have been read as Christian, though those readings are debated. A Byzantine church here remembered Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows real Jewish burials on this hill in Jesus' time. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated.

There is something striking here. On a hillside full of tombs, Jesus speaks of being in the heart of the earth for three days. Picture him looking over the graves toward the city, knowing what that sign would cost.

stops.panel_truth_line: Golgotha — "heart of the earth" begins at the cross.
stops.narration:
Jesus said that the Son of Man would be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights, like Jonah (Matthew 12:40, LSB). At Golgotha, that journey begins. Matthew tells of the crucifixion and death of Jesus (Matthew 27:33–50, LSB). Jesus himself made the link to Jonah. Burial follows, and the third day is coming.

The traditional site of Golgotha, or Calvary, in Jerusalem is commonly marked inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre area. Many Protestants honor another tradition at the Garden Tomb.

The ground and the Bible line up well on Jerusalem as the place.

Jonah ran from God and was swallowed by the sea. Jesus walked straight toward this hill on purpose. Stand here and remember: the sign he promised was not a trick for the curious. It was his own death, and what would happen three days later.

stops.panel_truth_line: Emmaus — third-day appearance tradition.
stops.narration:
The sign of Jonah is fulfilled. On the third day, the women find the tomb empty and meet the risen Jesus (Matthew 28:1–10, LSB). That same day, two followers on the road to Emmaus walk with a stranger who turns out to be the Lord (Luke 24:13–35, LSB). The sign was never a fish story for curious minds. It is a risen Lord.

Which village was Emmaus? That is debated. This stop uses the Emmaus Nicopolis tradition. Work here began in the 1880s, with major church digs in the 1900s and more off and on since. Teams found a Roman and Byzantine city, churches remembering the Luke 24 meeting, mosaics, and earlier settlement.

Other candidates include Motza or Qaloniyeh, el-Qubeibeh, and Abu Ghosh. Luke says 60 stadia from Jerusalem, but some manuscripts say 160. Nicopolis has a strong Byzantine pilgrim tradition. Archaeology shows a real town remembered as Emmaus, but not which village Luke meant.

Picture the moment of recognition at the table. Three days earlier, all hope seemed buried. Now the sign has come true.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — Galilee base where "greater than Jonah" teaching landed.
stops.caveats: Ministry base; optional Judea close could be WW-01.
stops.narration:
In Galilee, Jesus told the crowds that the people of Nineveh would rise up at the judgment, because they repented at Jonah's preaching, and something greater than Jonah is here (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:29–32, LSB). The Galilee towns heard it first, and Capernaum was his base.

In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of Capernaum's white limestone synagogue. They recorded its architecture, which set up later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. The dig confirmed a grand synagogue ruin in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base. But the synagogue you see is later, from the 300s–400s AD. Whether an earlier first-century phase lies under its floors is debated.

This path has traveled from a fleeing prophet at Joppa, to a city that repented, to a cross and an empty tomb. It ends back where Jesus first spoke these words. Picture the people of this lakeside town hearing that Nineveh, a pagan city, listened better than they did. The question still hangs in the air, but it comes with good news. Jonah only preached; Jesus died and rose. His invitation is the one Peter gave: repent and return, so that your sins may be wiped away (Acts 3:19).

paths.title: Son of David — Bethlehem's shepherd-king to Zion's Son
paths.theme: Bethlehem/David's rise to Zion, then Jesus Son of David
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — David's town and Jesus' birth.
stops.narration:
This path follows a royal line, and it begins in a small town. In Bethlehem, the prophet Samuel anoints a shepherd boy named David (1 Samuel 16:1–13, LSB). Later the prophet Micah promises that a greater ruler will come from this same town (Micah 5:2, LSB), and Matthew tells how Jesus is born here (Matthew 2:1–6, LSB). David's town becomes Jesus' birthplace.

The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave long believed to be where Jesus was born, with building phases from the eras of Constantine and Justinian. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors. No clear first-century "manger house" layer has been published as a smoking gun.

The ground and the Bible line up well as tradition. Christians have honored a cave in Bethlehem since at least the 300s AD, and archaeology confirms that early memory. It has not found a census record or remains from the birth. The Bethlehem claim comes from the text. The digs show the shrine's history.

Picture a boy called in from the sheep to be anointed, and, centuries later, a baby born in the same town to be the greater Son.

stops.panel_truth_line: Gath — Philistine frontier (David/Goliath geography).
stops.caveats: Keep CBG-21 media-overclaim caution in panel, not as stop.
stops.narration:
In the valley, a young David faces the giant Goliath, a champion from the Philistine city of Gath, and wins (1 Samuel 17:1–50, LSB). The story makes David famous. Gath was on the Philistine frontier.

Bliss and Macalister first dug at Tell es-Safi in 1899. Since 1996, Maeir has led the Tell es-Safi/Gath Archaeological Project. The mound has many layers: Early Bronze walls, Middle and Late Bronze Canaanite remains, and an Iron Age Philistine city, the largest Philistine city footprint known. Teams also found a lower-city destruction from the 800s BC, often linked to the Aramean king Hazael, places of worship, and pottery with writing that includes names similar in sound to "Goliath."

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Most scholars agree this site is biblical Gath, one of the five main Philistine cities. But media claims that the pottery names the actual giant go too far. The site's identity is strong. The giant's name on a pot is not.

Stay with the Bible's own story. Picture a shepherd with a sling stepping out to face a warrior from this powerful city, trusting Yahweh rather than armor.

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — David reigns first over Judah.
stops.narration:
After King Saul dies, David asks Yahweh where to go. He is told to go up to Hebron, and there the men of Judah anoint him king. Years later, all the tribes of Israel come to Hebron and anoint him king over the whole nation (2 Samuel 2:1–4; 2 Samuel 5:1–5, LSB). Kingship comes in stages. Hebron first, Zion next.

On the ancient mound of Hebron, Tel Rumeida, digs took place in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, including huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. Ancient Hebron was a fortified city in the hill country. It fits the setting of the patriarch stories, and of David's first capital. The cave of Machpelah lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has not been dug.

This was Judah's capital before Jerusalem. Picture elders from every tribe streaming into this hill city to pledge their loyalty to the shepherd who had become a king.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — Zion; avoid treating CBG-22 "palace of David" as settled.
stops.caveats: Do not treat palace-of-David claims as settled.
stops.narration:
David captures the stronghold of Zion and calls it the City of David. He grows greater and greater, because Yahweh is with him (2 Samuel 5:6–10, LSB). Later, Isaiah promises a child who will sit on David's throne and rule forever (Isaiah 9:6–7, LSB). The prophets promise a throne that never ends.

From 1961 to 1967, Kenyon dug here on the Ophel and in the City of David. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge, the area known as David's city. But how big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still argued about, with some scholars seeing a small town and others a larger city.

Some say a large stone building here was David's palace. We do not treat that as settled. Picture instead a hilltop fortress becoming a king's city, and a promise that one day a Son of David would reign without end.

stops.panel_truth_line: Gihon — royal/anointing water geography memory.
stops.narration:
Below the City of David flows the spring of Gihon. The Bible remembers a royal moment connected with this spring in 1 Kings 1:32–40 (LSB). And at Hebron, the tribes recalled that Yahweh had told David he would shepherd his people Israel (2 Samuel 5:2, LSB). Memories of royal water belong to the shepherd-king's city.

From 1995 into the 2010s, the Reich–Shukron team dug around Gihon. They found the Spring Tower and other defenses guarding the water. They clarified the Siloam Tunnel, often called Hezekiah's Tunnel, and a channel called Channel II. They also found small clay seals called bullae, and in 2004 the Pool of Siloam from the Second Temple period.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. An inscription found in the tunnel in 1880, and studied by many teams since, matches the Bible's description of King Hezekiah bringing water into the city (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30).

Traditions of royal anointing cling to this spring area. Picture fresh water bubbling up at the foot of the hill, and the city of a shepherd-king growing up around it.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nazareth — "He will be called a Nazarene" upbringing.
stops.caveats: Modest archaeology; hometown of the Son of David.
stops.narration:
Matthew opens his Gospel by calling Jesus Christ the son of David (Matthew 1:1, LSB). Luke records the angel's promise that God will give him the throne of his father David (Luke 1:32–33, LSB). Yet the child grows up far from Bethlehem's fields, in Nazareth, and is called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:23, LSB).

In 2009, the Israel Antiquities Authority dug near the Marian Center in Nazareth. They found a first-century courtyard house, partly cut into rock and partly built, with storage pits and household features. It is one of the first well-published houses in Nazareth from Jesus' time.

The evidence is mixed but helpful. The dig shows Nazareth was a small Jewish village in the early first century, answering extreme claims that it did not exist then. But it does not identify the house as belonging to Jesus or Mary. It only shows that such houses stood when the Gospels say Jesus grew up there.

The finds are modest, and so was the town. Picture the heir of David's royal line growing up in a quiet village of simple courtyard homes, unnoticed by the powerful, while the promise waited.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — Son of David enters and teaches.
stops.narration:
As Jesus enters Jerusalem, the crowds shout praise and hail him as the Son of David (Matthew 21:9, LSB). Then he goes into the temple, drives out the buyers and sellers, and heals the blind and lame. Children in the temple courts take up the same cry, and the leaders are furious (Matthew 21:12–16, LSB). The city hears the royal title, and Jesus accepts it.

At Robinson's Arch, along the temple's western wall, you stand near the approaches he would have known. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, followed by later seasons on the Ophel and along the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, and massive stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70. They found Ophel walls, ritual baths, and broad stairways rising to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These were the real routes into the temple. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

This path began with a shepherd boy anointed in Bethlehem. Picture his greater Son now standing in the temple, with children singing his name.

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — triumphal approach / teaching facing Zion.
