stops.narration:
From the Mount of Olives, Jesus begins his royal approach to Jerusalem. The crowds spread their cloaks and praise God (Matthew 21:1–11, LSB). But as he comes near and sees the city, he weeps over it (Luke 19:37–44, LSB). From this hill he faces Zion as the Son of David, and as the One who will be rejected and raised.

From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at Dominus Flevit, on the slope of this hill. They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with ossuaries, or bone boxes, and tunnel-like tombs. Some inscriptions have been read as Christian, though those readings are debated. A Byzantine monastery and church here remembered Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows real Jewish burial customs on this hill in Jesus' time. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated, but the cemetery itself is real.

This is where the Son of David path ends. Picture the King looking out over the city of David, with cheering behind him and tears in his eyes, knowing both the throne and the cross lay ahead. The crowd's praise echoed Psalm 118:25–26, a prayer asking Yahweh to save. Yahweh had promised David a throne that would last forever (2 Samuel 7:16), and the angel told Mary her Son would reign on it with no end (Luke 1:32–33). This King came to save by giving himself.

paths.title: Lifted up — bronze serpent to the cross
paths.theme: Numbers 21 → John 3:14 typology Jesus authorizes
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Sinai / Horeb — covenant people formed before the wilderness judgment story.
stops.narration:
This path follows one strange object, a bronze serpent lifted up in the wilderness, all the way to the cross. It starts at Sinai, also called Horeb, where Yahweh gave his people the covenant and told them to have no other gods (Exodus 20:1–3, LSB). Later, on the road, comes the bronze serpent story, a story of judgment in the wilderness (Numbers 21:4–9, LSB).

The traditional site of the mountain is Jebel Musa, near St. Catherine in southern Sinai. But the exact location is debated, and the evidence for this stop is mixed.

The lesson to carry from here is simple. A people who received God's covenant still had to learn through failure on the road. Picture the crowd at the mountain making promises, not yet knowing how hard the journey ahead would be.

stops.panel_truth_line: Kadesh-barnea — wilderness failure/memory.
stops.narration:
Kadesh-barnea is a place of painful memory. It is where the spies came back from exploring the land (Numbers 13:26, LSB). Later, the people complained here about water, and even Moses failed in how he responded (Numbers 20:1–13, LSB). That memory of unbelief sits behind the bronze serpent story.

A possible location is Tell el-Qudeirat, near the border of northeast Sinai and the Negev. It is a candidate, and the evidence is mixed.

This was a wilderness station where the people waited, argued, and stumbled. Picture a camp in the desert, full of people tired of walking and tired of trusting. That is the mood that leads into the next stop.

stops.panel_truth_line: Punon — Num 33 station in copper district; classic association zone for bronze-serpent narrative geography.
stops.caveats: Num 21 locale not GPS-certain — narrate honestly. Not "the pole found."
stops.narration:
Numbers lists Punon as one of the camps on Israel's wilderness journey (Numbers 33:42–43, LSB). It lies in a copper-mining district, and people have long associated this area with the bronze serpent story (Numbers 21:4–9, LSB). The region is the approach to Edom and Moab, between the Arabah valley and Transjordan, in the area known as Faynan.

But be honest about what we know. The exact place of the Numbers 21 story is not certain. Copper country gives context. It is not a relic claim. No one has found "the pole."

The evidence is mixed. Still, it is striking to stand in a land known for copper and think of a serpent made of bronze. Picture a weary people in rocky, metal-rich hills, and a story about looking up to live.

stops.panel_truth_line: Timna Valley — regional copper-working context (supporting).
stops.caveats: Supporting copper context, not the serpent pole dig.
stops.narration:
Numbers 21:8–9 (LSB) says Moses made a serpent of bronze and put it on a pole. Timna Valley helps explain bronze as a real material in this region.

From 1959 to 1990, Rothenberg led the Timna Expedition. Since 2013, Ben-Yosef has led the Central Timna Valley Project. Teams found a Late Bronze Egyptian temple to the goddess Hathor, mining camps, and smelting sites. They also found a painted pottery called Qurayyah Painted Ware, often called "Midianite" pottery, spanning the Late Bronze and early Iron Ages. New radiocarbon dating by Ben-Yosef shifts the peak of copper production to the early Iron Age, while keeping the Late Bronze Egyptian presence.

The evidence is mixed in a specific way. This is mining archaeology for the Bible's lands of the Arabah, Midian, and Edom. It is not the town called Timnah in Judah, which is a different site. The Egyptian presence and the Midianite pottery are the hooks to the Bible. The dating of peak production is debated and has been revised.

This is supporting context, not a serpent-pole dig, and not a sensational find. Picture furnaces glowing in a desert valley, turning green rock into shining metal.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nebo approach — edge of the land before entry.
stops.narration:
The wilderness road ends on a mountain. After all the failures and the bronze serpent story (Numbers 21:4–9, LSB), Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and Yahweh shows him the whole land he promised (Deuteronomy 34:1–4, LSB).

Today you can stand at the Mount Nebo memorial in Jordan, on the Pisgah ridge. This is the traditional viewpoint, and the geography and the Bible fit well here.

Think back over this path: a covenant at Sinai, painful memories at Kadesh, copper hills, and a serpent of bronze lifted up so that people could look and live. Now the road ends looking toward promise. Picture Moses, old and tired, gazing out over the land, at the edge of everything God had promised.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — Nicodemus's Jerusalem world (John 3).
stops.narration:
One night in Jerusalem, a teacher named Nicodemus comes to talk with Jesus. Jesus tells him that as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes may have eternal life (John 3:1–16, LSB). The old wilderness story suddenly points to something new.

At Robinson's Arch, on the temple's western side, we stand in Nicodemus' Jerusalem. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later seasons on the Ophel and work at the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, and huge cut stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70. They found Ophel walls, ritual baths, and grand stairways up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. This was the busy religious center where a leader like Nicodemus lived and worked. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Picture these streets quiet after dark, and a respected teacher slipping away to ask Jesus his questions, then hearing about a serpent, a pole, and a Son lifted up.

stops.panel_truth_line: Golgotha — the Son lifted up.
stops.narration:
Jesus said the Son of Man must be lifted up, like the serpent in the wilderness, so that whoever believes may have life (John 3:14–16, LSB). Later he said that when he is lifted up from the earth, he will draw all people to himself, showing the kind of death he would die (John 12:32–33, LSB). Jesus himself made this link, and it ends here: look to the lifted Son and live.

The traditional site of Golgotha, or Calvary, in Jerusalem is commonly marked inside the Church of the Holy Sepulchre area. Many Protestants honor another tradition at the Garden Tomb.

The ground and the Bible line up well on Jerusalem as the place of the crucifixion.

This path began at a mountain in the desert and wound through places of failure and copper hills. In the wilderness, people looked at a bronze serpent on a pole. Here, the Son of God is lifted up on a cross. Stand still, look up, and remember the invitation: look and live.

paths.title: Priest-king of Salem — Melchizedek to our great High Priest
paths.theme: Genesis 14; Psalm 110; Hebrews 7 — Salem/Jerusalem geography
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — Abraham's sojourn country (Gen 14 war context nearby).
stops.narration:
This path is about a mysterious figure: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High. It begins in Abraham's home country around Hebron. Genesis 14:13–16 (LSB) tells how Abram hears that his relative has been captured in a war, gathers his men, and rescues him. On the way back from battle, he will meet Melchizedek. The exact spot of that meeting has no pin on our map.

On the ancient mound of Hebron, Tel Rumeida, digs took place in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, including huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. Ancient Hebron was a fortified hill city, fitting the setting of the patriarch stories, and it later became David's first capital. The cave of Machpelah lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has not been dug.

This is the country where Abraham lived as a traveler. Picture him returning tired from battle, with rescued family and recovered goods, about to meet a king who would bless him.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — Salem / Zion geography (tradition).
stops.caveats: Salem/Jerusalem tradition pins + caveat; no Melchizedek dig.
stops.narration:
Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, comes out with bread and wine and blesses Abram (Genesis 14:18–20, LSB). Psalm 76:2 (LSB) uses the name Salem alongside Zion, which is why many link Salem with Jerusalem.

That link is a tradition, and we hold it with care. There is no Melchizedek dig.

In the City of David, the oldest part of Jerusalem, Kenyon dug from 1961 to 1967. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

As background, there was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge known as David's city. How big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still debated. For Melchizedek himself, the evidence is mixed, because Genesis is the only source.

Still, picture a king who is also a priest, walking out to meet a weary traveler, carrying bread and wine, and speaking a blessing in the name of God Most High. Then he steps off the page as quietly as he came.

stops.panel_truth_line: Gihon — ancient Jerusalem water heart.
stops.narration:
Psalm 110:4 (LSB) contains a striking promise. Yahweh swears that a coming king will be a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek. Zion's ancient water lies beneath that priestly language.

The spring of Gihon was the water heart of ancient Jerusalem. From 1995 into the 2010s, the Reich–Shukron team dug here. They found the Spring Tower and other defenses guarding the spring. They clarified the Siloam Tunnel, often called Hezekiah's Tunnel, and a channel known as Channel II. They found small clay seals called bullae, and in 2004 they uncovered the Pool of Siloam from the Second Temple period.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. An inscription found in the tunnel in 1880, studied by many teams since, matches the Bible's description of King Hezekiah bringing water into the city (2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:30).

On this path, Gihon reminds us that Zion was a real city with real needs. Picture the water rising at the foot of the hill, flowing on through the ages, as the psalm's promise of a forever priest waited to be fulfilled.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple west — Second Temple priesthood world.
stops.narration:
The book of Hebrews picks up Psalm 110 and says that Jesus is a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 5:5–10, LSB). It describes Melchizedek as king of righteousness and king of peace, without a recorded beginning or end, made like the Son of God (Hebrews 7:1–3, LSB). Hebrews reads a forever priest in Melchizedek's line, fulfilled in Jesus.

At Robinson's Arch, along the western side of the temple platform, we stand in the world of Second Temple priests. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later seasons on the Ophel and along the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, giant cut stones that fell when Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and great stairways leading up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Priests and worshipers used these approaches every day. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Look at those fallen stones. The temple priesthood ended with them. Hebrews points to a priest whose service never ends.

stops.panel_truth_line: Western Wall Tunnels — temple mount western approaches.
stops.narration:
Hebrews explains why Jesus is a different kind of priest. The earlier priests were many, because death kept stopping them from continuing. But Jesus lives forever, so he holds his priesthood permanently (Hebrews 7:23–28, LSB). He has entered behind the curtain as a forerunner for us, a high priest forever like Melchizedek (Hebrews 6:19–20, LSB).

Under the city, along the temple's western side, run the Western Wall Tunnels. Warren explored shafts here in 1867–1870, and the tunnel system has been dug since 1967. Teams exposed the huge cut stones from Herod's era in the temple's supporting wall, its underground continuation to the north, a first-century street with shops, the area of Warren's Gate, and massive blocks including the "Western Stone."

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The temple platform Jesus' disciples admired in Mark 13 is physically present. The size of the stones matches the historian Josephus and the Gospels' talk of great stones. That does not prove Jesus' words about destruction, but it shows what they saw. The platform itself is off-limits to dig teams under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf.

Picture priests coming and going for generations, each one serving for a time, until a priest came who serves forever.

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — priest-king who suffers then is exalted.
stops.narration:
Hebrews describes the high priest we need: holy, innocent, set apart from sinners, and raised higher than the heavens (Hebrews 7:26–28, LSB). Acts tells how, from the Mount of Olives, Jesus was taken up into heaven while his followers watched (Acts 1:9–11, LSB). Our great High Priest is no mythic idea. He walked these ridges, suffered, and was raised up.

From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at Dominus Flevit, on the slope of this hill. They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with ossuaries, or bone boxes, and tunnel-like tombs. Some inscriptions have been read as Christian, but those readings are debated. A Byzantine church here remembered Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows real Jewish burials on this hill in Jesus' time, the landscape of Gethsemane and the Ascension tradition. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated.

This path began with a mysterious priest-king meeting Abraham. It ends where Jesus, the priest-king who suffered, rose into heaven. Picture his followers staring up at the sky over this hill, then going back to the city with a priest who lives forever. Hebrews draws out the comfort: because he lives forever, he is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him (Hebrews 7:25). That rests on Yahweh's sworn word (Psalm 110:4), and it still stands.

paths.title: The Good Shepherd — from Bethlehem's fields to the door of the sheep
paths.theme: David shepherd → Ezek 34 → John 10 → cross
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — David's town & Messiah's birth.
stops.narration:
This path follows the image of a shepherd. It begins in Bethlehem, where young David is called in from keeping the sheep and anointed by Samuel (1 Samuel 16:11–13, LSB). Centuries later, a greater Shepherd is born here. Jesus will say: I am the good shepherd (John 10:11, LSB).

The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave long believed to be Jesus' birthplace, with buildings from the eras of Constantine and Justinian. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors. No clear first-century "manger house" layer has been published as a smoking gun.

The ground and the Bible line up well as tradition. Christians have honored a cave in Bethlehem since at least the 300s AD, and archaeology confirms that early pilgrim memory. It has not found a census record or remains from the birth. The Bethlehem claim, including Micah 5:2, comes from the text, while the digs show the shrine's history.

Picture the fields around a small town, a boy with his flock being called home to be anointed, and, long after, another birth in the same town that would change everything.

stops.panel_truth_line: Tel Dan Stele — extrabiblical "House of David" witness (museum object).
stops.caveats: language-careful wording on House of David consensus; museum object.
stops.narration:
This stop is a stone in a museum. It is made of broken pieces of a monument from the 800s BC, found at Tel Dan in northern Israel and written in Aramaic. The inscription refers to the "House of David." Most scholars read it that way, and it is a key witness outside the Bible to David's royal family in Judah.

At Hebron, the tribes remembered that Yahweh had told David he would shepherd his people Israel and be their leader (2 Samuel 5:2, LSB).

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone was set up by an enemy king, not a friend. Even enemies' stone remembered David's house. That helps show that Scripture's shepherd-king was not a late invention.

We still use careful words about exactly what the stone says, since scholars discuss the wording. But picture a proud foreign king carving his victories in stone, and in the middle of his boasting, naming the family of the shepherd from Bethlehem.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — shepherd-king's Zion.
stops.narration:
David, the shepherd from Bethlehem, became king in Zion. Yahweh had said he would shepherd Israel (2 Samuel 5:2, LSB). But many of Israel's later leaders were bad shepherds. So Ezekiel brings a promise: Yahweh himself will search for his sheep, gather them, and care for them (Ezekiel 34:11–16, LSB).

In the City of David, Kenyon dug from 1961 to 1967. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge known as David's city. How big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still debated, with some scholars thinking small and others thinking larger.

Some people claim a building here was David's palace, but we do not overclaim that. Picture this ridge as the shepherd-king's city. Then hear the prophet's surprising promise that one day God himself would come to shepherd his people.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — Jesus' ministry base where shepherd teaching lands in Galilee life.
stops.narration:
In Galilee, Jesus made Capernaum his base (Matthew 4:13, LSB). He taught that he is the good shepherd. His sheep hear his voice, and he lays down his life for them (John 10:1–18, LSB). The sheep heard his voice in ordinary days by the lake.

In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of Capernaum's white limestone synagogue. They recorded its architecture, preparing the way for later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well here as background. The dig confirmed a grand synagogue ruin in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base. But the synagogue you see is a later building, from the 300s–400s AD. Whether a first-century phase lies under its floors is debated. So we call this his teaching base, without claiming these exact walls.

Picture fishing boats coming in, families going about their day, and a teacher whose voice people learned to know and trust, like sheep who know their shepherd.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethany — the shepherd who raises the dead (Lazarus).
stops.narration:
In Bethany, Lazarus has died, and his sisters are grieving. Jesus comes to the tomb and calls him by name, and the dead man comes out (John 11:1–44, LSB). Jesus had said: I am the good shepherd (John 10:11, LSB). Here the shepherd calls a dead man by name.

This stop is the miracle pin at Bethany. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

On a path about the Good Shepherd, this may be the most powerful moment. A shepherd knows each sheep by name. Picture a crowd standing around a sealed tomb, the stone rolled away, and a single voice calling a friend's name, and that friend walking out alive.

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — shepherd struck / flock scattered night.
stops.narration:
On the night he is arrested, Jesus tells his disciples they will all fall away, quoting the prophet: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Zechariah 13:7; Mark 14:27, LSB). And it happens. But the story does not end there. He gathers them again.

This is the Mount of Olives, the landscape of Gethsemane. From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at Dominus Flevit on its slope. They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with ossuaries, or bone boxes, and tunnel-like tombs. Some inscriptions have been read as Christian, though those readings are debated. A Byzantine church here remembered Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows real Jewish burial customs on this hill in Jesus' time. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated, but the cemetery is real.

Picture the dark hillside, the arrest coming closer, and frightened disciples running in every direction. The shepherd is struck. The sheep scatter. Yet he already knows he will bring them back together.

stops.panel_truth_line: Golgotha — lays down His life for the sheep.
stops.narration:
The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11, LSB). And the God of peace brought him up from the dead, the great Shepherd of the sheep (Hebrews 13:20, LSB). He lays down his life, and he takes it up again.

The traditional site of Golgotha, or Calvary, in Jerusalem is commonly marked within the Church of the Holy Sepulchre area. Many Protestants honor another tradition at the Garden Tomb.

The ground and the Bible line up well on Jerusalem as the place of the crucifixion.

This path began in Bethlehem's fields, with a shepherd boy anointed. It passed a stone naming David's house, a lakeside town, a tomb in Bethany, and a dark night on the Mount of Olives. Now it ends here. Most shepherds risk their lives for their sheep. This Shepherd gave his life on purpose, and then rose as the great Shepherd who leads his flock forever.

paths.title: Glory in the house — dedication memory to Jesus' temple confrontations
paths.theme: 1 Kgs 8 glory → Jesus cleanses His Father's house
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Shiloh — earlier dwelling of Yahweh's name.
stops.narration:
This path follows the glory of God's house, and it starts with a warning. Long ago, Shiloh was where Yahweh's name dwelt, and families came here to worship each year (1 Samuel 1:3, LSB). Centuries later, Jeremiah told the people of Jerusalem to go and look at Shiloh and see what happened to it, because they treated the temple like a lucky charm (Jeremiah 7:12–14, LSB).

Danish teams dug here in the 1920s and 1930s, Finkelstein in 1981–1984, and the ABR team since 2017. They found Iron I religious and storage remains, deposits of animal bones, walls, and later remains. ABR has claimed finds related to the tabernacle, but those claims are debated among scholars.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Shiloh shows significant activity in the Iron I period, fitting the tradition of a sanctuary in Samuel's day. The exact tabernacle has not been proven, and scholars discuss destruction layers in light of Jeremiah's words.

So Shiloh becomes a lesson. A holy place does not protect people who ignore the God it honors. Picture these quiet hills, once busy with worshipers, and a prophet pointing to them as a warning.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — ark/temple approach history.
stops.narration:
Glory's path into Jerusalem runs through David's city. First David brings the ark up to Zion with music and joy (2 Samuel 6:12–17, LSB). Later Solomon brings the ark into the new temple, and a cloud fills the house of Yahweh (1 Kings 8:1–11, LSB).

In the City of David, Kenyon dug from 1961 to 1967. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge known as David's city. But how big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still argued over, with some scholars seeing a small town and others a larger city.

Some say a large building here was David's palace. We do not overclaim that. Instead, picture a procession winding up this ridge, first with David dancing, later with priests carrying the ark into a temple filled with glory.

stops.panel_truth_line: Southern Temple Mount — dedication / teaching / confrontation geography.
stops.caveats: Herodian west as Second Temple approaches.
stops.narration:
When Solomon dedicated the temple, the glory of Yahweh filled the house so the priests could not stand to serve. Solomon said he had built a lofty house for Yahweh to dwell in (1 Kings 8:10–13, LSB). Centuries later, in that same place, Jesus cleared the temple courts. When challenged, he spoke of the temple being destroyed and raised up in three days, and John explains he was talking about his body (John 2:13–22, LSB).

At Robinson's Arch, on the temple's western side, you stand by the approaches to the temple of Jesus' day. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later seasons on the Ophel and at the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, giant stones thrown down when Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and grand stairways rising to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These are real Second Temple approaches. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Look at the fallen stones. The stone house was torn down. Jesus pointed to a temple that would rise again.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pilgrimage Road — pilgrim ascent to the house He cleanses.
stops.narration:
As Jesus enters the temple, he overturns the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. He says God's house should be a house of prayer, but they have made it a den of robbers (Mark 11:15–18; Matthew 21:12–13, LSB). Zeal for his Father's house consumes him.

Since the 1990s, with major sections uncovered in the 2000s and 2010s, archaeologists in the City of David have exposed a grand stepped street. Paved in the Early Roman period, it climbs from the Siloam area toward the Temple Mount. Shops lined it, and a drainage channel ran underneath. Coins found under the paving, including some from Pontius Pilate's time, date its construction to about AD 30–40s.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. This street shows the pilgrim route and city life of Jerusalem in the lifetimes of Jesus and the apostles. The coins place it in the years of Pilate or Agrippa. It does not prove any single Gospel walk, but it is a real street that pilgrims used.

Picture the crowd climbing this road toward the temple, with traders and animals and noise everywhere, and then the shock when word spreads that a man from Galilee has turned over the tables.

stops.panel_truth_line: Siloam — water/festival context tied to the temple city.
stops.narration:
On the last day of a great feast, Jesus stands up in the temple city and cries out: if anyone is thirsty, let him come to me and drink, and rivers of living water will flow from within (John 7:37–38, LSB). Later he sends a man born blind to wash in the Pool of Siloam, and the man comes back seeing (John 9:1–11, LSB). Talk of living water belongs to the feast and the temple city together.

In 2004–2005, the Reich–Shukron team uncovered a large pool at Siloam, at a spot called Birkat el-Hamra, with more exposure work in the 2020s. It is stepped and plastered, from the late Second Temple or Early Roman period, with a stone plaza to the north and stairs leading down into the water. Work continues with the Israel Antiquities Authority and the City of David.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The pool fits John's account of the blind man washing. It does not prove the miracle, but it shows a large public pool stood here in Jesus' time, very likely used by pilgrims for ritual washing.

Archaeology and daily life collide here too. In March 2008, Israel's High Court of Justice briefly halted a dig in Silwan near the pool after residents said work ran under their homes without proper notice. Picture festival crowds at these steps, and a voice offering water that never runs dry.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethesda — Sheep Gate pools near temple north.
stops.narration:
North of the temple, near the Sheep Gate, lay the Pools of Bethesda. Here Jesus found a man who had been sick for thirty-eight years and told him to get up and walk (John 5:1–9, LSB). Mercy at the pools sat right beside the arguments and judgment of the temple courts.

People discovered this complex near St. Anne's Church in the 1800s. Major digs followed from the 1870s to the 1960s, and study continues. Teams found two pools with covered walkways, phases of a healing shrine, and a later Roman healing temple, though that last idea is debated. A Byzantine church was built to remember the miracle, and there were water works from the Second Temple and Early Roman periods.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. John describes a pool with five porticoes near the Sheep Gate, and a real complex of several basins fits that. The exact design of the "five porticoes," and the miracle itself, remain matters of interpretation. But archaeology confirms a major pool site right where John places the healing.

On this path about glory in God's house, picture a quiet act of mercy just outside the temple's walls, done for a man everyone else had passed by.

stops.panel_truth_line: Olivet — Jesus weeps over the city / speaks temple judgment.
stops.narration:
As Jesus comes near Jerusalem, he weeps over it, because the city does not recognize the time of God's visit (Luke 19:41–44, LSB). Later, his disciples point out the temple's huge stones and buildings. Jesus tells them that not one stone will be left on another (Mark 13:1–2, LSB). Someone greater than the house is here.

From 1953 to 1955, archaeologists dug at Dominus Flevit on the Mount of Olives. They found a large Jewish cemetery from the late Second Temple period, with ossuaries, or bone boxes, and tunnel-like tombs. Some inscriptions have been read as Christian, though those readings are debated. A Byzantine monastery and church here remembered Jesus weeping over Jerusalem.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig shows real Jewish burials on this hill in Jesus' time. Claims about Christian ossuaries are often overstated, but the cemetery is real.

This path began at Shiloh, a sanctuary that became a warning. It ends here, with Jesus looking at the glorious temple and weeping. Picture the gleaming buildings across the valley, and the One who truly filled God's house grieving for a city that missed him. Yet his tears were not the end. Jesus spoke of the temple of his body, raised in three days (John 2:19–21), and he said he came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). God's glory is found in him, and his welcome is still open.

paths.title: Naaman the Syrian — wash and worship
paths.theme: 2 Kings 5 — Gentile commander healed; confesses Yahweh (NOT Haman)
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Damascus hub — Naaman's Aram/Damascus world (trade hub marker, not a dig).
stops.caveats: Trade hub, not a dig. No Damascus dig pin. DGAM Syria authority-only caveat. Abana/Pharpar: narrate only, no pins.
stops.narration:
Naaman is a great commander of the army of Aram, the kingdom around Damascus. He is also sick with a skin disease. A young servant girl from Israel tells his household about a prophet in Samaria who could heal him, and he sets out (2 Kings 5:1–5, LSB). Pride is about to meet the waters of the Jordan.

This stop marks Damascus as a trade hub on our map, standing for Naaman's world. It is not a dig, and there is no Damascus dig pin. The evidence for this stop is mixed.

Later in the story, Naaman will brag about the rivers of his homeland, the Abana and the Pharpar. We name them here in words only, without map pins.

Picture a powerful, proud man with everything except health, packing silver and gold and fine clothes, setting off to find a cure in a land he looked down on.

stops.panel_truth_line: Samaria — letter to the king; prophet's city (2 Kgs 5).
stops.caveats: OT Samaria dig; Elisha city geography.
stops.narration:
Naaman arrives in Samaria with a letter for the king of Israel, asking him to heal the commander. The king tears his clothes in panic, thinking it is a trick to start a war. But the prophet Elisha sends word: let him come to me (2 Kings 5:5–8, LSB).

Samaria was Israel's capital. The Harvard Expedition dug here in 1908–1910, more digs followed in 1931–1935, and others off and on since. Under the later city lies the Iron Age capital of the Old Testament. On top, the Roman city of Sebaste had a temple to Augustus built by Herod, a forum, a stadium, and a basilica. That later city was the stage for Philip's preaching in Acts 8.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. Sebaste shows how Herod and Rome turned Samaria into a pagan capital. That is a different place from the village well at Sychar, near Shechem, in John 4. Acts 8's mission fits a real city here.

For Naaman's story, this was the city of the prophet. Picture a frightened king with a torn robe, and a calm message from Elisha that changes everything.

stops.panel_truth_line: Elisha — Abel-meholah / Jordan-valley call geography (context).
stops.caveats: Prophet's Jordan-valley call geography as context.
stops.narration:
When Naaman comes to Elisha's door, the prophet does not even come out. He sends a messenger: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and you will be clean (2 Kings 5:8–10, LSB). A prophet's word, not palace gold, will heal.

Elisha himself had been called years earlier, when Elijah found him plowing and threw his cloak over him (1 Kings 19:16–21, LSB). Elisha came from Abel-meholah, in the Jordan Valley region where he was called. This stop marks that area as context.

The evidence for this stop is mixed, and the place is approximate. But it helps us see that Elisha was a man of the Jordan Valley, and now he sends a proud foreigner to the river in his own home region.

Picture Naaman waiting with his horses and chariots at a simple door, expecting a grand ceremony, and getting only a short message about a muddy river instead.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jordan crossing approach / Gilgal — Jordan wash geography (seven dips).
stops.caveats: Exact ford unconfirmed — narrate as river approach. NOT Haman.
stops.narration:
At first Naaman is furious. But his servants persuade him to try. So he goes down and dips seven times in the Jordan, as the prophet said, and his flesh is restored like the skin of a little child (2 Kings 5:10–14, LSB). Much later, Jesus names Naaman as a sign of God's mercy reaching beyond Israel (Luke 4:27, LSB).

This stop is the approach to the river, in the Jordan Valley west of Jericho, where several candidates for Gilgal lie. The exact spot where Naaman washed is not known. So we tell the story as a river approach, not a confirmed ford. The evidence is mixed.

Picture a great commander stepping into a muddy river while his soldiers watch. Once. Twice. Seven times. Then he looks down at his skin and sees it new, like a child's. The proud man had to become humble to be healed.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jericho — Jordan Valley city near river approach (supporting geography).
stops.caveats: Supporting geography near the river approach.
stops.narration:
Healed at last, Naaman goes back to Elisha with a new confession (2 Kings 5:14–15, LSB). Jericho lies near this river approach in the Jordan Valley, and here it serves as supporting geography.

From 1930 to 1936, Garstang dug at Jericho. He found city walls and destruction debris that he dated to about 1400 BC and linked to Joshua. Earlier work had found a Neolithic stone tower, and there are Bronze Age town remains.

But be careful: this is debated. Later, Kenyon redated the main destruction to earlier, in the Middle Bronze Age, and found little of a Late Bronze city. That dating dispute is still discussed.

Politics have shaped the digging too. An Italian-Palestinian team from Sapienza University records that its autumn 2000 fieldwork at Tell es-Sultan was interrupted by the severe political situation during the Intifada, and work stopped into the mid-2000s before joint digs returned.

For Naaman, Jericho is simply a landmark near the river. Picture him passing this ancient city on his way back up the road, healed, eager to thank the prophet.

stops.panel_truth_line: Elisha Samaria — return / confession: no God in all the earth except in Israel.
stops.caveats: Confession beat; earth for Yahweh request. Naaman—not Haman.
stops.narration:
Naaman returns to Elisha and stands before him with a confession: now I know there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. He asks for a load of earth to take home, so he can worship Yahweh alone (2 Kings 5:15–19, LSB). Jesus later remembers him (Luke 4:27, LSB). A Gentile finds healing, and he finds Yahweh.

This stop is in Samaria, the prophet's city. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

This is the heart of this path. Naaman came proud, rich, and sick. He leaves humble, healed, and worshiping the true God. Picture a foreign general loading dirt onto mules to carry back to Damascus, so that even in a far country he could stand on ground that reminded him of the God who made him clean. Jesus would later touch and cleanse lepers himself (Matthew 8:2–3), and John writes that his blood cleanses us from all sin (1 John 1:7). The cleansing Naaman found is offered to every nation in Jesus.

paths.title: Ruth the Moabitess — under Yahweh's wings
paths.theme: Ruth 1–4 — Moabite widow clings to Yahweh; enters Messiah's line
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Plains of Moab — Moab geography east of the Jordan.
stops.narration:
The story of Ruth starts with a family leaving home. During a famine, a man from Bethlehem in Judah takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to live in Moab. There, the man dies, and later both sons die too (Ruth 1:1–5, LSB). A Judean family goes to Moab and tastes death.

This stop marks the plains of Moab, in the lower Jordan Valley east of Jericho, along the Sweimeh and Shittim corridor. The evidence for this stop is mixed, and it is general geography.

Picture three women left alone in a foreign land: Naomi, far from home, and her two Moabite daughters-in-law. One of them is Ruth. Their story is about to turn on a single choice.

stops.panel_truth_line: Dibon — Moabite city (Mesha findspot region).
stops.narration:
Ruth's story is set partly in Moab, a real people with real towns (Ruth 1:1–7, LSB). It is not a parable without a map. Dibon was one of Moab's cities.

ASOR teams dug at Dibon in 1950–1953, with later seasons and new work in the 2000s. They found Moabite walls and Iron Age buildings. This is also the region where the Mesha Stele was found in 1868, though not by these digs.

The evidence is mixed but rich. On that stone, Mesha, king of Moab, names Omri, Israel, Yahweh, and towns in a conflict that parallels 2 Kings 3. It is a rare royal witness from Moab that overlaps with the book of Kings. The digs give the city context.

Picture Naomi deciding to leave Moab and go home to Bethlehem, and her two daughters-in-law setting out with her from a land of walled towns like this one.

stops.panel_truth_line: Mesha Stele — Moabite inscription naming YHWH/Israel (Louvre object).
stops.caveats: 2 Kgs 3 backdrop—not Ruth's century claim. Museum object.
stops.narration:
At the edge of Moab, Ruth makes one of the most famous promises in the Bible. She tells Naomi: where you go, I will go, your people will be my people, and your God my God (Ruth 1:16–17, LSB).

This stop is an object now in the Louvre: the Mesha Stele. It is a basalt stone set up by Mesha, king of Moab, reporting his conflict with Israel. It is a major witness from the Iron Age outside the Bible, and it names Yahweh.

The evidence for linking it to Ruth is mixed. The stone is not about Ruth. But it shows that even a Moabite king's stone remembered Israel and the name of Yahweh.

Think about that. A Moabite king carved Yahweh's name in stone as an enemy. A Moabite woman named Ruth spoke of Yahweh as her own God. Picture her standing at the crossroads, choosing a people and a God that were not her own.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — fields / gleaning / marriage geography (Ruth 1–4).
stops.caveats: No Boaz-house pin—city pin carries the beat.
stops.narration:
Ruth keeps her promise. She comes to Bethlehem with Naomi, saying your people will be my people and your God my God (Ruth 1:16–17, LSB). In Bethlehem's fields she gleans grain, and Boaz blesses her as one who has come to take refuge under the wings of Yahweh (Ruth 2:12, LSB). In the end she marries Boaz and has a son, and the family line leads to King David (Ruth 4:13–22, LSB).

There is no map pin for Boaz's house, so the town itself carries this part of the story. Today, Bethlehem's most famous site is the Church of the Nativity, built in the eras of Constantine and Justinian over a cave long linked to Jesus' birth. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors.

The ground and the Bible line up well as tradition. Christians have honored the cave since at least the 300s AD, and archaeology confirms that early memory, not anything from the birth itself.

But on this path, picture an older Bethlehem: grain fields at harvest, a foreign widow gathering leftover grain, and a kind landowner noticing her faith.

stops.panel_truth_line: Hebron — Judah hill-country context (David-line bridge).
stops.narration:
The book of Ruth ends with a family list. It traces the line from Perez down to Boaz, then to Obed, Jesse, and finally David (Ruth 4:18–22, LSB). Judah's hills will carry the line forward.

Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, is a bridge on this path toward David. On its ancient mound, Tel Rumeida, digs took place in 1984–1986 and in later seasons from the 1990s into the 2010s. Teams found Bronze and Iron Age walls and homes, including huge Middle Bronze stone walls reported in phases.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. Ancient Hebron was a fortified city in the hills. It fits the setting of the patriarch stories, and it became David's first capital. The cave of Machpelah lies under a monument built in Herod's style and has not been dug.

This is an optional stop, linking Ruth's family to David's rise. Picture the line of names in Ruth's last chapter turning into real people walking these hills, generation after generation, until a king from that family is crowned in this very city.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — where Ruth's great-grandson reigns.
stops.narration:
Ruth's great-grandson became king, and he reigned from Zion (Ruth 4:18–22, LSB). Centuries later, Matthew names Ruth in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5, LSB). An outsider's faith is woven right into Israel's story of redemption.

In the City of David, Kenyon dug from 1961 to 1967. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge, the area known as David's city. How big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still debated, with some scholars seeing a small town and others a larger city.

This path began with a grieving family in Moab. It ends in the city of a king. Picture Ruth, the woman from Moab who chose Yahweh, never knowing that her great-grandson would rule here, or that her name would one day appear at the start of the New Testament. Boaz once prayed that Ruth would be rewarded by Yahweh, under whose wings she had come for refuge (Ruth 2:12). In Jesus that refuge opens to everyone: those who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Ephesians 2:13).

paths.title: Rahab of Jericho — faith on the wall
paths.theme: Joshua 2 & 6 — Canaanite woman confesses Yahweh; spared by faith
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Shittim — camp east of Jordan before spies sent.
stops.narration:
Before Israel crosses the Jordan, the people are camped at Shittim, east of the river. From here Joshua secretly sends two spies to look over the land, especially Jericho (Joshua 2:1, LSB). A Canaanite woman will hide them.

Shittim, also called Abel-shittim, was in the plains of Moab. Candidates include Tell el-Hammam. This is a wilderness station, and the evidence for this stop is mixed.

Picture two men slipping out of a huge camp at night, crossing the river, and heading toward a walled city. They do not know it yet, but their lives will depend on a woman named Rahab.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jordan crossing / Gilgal — entry after the spy mission.
stops.narration:
After the spies return, Yahweh brings the people across the Jordan (Joshua 3:1, LSB). Later, when Jericho's walls fall, Rahab and her family are spared, because she had tied a scarlet cord in her window as the spies told her (Joshua 6:22–25, LSB).

This stop is in the Jordan Valley west of Jericho, where several candidates for Gilgal lie. The evidence for this stop is mixed, and it marks the entry into the land.

Picture a whole nation crossing the river and setting up camp within sight of Jericho. Inside those walls, a woman watches and waits, a red cord hanging from her window as a sign of trust.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jericho — Rahab's city (Tell es-Sultan); no house footprint pin.
stops.caveats: Rahab's house = narration on city pin. Contested dating (CBG-02) not required stop.
stops.narration:
Inside Jericho, Rahab hides the two spies. She tells them she knows that Yahweh their God is God in heaven above and on earth below. She asks them to spare her family, and they agree (Joshua 2:8–21, LSB). When the city falls, she and her household are saved (Joshua 6:22–25, LSB). Later, Hebrews and James both praise her faith.

Jericho's ancient mound is Tell es-Sultan. There is no map pin for Rahab's house, so we tell her story at the city. From 1930 to 1936, Garstang dug here. He found city walls and destruction debris that he dated to about 1400 BC and linked to Joshua. Earlier work had found a Neolithic tower, and there are Bronze Age town remains.

But this is debated. Kenyon later redated the main destruction to the earlier Middle Bronze Age and found little of a Late Bronze city. That dating dispute is still discussed.

Politics have shaped the trenches too. A Sapienza University team records that its autumn 2000 season was interrupted by the severe political situation, with work stopped into the mid-2000s.

Picture a woman in a house on the wall, choosing to trust a God she had only heard about.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ai — next conquest geography after Jericho.
stops.narration:
After Jericho, the campaign moves on to Ai. At first Israel is defeated there, because someone in the camp has disobeyed. After that sin is dealt with, Ai is taken (Joshua 7:1–5; Joshua 8:1–29, LSB). Grace to Rahab does not cancel the call to holiness among God's people.

Many have identified Ai with a mound called et-Tell. Marquet-Krause dug here in 1933–1935, and Callaway in 1964–1976. They found a major Early Bronze city, but little or no Late Bronze settlement.

This is a careful, problem site. If et-Tell is Ai, archaeology does not show a city from the right period for Joshua 7–8 to conquer. Other sites have been proposed, such as Khirbet el-Maqatir. It is a classic tension between the text and this identification, and we leave it honestly open.

Picture an army shaken by an unexpected defeat, learning that how they live matters as much as who they fight.

stops.panel_truth_line: Shechem — covenant renewal in the land.
stops.narration:
At Shechem, Joshua gathers all Israel and challenges them: choose this day whom you will serve. The people answer that they will serve Yahweh, and Joshua makes a covenant with them (Joshua 24:14–25, LSB). Hebrews 11:31 (LSB) remembers that by faith Rahab did not perish. The God who rescued an outsider is now confessed in the land.

The ruins of Shechem are at Tell Balata. Sellin dug here in 1913–1914 and 1926–1927, and Wright led the Drew-McCormick and ASOR excavations from 1956 to 1973. They uncovered massive Middle Bronze walls, a temple-fortress, a gate complex, destruction layers, and Iron Age homes.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Shechem was a major city in the Bronze and Iron Ages, a fitting place for the covenant gathering in Joshua 24, and for the Abimelech story in Judges 9.

Picture the whole nation gathered before these great walls, and somewhere among them, Rahab's family, once Canaanites in Jericho, now standing with Israel to promise loyalty to Yahweh.

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — genealogy close (Matt 1:5 Rahab → Boaz line).
stops.narration:
Matthew begins his Gospel with Jesus' family tree, and he includes a surprising name. Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab (Matthew 1:5, LSB). Matthew will not let the church forget her name in the Messiah's line.

Bethlehem was Boaz's town, and later the birthplace of Jesus. The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave long linked to Jesus' birth, with buildings from the eras of Constantine and Justinian. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors. No clear first-century "manger house" layer has been published as a smoking gun.

The ground and the Bible line up well as tradition. Christians have honored the cave since at least the 300s AD, and archaeology confirms that early pilgrim memory. The Bethlehem birth claim comes from the text, while the digs show the shrine's history.

This is an optional close for the path. Picture the woman from Jericho's wall, saved by a scarlet cord, becoming part of the family that led to Bethlehem and to Jesus. Hebrews remembers her faith (Hebrews 11:31). Her rescue came by trusting Yahweh's word, not by her own record, and so does ours: by grace you have been saved through faith (Ephesians 2:8).

paths.title: Widow of Zarephath — flour, oil, and the living God
paths.theme: 1 Kings 17 — Sidonian widow trusts Yahweh; Jesus cites her (Luke 4)
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Brook Cherith — Elijah hid before Sidon.
stops.narration:
During a drought, Yahweh sends the prophet Elijah to hide by the brook Cherith. There he drinks from the brook, and ravens bring him food. When the brook dries up, Yahweh sends him on, to a Gentile widow (1 Kings 17:2–7, LSB).

This stop marks the Brook Cherith. Its location is traditional, and the evidence is mixed.

Picture a lonely prophet hiding in a ravine, with a trickle of water and birds dropping off bread and meat each morning and evening. Then one day the water stops. Yahweh had fed him in the wild. Now he will feed him through someone who has almost nothing.

stops.panel_truth_line: Sidon — Phoenician coast; Zarephath is in Sidon's district.
stops.narration:
Yahweh tells Elijah to go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, where a widow will feed him (1 Kings 17:8–9, LSB). Much later, Jesus reminds his hometown that there were many widows in Israel, but Elijah was sent to this one, in the land of Sidon (Luke 4:25–26, LSB). Jesus holds her up as a picture of mercy beyond Israel's borders.

Sidon was a Phoenician city on the coast. Finds here go back to the 1850s, including tombs from the Ottoman era. Since 1998, Doumet-Serhal has led digs at the College Site, with Lebanese and international teams. They found Phoenician burials, temple and settlement remains, Middle Bronze warrior burials, and Iron Age layers.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Sidon was a lasting Phoenician center, named from the table of nations in Genesis through the prophets. It was also the homeland of Jezebel.

The exact village of Zarephath is traditional, placed within Sidon's district. Picture Elijah walking right into Jezebel's homeland, sent by Yahweh to find a poor widow.

stops.panel_truth_line: Elijah — Zarephath — widow's house narrative locale.
stops.narration:
At the town gate of Zarephath, Elijah meets a widow gathering sticks. She has just enough flour and oil for one last meal for herself and her son. Elijah asks her to make him a cake first. She does, and her flour and oil do not run out. Later, when her son dies, Elijah prays and the boy is raised. She says: now I know that the word of Yahweh in your mouth is truth (1 Kings 17:8–24, LSB).

This stop marks Zarephath as the place of the widow's house. Its exact location is placed by district and tradition, and the evidence is mixed.

This is one of the most tender stories in the Bible. Picture a mother at the edge of starvation, sharing her last bit of food with a stranger. Then picture her checking the jar, day after day, and finding there is still enough. A Gentile woman, in Jezebel's homeland, comes to trust the living God.

stops.panel_truth_line: Tyre — Phoenician sister port (regional Gentile coast).
stops.narration:
Yahweh sent Elijah to Zarephath in the land of Sidon (1 Kings 17:9, LSB). Tyre was Sidon's sister port along the same coast. A Gentile coast receives a prophet whom Israel's own king is fighting.

Tyre has been dug off and on since the 1800s, with major modern work from the 1960s through the 1990s and beyond, by UNESCO, Lebanese authorities, and international teams. They found remains of settlements on the island and the mainland, harbors, Phoenician and later Classical layers, and evidence of the causeway built by Alexander the Great.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Tyre was a wealthy sea power, the setting for King Hiram's alliance with Solomon and for Ezekiel's prophecies. The mainland was destroyed while the island survived longer, and scholars debate how this relates to Ezekiel 26, speaking of partial fulfillment or layered history.

This is regional supporting geography. Picture busy harbors full of ships and traders, a rich and powerful coast, and, nearby, a poor widow's kitchen where the true God was at work.

stops.panel_truth_line: Mount Carmel — later showdown; Yahweh vs Baal after Zarephath mercy.
stops.narration:
After the drought and the widow's story, Elijah faces the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel. Each side prepares a sacrifice and calls on its god. Baal is silent. Yahweh answers by fire (1 Kings 18:20–39, LSB). The living God who fed a widow from Sidon shows himself before all Israel.

This stop marks Mount Carmel, by tradition. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

Think back over this path: a hidden brook, a foreign coast, a widow's last meal, and a son raised to life. Now comes the great public showdown. Picture a crowd on the mountain, hundreds of prophets shouting all day, and then one prophet's short prayer, and fire falling from heaven. The God who cared for one poor widow is the same God who rules over all. Jesus later pointed to this widow to show that God's mercy was never for one nation only (Luke 4:25–26). He also called himself the bread of life: whoever comes to him will not hunger (John 6:35). Flour and oil that never ran out point to a love that does not run out.

paths.title: Nineveh repents — a great city turns
paths.theme: Jonah 3 city repentance (distinct from Passion typology path)
paths.yahweh_rule: Narration says Yahweh untranslated; on-screen verses stay LSB wording

stops.panel_truth_line: Joppa — flight port.
stops.caveats: Sea/fish: no pin—narrate between Joppa and Nineveh.
stops.narration:
This path follows one great city's turn toward God. It begins with a prophet running away. Yahweh tells Jonah to go to Nineveh, but Jonah goes down to Joppa and boards a ship sailing the opposite way (Jonah 1:1–3, LSB). A prophet flees, and a city still waits to hear.

Joppa is today's Jaffa. Kaplan dug here from 1955 to 1974, and new projects by the Israel Antiquities Authority, UCLA, and others have continued since the 1990s. Earlier work found a Late Bronze gate with Egyptian inscriptions. Above it lie Iron Age, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman port cities. This harbor is tied to Jonah's flight and to Peter's stories in Acts.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Joppa is confirmed as Jaffa, with harbor remains from the Bronze Age to Roman times.

The sea and the great fish have no pin on our map, so we tell them in words between Joppa and Nineveh. Picture a busy port, sailors loading cargo, and one passenger trying very hard to get as far from God's call as he can.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jonah — Joppa — prophet locale pin at the flight port.
stops.narration:
Jonah went down to Joppa, found a ship going to Tarshish, paid the fare, and boarded it to get away from Yahweh's presence (Jonah 1:3, LSB). Disobedience has a dock.

This stop is a prophet pin placed at the port of Joppa. It lays the story of Jonah over the harbor's geography. The evidence for this stop is mixed.

It is worth pausing here. Running from God took planning. Jonah had to walk to the coast, find the right ship, and pay for it. Picture him handing over his money, stepping on board, and finding a place below deck, hoping that distance would quiet the call he had heard. On this path, it is the last moment before everything starts to turn.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nineveh — preaching and repentance.
stops.caveats: City faith beat—not Passion typology (see Sign of Jonah path).
stops.narration:
At last Jonah goes to Nineveh and preaches. The people believe God. They call a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least. Even the king steps down from his throne. They turn from their evil ways, and God relents (Jonah 3:1–10, LSB). A great city turns.

Layard dug at Nineveh from 1845 to 1851, and Rassam continued into the 1850s–1880s. They uncovered Sennacherib's Southwest Palace, carved wall scenes of the siege of Lachish, giant winged guardian statues, and Ashurbanipal's library of clay tablets.

The ground and the Bible line up well with Assyria's history. Assyrian records and the Lachish carvings back up Sennacherib's 701 BC campaign against Judah (2 Kings 18–19). The libraries shed light on the world of Isaiah and Nahum, and Nineveh's fall in 612 BC matches the prophets' warnings. During ISIS control of Mosul from 2014 to 2017, the site suffered documented destruction, and war stopped the digging.

On this path, the focus is the city's faith, its turning to God. Picture a vast capital going quiet, its people in rough cloth, waiting to see if God would show mercy.

stops.panel_truth_line: Jonah — Nineveh — prophetic locale of the warning.
stops.narration:
Jonah walks into Nineveh and announces that in forty days the city will be overthrown. The people respond with repentance, and God spares them (Jonah 3:4–10, LSB). Jesus later says the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment, because they repented at Jonah's preaching (Matthew 12:41, LSB).

This stop is a prophet pin marking Nineveh as the place of the warning. The evidence for this stop is mixed.

A pagan city becomes a map of Gentile repentance. Picture a lone foreign prophet shouting a short, hard message in the streets of the most powerful city of his day. He did not expect them to listen. They did. That surprise is the heart of this whole path.

stops.panel_truth_line: Lachish Reliefs — Assyrian power visual (Nineveh palace reliefs; museum object).
stops.caveats: Museum object; empire that later menaced Judah.
stops.narration:
Jonah calls Nineveh a great city (Jonah 3:3, LSB). Later the prophet Nahum calls it a city of bloodshed (Nahum 3:1, LSB). Both are true.

This stop is a set of carved stone panels now in a museum. They come from the walls of an Assyrian palace at Nineveh and show Sennacherib capturing the city of Lachish. They are a visual match to his 701 BC campaign against Judah.

The evidence for this path is mixed, since the carvings are about a later war, not about Jonah. This empire later threatened Judah.

But look at the carvings and think. This empire could carve its conquests in stone for everyone to admire. Yet once, the same city sat in sackcloth at a prophet's word. Picture the proud carvings on the palace walls, and remember the day when that same city bowed low before God.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — Jesus says Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation.
stops.narration:
In Galilee, Jesus told the crowds that the people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at Jonah's preaching, and now something greater than Jonah is here (Matthew 12:41; Luke 11:32, LSB). Nineveh's turning still stands against hard hearts.

Capernaum was Jesus' teaching base by the lake. In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of its white limestone synagogue. They documented its architecture, preparing the way for later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig confirmed a grand synagogue ruin in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base. But the synagogue you see is later, from the 300s–400s AD. Whether an earlier first-century phase lies under its floors is debated.

This path began with a prophet running from Joppa. It ends here, with Jesus holding up that pagan city as an example. Picture the people of this lakeside town, who had seen far more than Nineveh ever did, being told that the Ninevites listened better. The question is left for every listener, and so is the hope. Jonah knew Yahweh as gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in lovingkindness (Jonah 4:2). The same welcome stands in Jesus: whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13).

paths.title: Magi from the east — seeking the newborn King
paths.theme: Matthew 2 — Gentile seekers worship; Herod plots
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Bethlehem — where they find and worship the child.
stops.caveats: Exact Magi origin city: no pin — keep textual "from the east."
stops.narration:
Wise men from the east arrive in Jerusalem looking for the newborn King of the Jews. They are sent to Bethlehem, because the prophet Micah named it as the birthplace of a ruler (Micah 5:2, LSB). There they find the child and bow down to worship him (Matthew 2:1–12, LSB). Gentile seekers bow, while a troubled royal court plots.

The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave long believed to be Jesus' birthplace, with buildings from the eras of Constantine and Justinian. Harvey studied it in 1932–1934, and restoration work in the 2010s added more. Researchers found earlier quarry and cave use and mosaic floors. No clear first-century "manger house" layer has been published as a smoking gun.

The ground and the Bible line up well as tradition. Christians have honored this cave since at least the 300s AD, and archaeology confirms that early pilgrim memory, not anything from the birth itself. The Bethlehem claim comes from the text.

Where exactly were the Magi from? Matthew only says they came from the east, and we have no pin for their hometown. Picture travelers from far away kneeling before a small child in a small town.

stops.panel_truth_line: Herodium — Herod the Great's fortress-palace near Bethlehem.
stops.caveats: Herod context; tomb attribution debated. Not Magi lodging.
stops.narration:
When King Herod hears that a new king has been born, he is deeply troubled. He secretly questions the Magi and sends them to Bethlehem, pretending he wants to worship too (Matthew 2:1–8, LSB). Later, the child's family must flee to Egypt to escape Herod's fury (Matthew 2:13–18, LSB). Herod's power casts a shadow over the child's town.

Herodium, a fortress-palace near Bethlehem, was built by Herod the Great. Hebrew University's team under Netzer dug here from 1972 to 1987 and again from 1997 to 2010, and study continues. Teams found the palace-fortress, a theater, a grand stairway, ritual baths, wall paintings, and debris from the First Jewish Revolt. In 2007, Netzer announced a proposed tomb of Herod.

The evidence is strong as background for Herod, the king in Matthew 2. The buildings match the historian Josephus' description. Whether the tomb is truly Herod's is debated among experts, but Herod's existence and his building program are certain.

The Magi did not stay here. Picture this towering palace on its hill, visible from Bethlehem, a symbol of a jealous king who feared a baby.

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — chief priests/scribes consulted in Jerusalem.
stops.narration:
Herod gathers the chief priests and scribes in Jerusalem and asks where the Messiah is to be born. They open the Scriptures and answer: in Bethlehem of Judea, as the prophet wrote (Matthew 2:4–6, LSB). Scripture is opened in the capital, but it is the foreign Magi who keep moving toward worship.

Here, at Robinson's Arch on the temple's western side, we stand in the religious heart of that capital. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later seasons on the Ophel and along the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's own era under the arch, massive stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and grand stairways up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These are the approaches built in Herod's time. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

Think about the irony. The experts knew exactly where to look, just a short walk away. Picture them reading the answer aloud, and then staying home, while travelers from far away set out again for Bethlehem.

stops.panel_truth_line: City of David — Jerusalem inquiry geography.
stops.caveats: Jerusalem geography for the Magi's question.
stops.narration:
The Magi arrive in Jerusalem asking a question that shakes the city: where is he who has been born King of the Jews? Herod is troubled, and all Jerusalem with him (Matthew 2:1–6, LSB).

Jerusalem's oldest quarter is the City of David. Kenyon dug here from 1961 to 1967. Her team exposed the Stepped Stone Structure, found Bronze and Iron Age wall lines, and studied layers that explain the city's eastern slope.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. There was a large Iron Age settlement on this southeast ridge known as David's city. How big Jerusalem was in the 900s BC is still debated.

This is the city of David, and the Magi are asking about David's true heir. Picture foreign visitors in the streets of the old royal city, asking everyone they meet where the new king is, while the man on the throne listens with growing fear.

stops.panel_truth_line: Nazareth — holy family's later home after Egypt sojourn.
stops.caveats: Egypt sojourn narrated without inventing new stop IDs.
stops.narration:
After Herod dies, an angel tells Joseph in a dream that it is safe to return from Egypt. The family settles in Nazareth, in Galilee, and Jesus is called a Nazarene (Matthew 2:19–23, LSB). God draws the nations to his Son, and he protects the child on the road home. We tell the time in Egypt in words only, without adding a new stop.

In 2009, the Israel Antiquities Authority dug near the Marian Center in Nazareth. They found a first-century courtyard house, partly cut into rock and partly built, with storage pits and household features. It is one of the first well-published houses in Nazareth from Jesus' time.

The evidence is mixed but helpful. The dig shows Nazareth was a small Jewish village in the early first century, answering extreme claims that it did not exist. But it does not identify this house as belonging to Jesus or Mary. It only shows such houses stood when the Gospels say he grew up there.

Picture a tired young family finally arriving in a quiet village, far from Herod's palaces, ready to begin an ordinary life in simple rooms like these.

stops.panel_truth_line: Babylon — optional "from the east" cultural horizon (not claimed Magi hometown GPS).
stops.caveats: NOT claimed Magi hometown. Cultural horizon only.
stops.narration:
Matthew says only that the Magi came from the east (Matthew 2:1–2, LSB). We refuse to invent a hometown pin for them. Babylon is here as an optional stop, to give a sense of the eastern world, not as the place they came from.

From 1899 to 1917, Koldewey's team for the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft dug at Babylon. They uncovered the Ishtar Gate and the Processional Way, Nebuchadnezzar's city walls and palaces, the remains of the Esagila temple and the Etemenanki ziggurat, and building inscriptions in cuneiform.

The evidence for this stop's link is mixed. Babylon's history does match the Bible in other places: Nebuchadnezzar II's empire destroyed Jerusalem (2 Kings 25), and inscriptions record Cyrus taking the city later. Many link the Tower of Babel to Etemenanki, but that is traditional background.

So treat this as a cultural horizon. Picture the great old cities of the east, with their gates and towers, and somewhere beyond the map, travelers packing for a long journey west to find a king. When they found him, they rejoiced greatly and bowed down to worship (Matthew 2:10–11). Isaiah had said the nations would come to the light Yahweh would raise over his people (Isaiah 60:1–3). The King they sought came for seekers from every land, and he still welcomes those who look for him.

paths.title: Capernaum's centurion — great faith under a Gentile roof
paths.theme: Matthew 8 / Luke 7 — Roman centurion's faith marvels Jesus
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — town of the centurion.
stops.caveats: Avoid contested House of Peter CBG-05 as required stop.
stops.narration:
This path is about a Roman officer, a centurion, living in Capernaum. When his servant is sick, he asks Jesus for help, and he believes Jesus can heal with just a word (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10, LSB). Great faith appears under a Gentile roof.

Capernaum was Jesus' base by the lake. In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of its white limestone synagogue. They recorded its architecture, setting up later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig confirmed a grand synagogue ruin in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base. The synagogue you see is later, from the 300s–400s AD, and whether a first-century phase lies under its floors is debated.

A nearby site is shown as the "House of Peter," but that identification is contested, and this path does not depend on it. Picture a busy lakeside town where Jewish fishermen and a Roman officer lived side by side, and where that officer was about to surprise everyone.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — centurion's servant miracle pin.
stops.narration:
This stop marks the miracle itself, in Capernaum. The centurion tells Jesus he is not worthy to have him come under his roof. Just say the word, he says, and my servant will be healed. Jesus marvels and says he has not found such faith in Israel. The servant is healed (Matthew 8:5–13; Luke 7:1–10, LSB).

The geography and the Bible fit well here.

Think about what this officer understood. He was used to giving orders and having them obeyed from a distance. He saw that Jesus had that kind of authority over sickness. Picture Jesus stopping in the street, amazed, turning to the crowd, and praising the faith of a foreign soldier. It was a moment no one there expected.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — Jesus' authority in the same town.
stops.narration:
In the same town of Capernaum, Jesus heals many. Matthew and Mark describe his healings here, showing his authority over sickness and evil (Matthew 8:14–17; Mark 1:29–34, LSB). The power that unsettled the town is the same power that welcomed a Gentile's trust.

This stop marks those base healings in Capernaum. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

On this path, it helps to see that the centurion's servant was not an isolated case. Capernaum was full of stories like it. Picture a town where word spread quickly, where neighbors brought the sick to Jesus, and where a Roman officer had surely heard the news before he ever asked for help.

stops.panel_truth_line: Cana — related heal-at-a-distance sign (humble on official's identity).
stops.caveats: Official may be Herodian/Gentile-adjacent — keep humble.
stops.narration:
In Cana of Galilee, a royal official comes to Jesus begging him to heal his son, who is near death in Capernaum. Jesus tells him: go, your son lives. The man believes the word and goes, and he learns that his son got better at that very hour (John 4:46–54, LSB). Distance is no barrier when the word is trusted.

This stop marks Cana as the place where Jesus spoke the word. The evidence for the stop is mixed.

Who was this official? John does not say much. He may have served Herod's family, and he may have had ties to the Gentile world, but we keep that humble and do not claim more. What matters is the pattern. Like the centurion, he had to trust Jesus' word and walk away without seeing the healing first. Picture a father hurrying home, hoping, and then his servants running to meet him with good news.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pilate Stone — Roman prefect inscription from Caesarea (Roman authority world).
stops.caveats: Museum/findspot context for Roman Gospel world.
stops.narration:
Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea (Luke 3:1, LSB). Matthew tells how Jesus was handed over to Pilate (Matthew 27:2, LSB). The centurion's great faith lived inside a real Roman empire.

This stop is the Pilate Stone, an inscription found at Caesarea and now a museum object. It is the only known stone inscription from Pilate's own time that names him, and it calls him prefect of Judea. A small ring from Herodium reads "of Pilatus," but scholars debate whether it has anything to do with Pontius Pilate, and his coins carry the emperor Tiberius' name, not his.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone shows that the Gospels' Roman world was real, with real officials and real titles.

On this path, it reminds us of the world the centurion served in. He was part of the same Roman system that would one day put Jesus on trial. Picture the governor's name carved in stone for all to see, and remember a humble officer in that same empire who said he was not worthy to have Jesus under his roof. Jesus marveled at that faith and said many will come from east and west to share the feast of the kingdom (Matthew 8:10–11). No one earns a seat there; it is given to those who trust him.

paths.title: Syrophoenician mother — crumbs of mercy
paths.theme: Matthew 15 / Mark 7 — Canaanite / Syrophoenician mother's faith
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Tyre — Phoenician port region of the encounter.
stops.narration:
Jesus leaves Galilee and goes into the region of Tyre and Sidon, Gentile coast country (Matthew 15:21–28; Mark 7:24, LSB). There a mother will come to him with a desperate request.

Tyre has been dug off and on since the 1800s, with major modern work from the 1960s through the 1990s and beyond, by UNESCO, Lebanese authorities, and international teams. They found settlement remains on the island and the mainland, harbors, Phoenician and later Classical layers, and evidence of the causeway built by Alexander the Great.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician sea power, the setting for King Hiram's alliance with Solomon and for Ezekiel's prophecies. The mainland was destroyed while the island survived longer, and scholars debate how that fits Ezekiel 26, speaking of partial fulfillment or layered history.

This pin marks the region, not an exact house. Picture Jesus stepping into a foreign land of rich ports and ships, perhaps hoping for quiet, and a woman who had heard about him already on her way.

stops.panel_truth_line: Tyre/Sidon region — Canaanite woman's daughter miracle pin.
stops.narration:
A mother from this region comes to Jesus, crying out for her daughter, who is troubled by a demon. Jesus answers with a hard saying about bread for the children and not for the dogs. She replies that even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from the table. She accepts the crumbs. Jesus praises her great faith, and her daughter is healed (Matthew 15:21–28; Mark 7:24–30, LSB).

This stop marks the miracle in the region of Tyre and Sidon. The geography and the Bible fit well here.

Matthew calls her a Canaanite woman, and Mark calls her Syrophoenician. Either way, she was an outsider. She did not argue that she deserved help. She simply trusted that even a crumb of Jesus' mercy was enough. Picture a mother on her knees, quick-witted and humble, refusing to give up, and Jesus delighting in her answer.

stops.panel_truth_line: Sidon — Mark's "Syrophoenician" coast.
stops.narration:
