Mark calls the mother a Syrophoenician by birth, a woman of the coast around Tyre and Sidon (Mark 7:24–30, LSB). Her persistence is welcomed at the Redeemer's feet.

Sidon was the other great Phoenician city on this coast. Finds here go back to the 1850s, including tombs from the Ottoman era. Since 1998, Doumet-Serhal has led digs at the College Site, with Lebanese and international teams. They found Phoenician burials, temple and settlement remains, Middle Bronze warrior burials, and Iron Age layers.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Sidon was a lasting Phoenician center, named from the table of nations in Genesis all the way through the prophets. It was the homeland of Jezebel, and the prophets often speak of Tyre and Sidon together.

This coast had a long and troubled history with Israel. That makes this mother's story even more striking. Picture a land once known for its proud kings and foreign gods, and in it, a mother who saw in Jesus the only hope for her child.

stops.panel_truth_line: Hub — Tyre — Phoenician maritime hinge (supporting).
stops.caveats: Trade hub marker supporting regional geography.
stops.narration:
Long before Jesus' day, Ezekiel described Tyre as a glorious trading ship, built from the finest materials and sailed by skilled crews (Ezekiel 27:1–9, LSB). Matthew 15:21 (LSB) says Jesus went into the region of Tyre and Sidon. A coast famous for commerce becomes a coast of mercy.

This stop is a trade hub marker for Tyre, supporting the regional geography. It is not a dig site, and the evidence for this stop is mixed.

Think about the contrast. Ezekiel's Tyre was all about wealth, cargo, and pride. Jesus came to the same coast, and the thing that mattered most there was not a shipment of goods but a desperate mother's faith. Picture the busy harbors, full of trade from around the world, and the quiet moment when mercy was the most valuable thing exchanged.

stops.panel_truth_line: Capernaum — return to Galilee ministry base after the district trip.
stops.narration:
After his trip to the coast, Jesus returns to the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 15:29, LSB). Capernaum was his base in Galilee. The crumbs given to the nations do not empty the table of promise. They show how wide that table really is.

In 1905, Kohl and Watzinger carried out the first scientific clearing of Capernaum's white limestone synagogue. They documented its architecture, which framed later Franciscan work.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. The dig confirmed a grand synagogue ruin in the town the Gospels call Jesus' home base. The synagogue you see is a later building, from the 300s–400s AD, and whether a first-century phase lies under its floors is debated.

This path went from Galilee out to the Gentile coast, and back again. Picture Jesus walking home along the lake, with a story about a foreign mother's faith that his disciples would never forget. Paul later put it plainly: the same Lord is Lord of all, rich in mercy toward all who call on him (Romans 10:12). There is room at his table for you.

paths.title: Ethiopian on the Gaza road — Isaiah open, Jesus named
paths.theme: Acts 8 — Ethiopian official believes and is baptized
paths.yahweh_rule: NT path — Jesus named normally; no forced Yahweh in NT speech

stops.panel_truth_line: Temple approaches — he had come to Jerusalem to worship.
stops.caveats: Exact baptism water spot: no pin.
stops.narration:
A court official from Ethiopia, a Gentile, has traveled all the way to Jerusalem to worship (Acts 8:27, LSB). He comes to worship, and he leaves reading the prophet Isaiah.

Robinson's Arch, on the western side of the temple platform, shows the kind of approach a worshiper from far away would climb. B. Mazar dug here from 1968 to 1978, with later seasons on the Ophel and work along the southwest corner. His teams uncovered a street from Herod's time under the arch, giant cut stones that fell when Rome destroyed the city in AD 70, Ophel walls, ritual baths, and broad stairways up to the Temple Mount.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. These were real routes into the temple in the apostles' day. On the platform itself, licensed digging is not allowed under the agreement with the Jerusalem Islamic Waqf, so the Sifting Project studies soil dumped elsewhere.

This path will follow him home along the road. The exact spot where he is later baptized has no pin. Picture a traveler from the far south, after a long journey, climbing these great steps, and then heading home with a scroll he does not yet understand.

stops.panel_truth_line: Samaria — Philip's prior preaching.
stops.narration:
Before the desert road, the evangelist Philip is busy in Samaria, preaching Christ to the city. Crowds listen, and many believe. Then the Spirit redirects him to a lonely desert road (Acts 8:5–25, LSB).

Samaria, rebuilt in Roman times as Sebaste, has been dug by the Harvard Expedition in 1908–1910, again in 1931–1935, and off and on since. On top lies Herod's Roman city, with a temple to Augustus, a forum, a stadium, and a basilica. Beneath it is the Iron Age capital of the Old Testament.

The evidence for this stop is mixed, but the background is clear. Sebaste shows how Herod and Rome turned Samaria's capital into a pagan city. That is separate from the village well at Sychar, near Shechem, in John 4. Philip's city mission in Acts 8 fits a real city here.

Picture Philip in the middle of a revival in a busy Roman city, and then being told to leave it all and go stand by an empty road in the desert. It would have made little sense, until he met the traveler.

stops.panel_truth_line: Philip route — Samaria → Gaza road → Azotus → Caesarea.
stops.narration:
This stop is the route itself. Philip's path runs from Samaria, down the Gaza road, up to Azotus, and on to Caesarea (Acts 8:26–40, LSB). The road becomes the backbone of this story.

The evidence for this route stop is mixed. It is a map line, not a dig. We do not invent a location for the baptism.

Think about what happens along this road. An angel sends Philip south. He meets a traveler reading Isaiah. He explains the good news about Jesus. Water is found, and the traveler is baptized. Then Philip is taken away and keeps preaching town to town. Picture the long, dusty road stretching across the land, and how one conversation along it carried the good news toward the ends of the earth.

stops.panel_truth_line: Tell el-ʿAjjul / Gaza — Gaza approach geography (road region, not baptism GPS).
stops.narration:
On the road toward Gaza, Philip meets the Ethiopian official reading Isaiah. He is reading about the Suffering Servant, and he asks who the prophet means. Philip explains, and he tells him the good news about Jesus. Then they come to some water, and the official is baptized (Acts 8:26–39, LSB).

This stop marks the Gaza approach, the road region, not the exact place of the baptism. The pin uses an excavated mound in this area. Petrie dug at "Ancient Gaza" in 1930–1934 and 1938, and Fischer and Sadeq renewed work in 1999–2000. They found one of the richest Middle Bronze Canaanite centers in the southern Levant, with palaces, an elite cemetery, gold jewelry, Egyptian scarabs, imported pottery, and Late Bronze layers. The renewed work also noted pumice from the Thera volcano.

The big Bronze Age dig is not in doubt. But whether this mound is the city called Sharuhen is contested. Tell el-Far'ah South is another candidate. So this is an honest candidate, not a closed case.

Picture a traveler stopping by the side of the road, pointing to water, and asking what could stop him from being baptized right then.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ashdod (Azotus) — Philip appears there preaching.
stops.narration:
After the baptism, Philip suddenly finds himself at Azotus, and he keeps preaching the gospel in every town until he reaches Caesarea. The Ethiopian goes home rejoicing (Acts 8:40, LSB). The evangelist keeps moving.

Azotus is the Old Testament city of Ashdod. Moshe Dothan led excavations here from 1962 to 1972, and the Israel Antiquities Authority has done salvage digs from the 2000s into the 2020s. They found twenty-three layers, from the Middle Bronze Age to the Hellenistic period. There was a Canaanite city with Egyptian objects, Philistine pottery and figurines called "Ashdoda," and an Assyrian-period palace near the mound.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Scholars strongly identify this site with biblical Ashdod and New Testament Azotus, one of the five main Philistine cities named often in the Old Testament and in Acts. The Bronze Age city came before the Philistine one. The finds do not prove every detail of stories like 1 Samuel 5.

Picture Philip arriving in this old coastal city, ready to preach again, while far to the south a happy traveler rides home to Ethiopia.

stops.panel_truth_line: Ashkelon — coastal Philistine plain context (optional).
stops.narration:
Philip preached in the towns along the coast on his way to Caesarea (Acts 8:40, LSB). Ashkelon helps us picture that coastal plain. This is an optional context stop.

From 1985 to 2016, the Leon Levy Expedition dug at Ashkelon. They found Philistine city layers, a dog cemetery, defensive ramparts, a Canaanite gate, a marketplace, and inscriptions. They also found evidence of the Babylonian destruction of 604 BC.

The evidence for this stop's link to Philip is mixed, since Acts does not name Ashkelon. But the site itself is clear. It confirms Ashkelon as a major Philistine city named often in the Old Testament prophets. Its destruction layer fits the Babylonian campaigns in Jeremiah's time, giving a strong historical backdrop.

Picture the coastal road running north past old cities like this one, each with a long history, and a traveling preacher passing through with a new message.

stops.panel_truth_line: Caesarea — Philip later settles.
stops.narration:
Philip's journey ends in Caesarea (Acts 8:40, LSB). Years later, Paul stays at Philip's house there, where Philip is known as the evangelist (Acts 21:8, LSB). A Gentile from the ends of the earth went home rejoicing, and the preacher settled in Caesarea.

Caesarea Maritima was the governor's port city. From 1959 to 1964, an Italian mission dug its theater, built in Herod's time. In June 1961 they found a limestone block reused in stairs in the 300s AD. It names "Pontius Pilatus," calls him prefect of Judea, and mentions a building named for the emperor Tiberius. It is the only known stone inscription from Pilate's own time that names him, and it calls him prefect of Judea.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone confirms Pilate's name, title, and post in Judea under Tiberius, matching the Gospels and the historians Tacitus and Josephus. It is strong evidence that the governor was real and tied to this city.

This path began with a worshiper climbing the temple steps. It ends with two men far apart: one rejoicing on the road home, the other settling down in a busy port to keep preaching. What turned the traveler's question into joy was simple. Beginning from Isaiah, Philip told him the good news of Jesus (Acts 8:35). The Scripture he could not understand opened into a Savior who welcomed him.

stops.panel_truth_line: Joppa — Peter's vision of clean/unclean.
stops.caveats: Distinct from Paul-Greece "Good news for the nations" spine.
stops.narration:
On a rooftop in Joppa, Peter sees a vision of animals, clean and unclean, and hears that what God has cleansed he must not call unclean. At that moment, messengers from a Roman officer arrive (Acts 10:9–23, LSB). A rooftop vision reorders who can share a table in the gospel.

Joppa is today's Jaffa. Kaplan dug here from 1955 to 1974, and new projects by the Israel Antiquities Authority, UCLA, and others have continued since the 1990s. Earlier work found a Late Bronze gate with Egyptian inscriptions. Above it lie the remains of Iron Age, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman port cities. This harbor is linked to Jonah's flight and to Peter's raising of Tabitha.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Joppa is confirmed as Jaffa, and the setting of Acts is secure at the city level. The exact "house of Simon the tanner" is pilgrim tradition.

Picture Peter on a flat roof by the sea, hungry and confused by what he has seen, when a knock comes at the gate below. His old ideas are about to be tested.

stops.panel_truth_line: Lydda — Peter's prior Judea ministry stop (approach to Joppa).
stops.narration:
Before Joppa, Peter is already on the move through Judea. At Lydda, he finds a man named Aeneas who has been paralyzed for eight years, and heals him in Jesus' name (Acts 9:32–35, LSB). Peter is already traveling when messengers from Caesarea come to find him.

Lydda is today's Lod. Since the 1990s, the Israel Antiquities Authority has carried out salvage and research digs here. The city has Iron Age, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman layers, and a famous Roman-period mosaic in a villa. It lay on the coastal plain road.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. Lydda in Acts 9 is confirmed. Since a modern city sits on top, most of the digging has been salvage work. The city's identity is secure, but no specific miracle house has been dug.

Picture Peter walking from town to town on the coastal road, visiting believers, and word of a healing spreading fast to nearby Joppa.

stops.panel_truth_line: Caesarea — Cornelius's city.
stops.narration:
Cornelius is a Roman centurion in Caesarea, a devout man who prays and gives to the poor. An angel tells him to send for Peter. When Peter arrives and speaks about Jesus, the Spirit falls on Cornelius' household, and they are baptized. Peter says God shows no partiality (Acts 10:1–48, LSB).

Caesarea Maritima was the Roman and Herodian port city. From 1959 to 1964, an Italian mission dug its theater from Herod's time. In June 1961 they found a limestone block reused in stairs in the 300s AD. It names "Pontius Pilatus," calls him prefect of Judea, and mentions a building named for the emperor Tiberius. It is the only known stone inscription from Pilate's own time that names him, and it calls him prefect of Judea.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone confirms Pilate's name, title, and post under Tiberius, matching the Gospels and the historians Tacitus and Josephus. It is strong evidence that the governor was real and tied to this city.

Picture a Roman officer's home, full of relatives and friends gathered to listen, a Jewish apostle stepping through the door, and then the joyful shock when God pours out his Spirit on them all.

stops.panel_truth_line: Pilate Stone — Roman prefecture inscription from Caesarea.
stops.narration:
Cornelius was a centurion of the Italian cohort in Caesarea (Acts 10:1, LSB). Luke dates events in the Gospel to when Pontius Pilate governed Judea (Luke 3:1, LSB). Cornelius served inside the same Roman system the Gospels name.

This stop is the Pilate Stone, an inscription from Caesarea now shown as a museum object. It is the only known stone inscription from Pilate's own time that names him, and it calls him prefect of Judea. A small ring from Herodium reads "of Pilatus," but scholars debate whether it has anything to do with Pontius Pilate, and his coins carry the emperor Tiberius' name, not his.

The ground and the Bible line up well here. The stone shows that the Roman world of the Gospels and Acts was real, with real officials and real titles.

Picture the stone carved with the governor's name, standing in a city run by Roman soldiers. One of those soldiers, a man named Cornelius, would become one of the first Gentiles to receive the Spirit. The empire's power is carved in stone. God's grace reached right into its ranks.

stops.panel_truth_line: Peter Acts route — Judea / Samaria / Caesarea ministry path.
stops.narration:
This stop traces Peter's route through Judea, Samaria, and on to Caesarea (Acts 10:1–48, LSB). Afterward, Peter goes back to Jerusalem and reports what happened. When the believers hear it, they quiet down and praise God, saying that God has granted the Gentiles repentance that leads to life (Acts 11:1–18, LSB).

The evidence for this route stop is mixed. It is a map line for the apostle's travels, not a dig.

Think about how big that moment in Jerusalem was. Some believers were upset that Peter had eaten with Gentiles. But once they heard the full story, their complaints turned to praise. Picture a room full of tense faces relaxing into wonder as Peter tells them about the vision, the knock at the door, and the Spirit falling on a Roman household.

stops.panel_truth_line: Antioch — mixed church where Gentiles and Jews are called Christians.
stops.narration:
In Antioch, believers begin telling Greeks about Jesus, and a large number turn to the Lord. It is in Antioch that the disciples are first called Christians (Acts 11:19–26, LSB). Acts 15:7–11 (LSB) returns to the question of the Gentiles. Nations welcomed into the Redeemer's people get a name in Antioch.

From 1932 to 1939, a Princeton team led excavations at Antioch. They uncovered Roman and Byzantine city remains, a famous collection of mosaics, a racecourse called a circus, and villas. Very little early Christian building can be recovered, because the modern city sits on top.

The ground and the Bible line up well as background. Antioch was a major Roman capital in Syria, fitting its role as a mission hub in Acts. Early house churches are hard to find under modern Antakya. But the mosaics and the city's size set the scene for the debates about Gentile believers that Paul describes in Galatians 2.

This is an optional close for the Cornelius path. Picture a mixed church in a big city, Jews and Gentiles worshiping together, so new and different that their neighbors needed a new name for them. Peter summed it up at the council in Jerusalem: we believe we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are (Acts 15:11). One Savior, one grace, for Jews and Gentiles alike.
